design_detail: Randomized within-person comparison of two music playlists, reported as a short Letter: a secondary analysis of 10 participants in an open-label, single-arm pilot of psilocybin-assisted smoking cessation at Johns Hopkins. Each person had two psilocybin sessions (weeks 5 and 7), one with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist (singing bowls, gongs, didgeridoo, chimes, bells, sitar, overtone singing), in randomized, counterbalanced order, and then chose one playlist for a third session (week 13). Outcomes: mystical experience (MEQ30) and challenging experience (CEQ) after each session; biologically verified smoking abstinence, compared only between the groups formed by the playlist people chose.
can_establish: Whether, in 10 people who smoked and took psilocybin with preparation and support in a research setting, the genre of music played during a session made a detectable difference to self-rated mystical or challenging experience, within the limits of a very small randomized crossover.
cannot_establish: Whether music genre changes smoking abstinence or any clinical outcome (abstinence was compared only between self-selected groups of 6 and 4 who had all heard both playlists); whether music versus no music matters (there was no silent condition); or anything with precision: the intervals are wide (editors' calculation: for mystical experience from a small negative to a very large positive effect, for challenging experience from a moderate decrease to a moderate increase).

sample.recruitment: Participants in an open-label pilot study of psilocybin for smoking cessation (parent study reported in Johnson et al., 2014 and 2017); this analysis covers the subsample of 10 who were randomized to playlist order (p. 476, Methods › General Overview and Participants, 2nd paragraph, which starts on p. 475). How and why this subsample was chosen from the parent study is not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: At least 10 cigarettes a day, a current wish to stop smoking, physically healthy on medical screening, no family history of psychotic or bipolar disorder, and no substance use disorder other than nicotine in the past 5 years (pp. 475–476).
sample.demographics: Mean age 51 (range 37–65); 8 men and 2 women; 9 White and 1 Asian (p. 476).
sample.attrition: Not reported as such; the analyses and figures appear to include all 10 people in sessions 1–3 and in abstinence follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers for a psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot, screened for physical and psychiatric health; mostly White men around 50; the reason for analysing this subsample is not given. The findings may not apply to other people, other drugs, or use outside a supervised research setting.

exposure.measurement: Music condition assigned by the investigators: a Western classical playlist, similar to those used in earlier psilocybin studies, or an overtone-based playlist emphasizing instruments with a strong overtone signature, some tracks without identifiable melody or rhythm. Participants wore an eye mask and listened through headphones throughout; the music also played through room speakers (p. 476, Methods › Psilocybin Sessions and Musical Genres, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions, not patterns of use: oral psilocybin, 20 mg/70 kg in session 1 and 30 mg/70 kg in sessions 2 and 3; one participant, as the protocol allowed, received 20 mg/70 kg in sessions 1 and 2 because of concern about adverse reactions. Sessions in weeks 5, 7 and 13 of a 15-week programme that included four weekly preparatory meetings of cognitive-behavioural smoking-cessation treatment with mindfulness and guided imagery; staff gave non-directive support during sessions (pp. 475–476; note 19, p. 477).
exposure.polysubstance: Nicotine (cigarette smoking) was the behaviour being treated; other substance use disorders in the past 5 years were excluded; other drug use during the study is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to the music comparison; smoking abstinence was an outcome.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant's Western classical session against the same person's overtone session. No session without music.
comparison.matching: Same participants, staff and room. About 25% of the Western classical tracks also appeared in the overtone playlist, mostly at the start and at the come-down; nine of the ten participants supplied about 60 minutes of personally selected music, played in all of their sessions from roughly 4 h after psilocybin; one participant chose no personal music; the overtone playlist lost three tracks and was slightly reordered after the first 3 participants (p. 476; note 22, p. 477).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Musical preferences and familiarity with either genre were not measured; apart from the final choice, no measure of liking or resonance with the music was collected (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 475).

outcomes.instruments: MEQ30 (mystical-type experience) and the 26-item Challenging Experience Questionnaire, completed at the end of each session; smoking abstinence as 7-day point prevalence verified by timeline follow-back self-report, breath carbon monoxide ≤ 6 ppm and urinary cotinine < 200 ng/mL (p. 476, Methods › Outcomes). The Methods specify carbon monoxide and name the measuring instrument; the Results instead say carbon dioxide (p. 474), an apparent textual error recorded below.
outcomes.validity_norms: Both questionnaires are published and validated (cited). Scores are printed on a 0–1 scale; the scaling is not described.
outcomes.operationalization: A good experience is a higher MEQ30 total and a difficult one a higher CEQ total, both self-rated after the session about that session, that is after the drug and the music. The clinical outcome is verified abstinence at the end of treatment (8 weeks after the first session) and at 6, 12 and about 30 months.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; each comparison two-tailed at α = 0.05 (p. 476, Methods › Data Analysis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None possible for music: participants rated their own experience knowing which music they had heard, and psilocybin was open-label.

analysis.effect_sizes: Randomized sessions 1–2 (paired t-test, n = 10): MEQ30 overtone 0.68 (SD 0.20) vs Western classical 0.52 (SD 0.21), Cohen's dz = 0.57, p = 0.107; in a random-intercept mixed model adjusting for dose, overtone b = 0.14 (p = 0.108) and the 30 mg/70 kg dose b = 0.14 (p = 0.102) (p. 473). CEQ 0.33 (SD 0.20) vs 0.34 (SD 0.22), dz = −0.11, p = 0.74 (p. 474). Editors' calculation from the printed dz and n = 10 (noncentral t; approximate because the inputs are rounded): MEQ30 dz 95% CI about −0.12 to 1.23, mean difference about 0.16 (95% CI about −0.04 to 0.36); CEQ dz 95% CI about −0.73 to 0.51. Session 3 (chosen playlist; 4 vs 6 people): MEQ30 0.70 (SD 0.26) Western classical vs 0.58 (SD 0.16) overtone, p = 0.41; CEQ 0.29 (SD 0.17) vs 0.26 (SD 0.15), p = 0.79 (p. 474). Abstinence: end of treatment 5 of 6 who chose overtone vs 2 of 4 who chose classical; long-term 4 of 6 vs 2 of 4 (pp. 474–475). Editors' calculation: Fisher exact two-sided p = 0.50 at end of treatment and 1.0 at long-term follow-up.
analysis.covariates: Dose in the mixed model; nothing else.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration number is given in this Letter for the parent study or for the music comparison, which the author contributions describe as incorporated into the study design by one author (p. 476).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only total scores are reported (no MEQ30 or CEQ subscales). The abstract reports the non-randomized abstinence comparison by chosen playlist as a slight benefit for the overtone group.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors call the sample small. With n = 10 only very large differences could be detected (see the editors' intervals above).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 10 people, no detectable difference between the two playlists in mystical experience (dz 0.57, p = 0.107, with an interval running from a small negative to a very large positive effect) or in challenging experience (dz −0.11, p = 0.74). Six of ten chose the overtone playlist for the last session. Abstinence did not differ detectably between those who chose either playlist (5 of 6 vs 2 of 4 at the end of treatment).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says mystical scores "tended to be higher" with overtone music and reports a slight abstinence benefit for those choosing it (66.7% vs 50%), and concludes that the data call into question whether Western classical music holds a unique benefit. That conclusion is fair as a statement that no superiority of classical music was detected, but the study cannot show that the genres are equivalent (the intervals are wide) and compared only two genres. The abstinence difference is between self-selected groups of 6 and 4 people who had all heard both playlists, so it says nothing about the effect of genre. The discussion's suggestion that individually selected music may improve outcomes (p. 475) was not tested; in session 3, mystical scores were, if anything, higher among those who chose classical music. The description as the first fully randomized within-subject test of set and setting (pp. 473, 475) is accurate for the randomized part but rests on 10 people in an open-label, single-arm trial.

timeline.event: Ludwig et al.: 176 men in inpatient alcoholism treatment randomized to no drug or LSD with no therapy, talk therapy or hypnosis-based therapy; no substantial group differences in long-term outcomes; a manipulation of therapy rather than setting (as described here, pp. 472–473).

Gaston and Eagle: five musical conditions (including no music, familiar and unfamiliar music) during LSD sessions for alcohol use; no significant differences, in a between-subject, quasi-randomized design without an objective clinical outcome (as described here, p. 473).

Kaelen et al.: greater liking of, resonance with and openness to the standard music in psilocybin sessions went with larger reductions in depression a week later (correlational; as described here, p. 473).
Correction notice for this article (DOI 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119): read on 12 November 2026; it changes only the Acknowledgment (who suggested and recommended the overtone-based music).
Estric et al.: in 25 psychiatric trials of classic psychedelics, 16 played a predefined playlist through headphones and none compared settings; addiction trials such as this one were excluded.

replication.where_it_stands: This very small randomized comparison tested two music genres during psilocybin sessions, not music with silence. Its introduction also describes an older quasi-randomized comparison; it is not an exhaustive survey of all music experiments. Evidence that the experience of music matters for outcomes remains correlational (Kaelen et al., 2018, as described here).

Support for M.W.J. and A.G.-R. came from the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelics and Consciousness Research, funded by the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation and the Tim Ferriss, Matt Mullenweg, Craig Nerenberg and Blake Mycoskie Collaborative; support for J.C.S. from National Institute on Drug Abuse grant T32DA07209 (p. 477).

M.W.J. and A.G.-R. designed the genre comparison, developed the overtone playlist and collected the data (author contributions, p. 476; Methods, p. 476). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized trial, crossover or parallel, comparing music genres with a no-music condition and with participant-chosen music during psilocybin sessions, with outcomes registered in advance, enough participants to detect moderate differences in mystical and challenging experience, and clinical outcomes analysed by randomized condition rather than by later choice.

domains.note: Playlist order was randomized for each participant and counterbalanced (p. 476); the method of sequence generation and concealment is not described. From the selection paragraph (half of each choice group had its chosen genre in session 1), five participants had each order (editors' inference), so dose was close to balanced across genres; per-participant values in Figure 1 cannot be read reliably because symbols overlap.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: Session 1 was also the target quit date and used the lower dose, and session 2 came 2 weeks later at the higher dose after experience of the other playlist. Dose was adjusted for, but period and order effects were not analysed, and 10 people cannot test them.

Open-label: participants and session staff, including the two authors who built the overtone playlist and collected the data, knew which music was playing. The overtone playlist was changed after the first 3 participants, and shared tracks (about 25%) and about an hour of personal music in each session for nine of ten participants (one chose none) dilute the contrast.
All 10 participants appear to contribute both randomized sessions (text and Figures 1–2).
MEQ30 and CEQ were self-rated by participants who knew which music they had heard; expectations about classical or unusual music could colour the ratings, and blinding was not possible.
No registered analysis plan is reported for the music comparison; only total scores are given, and the abstract gives weight to the non-randomized abstinence comparison.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomized, counterbalanced within-person order protects the experience comparison against confounding by person, and both experience outcomes are reported with effect sizes, so bias is of some concern rather than high; the larger problem is imprecision with 10 people. The abstinence comparison by chosen playlist (and the session 3 comparison) is not randomized and is outside this judgment: it is open to confounding by whatever led people to choose a genre and cannot support any claim that genre affects quitting. Cite the study for no detectable difference between these two genres in self-rated mystical or challenging experience in 10 people, and for its design; not for equivalence, not for clinical effects of music, and not for music versus silence.

key_findings.finding: Design: 10 participants in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot had sessions 1 and 2 with a Western classical and an overtone-based playlist in randomized, counterbalanced order, with eye mask and headphones; they then chose a playlist for session 3.
key_findings.locator: Methods › General Overview and Participants, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 475; the subsample of 10 is on p. 476); Methods › Psilocybin Sessions and Musical Genres, 2nd paragraph (p. 476)

key_findings.finding: Participants: mean age 51 (range 37–65), 8 men and 2 women, 9 White and 1 Asian; all smoked at least 10 cigarettes a day, wanted to stop, were physically healthy, had no family history of psychotic or bipolar disorder and no other substance use disorder in the past 5 years.
key_findings.locator: Methods › General Overview and Participants, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 475)

key_findings.finding: Mystical experience (MEQ30) was 0.68 (SD 0.20) in overtone sessions and 0.52 (SD 0.21) in Western classical sessions: Cohen's dz 0.57, not statistically significant (p = 0.107). Adjusting for dose in a mixed model, overtone b = 0.14 (p = 0.108) and the higher dose b = 0.14 (p = 0.102).
key_findings.locator: Results › Mystical and Challenging Experiences, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (p. 474)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (noncentral t from the rounded dz, n = 10): dz 95% CI about −0.12 to 1.23.

key_findings.finding: Challenging experience (CEQ) did not differ: 0.33 (SD 0.20) with overtone vs 0.34 (SD 0.22) with Western classical, dz −0.11, p = 0.74; no pattern at group or individual level.
key_findings.locator: Results › Mystical and Challenging Experiences, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 473); Figure 2 (p. 474)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: dz 95% CI about −0.73 to 0.51.

key_findings.finding: For the third session, 6 of 10 (60%) chose the overtone-based playlist; in that session, mystical scores were 0.70 (SD 0.26) with Western classical and 0.58 (SD 0.16) with overtone (p = 0.41), and challenging scores 0.29 (SD 0.17) and 0.26 (SD 0.15) (p = 0.79).
key_findings.locator: Results › Musical Genre Selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Biologically verified abstinence by chosen playlist: 2 of 4 who chose Western classical were abstinent at the end of treatment and stayed abstinent through 6, 12 and about 30 months; 5 of 6 (83.3%) who chose overtone were abstinent at the end of treatment and 4 of 6 through long-term follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking Abstinence (one paragraph, starts on p. 474); Figure 4 (p. 474)
key_findings.note: Not a randomized comparison: everyone heard both playlists in sessions 1 and 2. Editors' calculation: Fisher exact two-sided p = 0.50 (end of treatment) and 1.0 (long-term).

key_findings.finding: Session conditions: music started when psilocybin was given; nine of ten supplied about 60 minutes of personally selected music, played in all their sessions from roughly 4 h after psilocybin, near the end of peak effects; one chose no personal music; about 25% of the classical playlist's tracks were shared with the overtone playlist, mostly before onset and during the come-down.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Psilocybin Sessions and Musical Genres, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: small sample; no measure of the musical experience (such as liking) other than the final choice; partial overlap of the playlists; open-label design, so interactions of genre with expectancy or placebo effects cannot be assessed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the study as the first experimental comparison of session set and setting reported in half a century and the first fully randomized within-subject study of session set and setting, and conclude that the data fail to show any clear superiority of Western classical music, long considered the standard.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (p. 473); Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs (p. 475)

reporting_issues.issue: The authors' correction (Strickland et al., 2021c; DOI 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119), read on 12 November 2026, changes only the Acknowledgment: who suggested overtone-based music for psychedelic sessions and who recommended some of the selections.
reporting_issues.consequence: No number, figure, table, method, funding or conflict-of-interest statement is changed, and no key finding or risk-of-bias judgment on this card is affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the long-term abstinence in the overtone group as 66.7%, the Results as 66.6% (4 of 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; 4 of 6 is 66.7%.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that controlling for dose did not attenuate the genre difference (p. 473), but the model coefficient (b = 0.14) is slightly smaller than the difference between the printed means (0.68 − 0.52 = 0.16).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, and the means are rounded; the p value hardly changed (0.107 vs 0.108).

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants given each playlist first is not stated; it can be inferred only from the selection paragraph (five each), and the overlapping symbols in Figure 1 do not allow per-participant values to be read.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose balance across genres has to be inferred; the paper's mixed model adjusts for dose.

reporting_issues.issue: Results describe abstinence verification using exhaled carbon dioxide, urinary cotinine and self-report, whereas Methods specify exhaled carbon monoxide (CO), name a CO instrument and define the CO threshold.
reporting_issues.consequence: This appears to be a textual slip in Results. The card follows the explicit Methods definition and retains the discrepancy; the authors' correction (read 12 November 2026) does not address it.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of the Global Drug Survey (GDS) 2017, an anonymous, self-nominating online survey open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages (119,108 responses). People who reported using magic mushrooms in the last 12 months (12,534) were asked whether they had sought emergency medical treatment (EMT) after using them in that year; 9233 answered, and the 19 who said yes completed a specialist section on that incident (symptoms ticked from a list, number of mushrooms, other substances, time to feel back to normal, hospital admission, perceived reasons, change in use). EMT seekers and the others were compared with univariate Mann–Whitney, chi-square and Fisher tests. Companion paper on LSD from the same survey and authors: kopra_2022b.
can_establish: How often respondents to a large self-selected online drug survey who had used magic mushrooms in the past year reported seeking emergency medical treatment afterwards (19 of 9233), and how those 19 described the incident, its course and its perceived causes.
cannot_establish: The rate among all people who use magic mushrooms (no sampling frame; the direction of selection bias is unknown); deaths, lasting harm or incidents in people who could not or did not answer (only people able to complete an online survey are counted); whether the reported symptoms, such as seizures or loss of consciousness, happened as described or were caused by psilocybin (no records, no toxicology, unknown mushroom content, 11 of 19 had taken another substance); or predictors of incidents, given 19 events.

sample.recruitment: Self-nominating online sample: the GDS is advertised on social networking sites in collaboration with media partners and harm-reduction organizations; anonymous, encrypted, in 10 languages, no payment (p. 966, Methods › Design, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). The 12,534 people who reported past-year use lived mainly in Germany (20.7%), the United States (17.0%), Canada (12.2%), Denmark (10.3%) and the United Kingdom (8.2%), with 31.6% elsewhere (Table 1, p. 968).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All GDS 2017 respondents who reported magic mushroom use in the last 12 months; no exclusions for other drug use or mental health. Each analysis used complete cases for its variables (p. 967, Data analysis, 4th paragraph).
sample.demographics: People who reported past-year use (n=12,534): 62.9% under 25, 28.5% aged 25–34, 8.5% 35 or older; 78.7% men and 21.3% women (no other category shown); of 7598 answering, 88.6% White, 4.4% mixed, 3.0% Hispanic/Latino; of 7706 answering, 26.9% reported a lifetime mental health diagnosis (depression 19.7%, anxiety 14.1%, ADHD 6.4%, bipolar 2.6%, psychosis 1.4%); 22.6% had used in the last month; median 2 days of use in the past year (IQR 1–3) (Table 1, p. 968; answering totals are editors' sums of the table rows). The 19 EMT seekers are described only by age: median 19 (IQR 18–23) (p. 967).
sample.attrition: Not a follow-up study, but item non-response is large: 9233 of 12,534 past-year respondents (73.7%, editors' calculation) answered the EMT question. The authors attribute most missing answers to people leaving the survey early: among 1895 who completed the whole survey, 1857 (98%) answered the item and 6 (0.3%) reported EMT, against 0.2% overall (p. 967, Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 3rd paragraph). Mental health (asked towards the end of the survey, pp. 966–967) and ethnicity were each answered by about 61% (editors' calculation from Table 1), while the age, gender and country rows are complete; the paper says a wide range of demographic information was collected at the start of the survey (p. 966) and does not explain the missing ethnicity answers. Time to recovery was answered by 18 of the 19 EMT seekers (Table 2 counts sum to 18).
sample.selection_effects: Self-nominated respondents reached through GDS media partners, social networks and harm-reduction organizations: mostly young, male, White, European or North American. There is no sampling frame and no response rate. People who died or were too unwell to take part are outside the design; people with bad experiences may be more or less likely to respond, and the authors say skipping the EMT item could bias the rate in either direction (p. 971, Discussion, 10th paragraph). The incident details come only from the 19 who said yes and went on to the specialist section.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: time since last use (never, last 30 days, 31 days to 12 months, more than 12 months); days of use in the last 12 months; first use in the last 12 months; number of mushrooms normally taken on a day of use; and, for EMT seekers, the number of mushrooms in the incident session and any other substances (p. 966, Methods › Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). No biological verification; species, potency and psilocybin content unknown (the authors say so, p. 971).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions. Past-year frequency: median 2 days (IQR 1–3) in the whole past-year group (Table 1); mean 3.72 days (SD 13.1) among the 9233 who answered the EMT item, the basis of the per-event estimate (p. 967). Number of mushrooms commonly taken on a day of use: median 4.0 in both EMT seekers (IQR 3.0–16.0) and others (IQR 2.0–6.0) (p. 967). EMT seekers reported a median of 10.0 mushrooms (IQR 2.0–33.8) in the incident session (p. 968). The authors call the number of mushrooms a vague indicator of quantity, because mushroom sizes vary and many people weigh dried mushrooms rather than count them (p. 971, Discussion, 11th paragraph). Route is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Asked only of EMT seekers, about the incident session: 11 of 19 had taken another substance (cannabis 7, alcohol 6; cocaine, MDMA, ketamine and opioids 1 each) and 8 (42%) nothing else (Table 3, p. 969). Co-use in the sessions of people who did not seek EMT is not reported; the authors note they do not know its prevalence in the whole sample and so cannot tell how far other substances, rather than mushrooms, are linked to incidents (p. 968, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective survey covering the previous 12 months).

comparison.controls: Within the sample: the 9214 EMT-item respondents who did not report EMT seeking, compared with the 19 who did, on age, sex, lifetime mental health diagnosis, first use in the past year, number of mushrooms commonly taken and past-year frequency. No group without mushroom use, and no other drug within this paper; the comparison with LSD comes from the companion paper (kopra_2022b).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality, earlier difficult experiences, setting and company on the day, and current medication (the Discussion mentions lithium, p. 968) are not reported; mental health entered the analysis only as a lifetime diagnosis.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported for people who did not seek EMT.

outcomes.instruments: One self-report item on seeking EMT after magic mushroom use in the past 12 months; EMT is not defined in the paper and the number of incidents per person was not recorded (p. 966, Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph). EMT seekers then ticked symptoms from a list of 21 compiled from the literature, gave the number of mushrooms in that session, other substances, duration of symptoms and whether they were hospitalized, chose up to 3 of 6 reasons for the incident, and reported any change in their use (p. 966, Methods › Measures, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of any item is reported. The reasons question offered no 'other' or free-text option, which the authors say may have led answers (p. 971). Two multiple correspondence analyses of symptoms and of reasons are shown as factor maps only in supplementary figures, which were not among the files; the Results describe the groupings in words (pp. 967–968).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm was operationalized as self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment; severity only through self-reported hospital admission (not defined; the LSD companion paper states the survey did not define it) and time to feel back to normal.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six predictor tests (age, mental health diagnosis, sex, first use in the past year, mushrooms commonly taken, past-year frequency); only age was significant (p=0.002), which would stay below a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/6 = 0.008 (editors' calculation).

analysis.effect_sizes: 19 of 9233 (0.2%) reported seeking EMT in the past year; editors' Wilson 95% CI 0.13% to 0.32% (about 1 in 490 respondents, editors' calculation). Per-event estimate: 19 divided by 34,347 estimated days of use (mean 3.72 × 9233) = 0.00055, given as 0.06% or about 1 in 1800 intakes (p. 967). Predictors (p. 967): age median 19 (IQR 18–23) vs 23 (IQR 20–27), Mann–Whitney z=3.09, p=0.002; lifetime mental health diagnosis 0.2% vs 0.2%, Fisher's exact p=0.546; men 0.2% vs women 0.2%, p=1.00; first use in the past year 0.2% vs 0.2%, χ2(1, N=9068)=0.43, p=0.512; mushrooms commonly taken median 4.0 vs 4.0, z=1.768, p=0.077; past-year frequency median 2.0 (IQR 1.0–6.5) vs 2.0 (1.0–3.0), z=1.479, p=0.139. Hospital admission 8 of 19 (42%; printed 95% CI 20–64%, a normal-approximation interval; editors' Wilson 23% to 64%). No effect sizes or intervals are given for the group comparisons.
analysis.covariates: None: univariate tests only (with 19 events a multivariable model would not be stable).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is reported; the authors describe the study as an exploratory analysis (p. 966, Introduction, 6th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The two multiple correspondence analyses are described in words in the Results (four symptom groupings, p. 967; wrong mind-set and mixing substances reported together, p. 968), but their methods and factor maps are only in the supplement, which was not among the files. The number of EMT seekers with a mental health diagnosis is not given. Figure 1 shows symptom frequencies as bars without printed values (read by the editors; see key findings). The change-in-use percentages (58% cut down, 37% no change) leave 1 of 19 undescribed.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally. The authors state that with 19 incidents predictors were difficult to establish and that very large samples would be needed to detect the trends they saw for frequency and quantity (p. 970, Discussion, 8th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a self-selected online sample, 19 of 9233 people (0.2%) who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered the question reported seeking emergency medical treatment afterwards; by the authors' per-day calculation, about 1 in 1800 days of use. Of the 19, 8 reported hospital admission. Anxiety/panic and paranoia were ticked by 13 each, but 7 ticked passing out, 6 difficulty breathing and 5 seizures, none verified. Eleven had taken another substance, most often cannabis or alcohol. Of 18 who answered, 17 felt back to normal within 24 hours and all within 7 days. Only younger age distinguished EMT seekers (median 19 vs 23 years).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the results “confirm psilocybin mushrooms are a relatively safe drug”, with serious incidents rare and short-lasting, and that providing harm-reduction information “likely plays a key role in preventing adverse effects” (p. 965). The final paragraph says mushrooms “rarely cause harm to the individual consuming them nor to other people” and that the results support reassessing psilocybin's legal status (p. 971). Gaps: (1) a survey of people able to answer an online questionnaire cannot confirm safety: deaths and lasting harm are outside its reach, and the 0.2% applies to self-selected GDS respondents who answered the item (the abstract presents the 9233 as the past-year group, but 12,534 reported past-year use); (2) harm to other people is not among the reported measures; (3) 'relatively' safe rests on the companion LSD paper and on cited rankings, not on a comparison in this paper; (4) the role of harm-reduction information was not studied; (5) 'back to normality' was not defined, and the authors themselves say it may mean only that acute effects resolved (p. 970, Discussion, 9th paragraph); (6) the per-event figure counts each person once although incidents per person were not recorded, and divides by days of use from a skewed distribution (mean 3.72, SD 13.1, median 2). A headline saying that only 1 in 1800 mushroom trips ends in the emergency room would overstate what was measured: self-reported help-seeking, per day of use, in a self-selected sample. Against this, the limitations section is candid about sampling, attrition, recall bias, the leading reasons question and the vague quantity measure (p. 971, Discussion, 10th and 11th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al., online survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms (J Psychopharmacol 30(12): 1268–1278), cited for cannabis co-use and for younger age predicting more difficult experiences; read here only as cited (pp. 969–970).

Leonard et al., exposures to LSD and psilocybin mushrooms reported to US poison centres 2000–2016, cited as finding fewer major outcomes and hospital admissions with mushrooms than with LSD; read here only as cited (p. 970).

Companion paper from the same GDS 2017 data on LSD: 102 of 10,293 (1.0%) reported EMT seeking, about five times the mushroom rate, and a lifetime mental health diagnosis went with EMT seeking there but not here.

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional estimate from one GDS wave (2016–17). The authors place it beside poison-centre data and earlier surveys of challenging experiences, read here only as cited. No validation of the self-reported EMT item against hospital or ambulance records is reported in this paper or its LSD companion.

Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the counts.

what_would_settle_it: Linkage of emergency-department, ambulance and poison-centre records to a population survey that counts use occasions in the same area and period, recording every incident per person, toxicology and mushroom identification, and following people for weeks afterwards; this would give a per-occasion risk with a known denominator and verified outcomes, including deaths and lasting harm.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: self-nominated GDS respondents reached through social media, media partners and harm-reduction organizations, while the target is people who use magic mushrooms in general.
Self-nominating convenience sample (p. 966).
9233 respondents give a precise headline proportion (Wilson 0.13% to 0.32%, editors' calculation), but every statement about the incidents rests on 19 people and the predictor tests on 19 events.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The past-year group is described by age, sex, country, ethnicity, diagnoses and use (Table 1); the 19 EMT seekers only by age, and where and what kind of emergency care they sought is not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 9233 of 12,534 (74%) answered the EMT item; the completer check (1857 of 1895 answered, 0.3% EMT) points to drop-out rather than selective skipping but cannot rule the latter out; recovery time has 18 of 19 answers; complete-case analyses throughout.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: One face-valid but undefined and unvalidated self-report item over a 12-month recall period, with the respondent attributing the incident to mushrooms (1 of 19 later named 'not magic mushrooms' as a reason); symptoms ticked from an unvalidated list and not verified.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online items for everyone, but in 10 languages without any described translation check; reliability not assessed.

No interval for the headline proportion; normal-approximation intervals truncated at zero for counts of 1 to 3 (Table 2); a per-event estimate that assumes one incident per person and equal risk on every day of use; univariate tests on 19 events, with non-significant results described as no difference.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed
domains.note: Open online survey with no denominator of people invited; item non-response on the EMT question is judged under item 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because what the encyclopedia uses are the proportion reporting EMT seeking and the shares describing the incidents. As an estimate for people who use magic mushrooms in general, the 0.2% could be biased in either direction: the sample has no frame, the outcome is an undefined self-report, and people who died, were badly harmed or did not answer are not represented. As a description of this sample the counts are transparent and arithmetically consistent. The source may be cited for the proportion of GDS 2017 respondents who reported seeking EMT after magic mushrooms (19 of 9233), how those 19 described their incidents, and the finding that only age differed detectably with 19 events. It may not be cited for a population risk per occasion, for the cause of the reported symptoms, or for safety beyond self-reported help-seeking.

key_findings.finding: GDS 2017 received 119,108 responses; 29,124 (24.5%) reported ever using magic mushrooms and 12,534 (43.0% of them) reported use in the last 12 months; 9233 of these answered the EMT question.
key_findings.locator: Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 1st paragraph (p. 967); Table 1 (p. 968)

key_findings.finding: 19 of the 9233 who answered (0.2%) reported having sought emergency medical treatment after using magic mushrooms in the past year.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 965); Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 1st paragraph (p. 967)
key_findings.note: Editors' Wilson 95% CI 0.13% to 0.32%, about 1 in 490 respondents. The abstract describes the 9233 as the past-year group; 12,534 reported past-year use and 9233 answered this item.

key_findings.finding: Per-event estimate: among the 9233, mean days of use in the past year was 3.72 (SD 13.1), giving an estimated 34,347 days of use; 19 divided by this is 0.00055, which the authors express as 0.06% or about 1 in 1800 intakes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing at the top of the right column); Data analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The numerator counts people, not incidents (the number of incidents per person was not recorded, p. 966), and the calculation treats every day of use as carrying the same risk; the denominator is days of use, not separate intakes.

key_findings.finding: Among 1895 past-year respondents who completed the whole survey, 1857 (98%) answered the EMT question and 6 of them (0.3%) reported EMT seeking, which the authors read as low risk of attrition bias.
key_findings.locator: Results › Frequency and risk of EMT incidents, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: EMT seekers were younger: median age 19 (IQR 18–23) vs 23 (IQR 20–27), Mann–Whitney z=3.09, p=0.002. No significant difference by lifetime mental health diagnosis (0.2% vs 0.2%, Fisher's exact p=0.546), sex (0.2% vs 0.2%, p=1.00), first use in the past year (0.2% vs 0.2%, χ2(1, N=9068)=0.43, p=0.512), mushrooms commonly taken on a day of use (median 4.0 in both; IQR 3.0–16.0 vs 2.0–6.0; z=1.768, p=0.077) or past-year frequency (median 2.0 in both; IQR 1.0–6.5 vs 1.0–3.0; z=1.479, p=0.139).
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of EMT seeking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: With 19 events these null results cannot exclude meaningful differences; the authors themselves describe the frequency and quantity results as trends needing much larger samples (p. 970, Discussion, 8th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: EMT seekers ticked a median of 5.0 symptoms (IQR 2.0–8.0). The most common were anxiety/panic (68%) and paranoia/suspiciousness (68%), then seeing/hearing things (42%) and passing out/unconsciousness (37%); the Discussion adds difficulty breathing (32%) and seizures (26%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 1st paragraph (p. 967); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 968)
key_findings.note: The authors note that passing out may in some cases have been transient memory loss or falling asleep, and that the reported seizures cannot be confirmed as epileptic rather than psychologically triggered (p. 968, Discussion, 2nd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Symptom counts of the 19 (editors' reading of Figure 1, which prints no values): anxiety/panic 13, paranoia/suspiciousness 13, seeing/hearing things 8, passed out/unconscious 7, difficulty breathing 6, confusion 6, memory loss 5, fits/seizures 5, palpitations 5, extreme agitation 5, very low mood in the days afterwards 4, headache 4, extreme sweating 4, overheating 4, nausea/vomiting 2, aggression/violence 2, chest pain 2, and 1 each for other, bladder/kidney problems, thoughts or acts of self-harm, and accident/trauma.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1
key_findings.note: The figure prints no values. Bar lengths were measured on a 300-dpi rendering against the gridlines; every bar falls on a whole number of the 19 respondents (steps of 5.3%), and the text's 68%, 42%, 37%, 32% and 26% match. Editors' reading.

key_findings.finding: 8 of the 19 EMT seekers (42%; printed 95% CI 20–64%) reported being admitted to hospital.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The printed interval is a normal approximation; editors' Wilson 95% CI 23% to 64%. Admission is not defined in this paper; the LSD companion paper states the survey did not define it (kopra_2022b, p. 960).

key_findings.finding: Time to feel back to normal, 18 respondents: 12 at 6 h (67%), 3 at 12 h, 1 at 18 h, 1 at 24 h and 1 at 5–7 days; the text says all but one were back to normal within 24 h and all within 7 days.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 969); Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 2nd paragraph (p. 967)
key_findings.note: Table 2 counts sum to 18, not 19, so its percentages are of 18 respondents (not stated). The rows are printed as time points (6 h, 12 h …) without saying whether each means 'up to'.

key_findings.finding: EMT seekers reported a median of 10.0 mushrooms (IQR 2.0–33.8) in the session that led to EMT, against a median of 4.0 (IQR 3.0–16.0) that the same group commonly took on a day of use; the authors call the number of mushrooms a vague measure of quantity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 3rd paragraph (p. 968); Results › Predictors of EMT seeking, 2nd paragraph (p. 967); Discussion, 11th paragraph (p. 971)
key_findings.note: Study conditions as reported, not a dose–risk relation: no test compares the incident session with usual use, and the incident-session quantity has no counterpart for people who did not seek EMT.

key_findings.finding: In the session that led to EMT, 8 of the 19 (42%) had taken nothing else; the others reported cannabis 7 (37%), alcohol 6 (32%), and cocaine, MDMA, ketamine and opioids 1 each (5%), so by the editors' subtraction 11 of 19 had taken at least one other substance.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 969); Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 3rd paragraph (p. 968)
key_findings.note: Co-use in ordinary sessions is not reported, so the share cannot be compared with sessions that did not end in EMT (the authors say so, p. 968, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Perceived reasons for the incident (up to 3 of 6 options, no 'other' option): wrong mood/mind-set 9 (47%), mixing substances 7 (37%), place/setting 7 (37%), took too much 5 (26%), don't know 4 (21%), not magic mushrooms 1 (5%).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 969); Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 4th paragraph (p. 968)

key_findings.finding: After the incident, 58% of EMT seekers said they cut down their magic mushroom use and 37% reported no change; 16% reduced and 0% increased their use of other illicit drugs or alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Symptom profile and nature of EMT incidents, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: These percentages correspond to 11, 7 and 3 of 19 (editors' calculation); 58% and 37% leave 1 of 19 undescribed.

key_findings.finding: Cross-references to the LSD companion paper: the authors state that EMT seeking after mushrooms was about five times less common than after LSD in the same survey, that 'taking too much' was named less often (26% vs 40%) and 'don't know' more often (21% vs 10%).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: From the companion paper (kopra_2022b): 102 of 10,293 (1.0%) per person and 0.19% per day of use for LSD, so the ratio is about 4.8 per person and 3.4 per day of use (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The authors contrast the null mental health result here with the LSD companion paper, where they say mental health conditions predicted EMT seeking with a large effect size, and suggest the mushroom result may be a false negative given 19 incidents.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: The LSD paper prints 1.8% vs 0.7%, χ2(1, N=8299)=19.33, without an effect size; the ratio is about 2.6 and phi about 0.05 (editors' calculation from kopra_2022b, p. 959).

key_findings.finding: Background stated in the introduction from cited sources, not from this survey: only three deaths are known to have been attributed to magic mushroom toxicity; the estimated lethal amount of psilocybin is about 1000 times the threshold amount, so lethal overdose from eating mushrooms is described as impractical; and a small number of deaths from falls or jumps have been attributed to mushroom use.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand: cited to Gerault and Picart (1996), Lim et al. (2012), Gable (2004) and Van Amsterdam et al. (2011), none read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: self-nominating sampling and volunteer bias; skipping the EMT item could bias the rate in either direction; recall and response bias; the reasons question had no 'other' or free-text option and may have led answers; purity, potency and the contribution of compounds other than psilocybin are unknown; and the exact circumstances of each incident were not established.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th and 11th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports 19 EMT seekers out of 9233 people described as the past-year group; the Results show 12,534 reported past-year use and 9233 answered the EMT question.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is item responders (74% of the past-year group), not everyone who reported past-year use; the Discussion repeats the 0.2% as a share of people reporting past-year use (p. 968).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 counts (12, 3, 1, 1, 1) sum to 18, not 19, and the table does not state that its percentages are of 18.
reporting_issues.consequence: One seeker's recovery time is missing; 'all but one within 24 h' means 17 of 18.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals in Table 2 and for hospital admission are normal-approximation intervals truncated at zero (for example 6% (0–17) for 1 of 18), and 67% (46–88) for 12 of 18 does not reproduce exactly (an editors' Wald calculation gives about 45–88).
reporting_issues.consequence: Such intervals are unreliable with 18–19 respondents; Wilson intervals are 1% to 26% for 1 of 18 and 23% to 64% for 8 of 19 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives first use in the past year as 3543 (38.9%) in a table of 12,534 people; by the editors' arithmetic 3543 is 28.3% of 12,534, so the valid percentage rests on an unstated denominator of about 9100. Ethnicity and mental health rows likewise use unstated denominators (7598 and 7706, editors' sums of the rows).
reporting_issues.consequence: Valid percentages in Table 1 rest on different, unprinted denominators. Mental health, asked towards the end of the survey (pp. 966–967, Methods › Measures, 3rd paragraph), was answered by about 61% of the 12,534 (7706), and ethnicity by about 61% too (7598), while the age, gender and country rows each sum to all 12,534 (editors' sums). The paper says a wide range of demographic information was collected at the start of the survey (p. 966, Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph) and does not explain the missing ethnicity answers.

reporting_issues.issue: The change in magic mushroom use after the incident is given as 58% cut down and 37% no change, leaving 5% undescribed (by the editors' arithmetic, 1 of 19).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether that person stopped, increased use or did not answer is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says mental health conditions predicted LSD-related EMT seeking with a large effect size; the LSD companion paper prints no effect size for that association.
reporting_issues.consequence: The LSD paper's printed figures (kopra_2022b, p. 959: 1.8% vs 0.7%; χ2=19.33, N=8299) correspond to a ratio of about 2.6 and phi about 0.05 (editors' calculation); the contrast between the two substances on mental health should not be described as large on this paper's authority.

reporting_issues.issue: The per-event formula counts each EMT seeker once although the number of incidents per person was not recorded (p. 966), and it does not say whether all 9233 answered the frequency question; this paper does not say the estimate may therefore be an underestimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 1 in 1800 figure is approximate and probably low if some people had more than one incident; the LSD companion paper states this caveat for its own per-event figure (kopra_2022b, p. 962).

reporting_issues.issue: This paper describes a list of 21 symptoms, and Figure 1 includes 'overheating'; the LSD companion paper describes a list of 20 for the same survey section, and its Table 2 has no 'overheating' row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Symptom profiles from the two papers are not fully comparable.

design_detail: Phase 2, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group randomized trial (1:1) at one UK centre (NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility), visits January 2019 to March 2020. 59 adults with long-standing major depressive disorder (HAM-D-17 of 17 or more at screening) were assigned to psilocybin (25 mg on two dosing days 3 weeks apart, with placebo capsules every day for 6 weeks) or escitalopram (1 mg psilocybin on the two dosing days plus daily escitalopram, 10 mg for 3 weeks then 20 mg for 3 weeks); both groups had the same psychological support from two assigned mental health professionals. Primary outcome: change in the self-rated QIDS-SR-16 from baseline to week 6. No placebo-only group: one was in the initial design but was dropped.
can_establish: Whether, over 6 weeks in a small, largely self-referred group of patients with moderate major depression, two psilocybin sessions with psychological support changed self-rated depression scores differently from 6 weeks of escitalopram given with the same support and two 1-mg psilocybin sessions, and how the adverse events of the two regimens differed.
cannot_establish: Whether psilocybin is as effective as or more effective than escitalopram (the trial was powered only for a large difference, was not designed for equivalence or non-inferiority, and the secondary outcomes favouring psilocybin were not corrected for multiplicity), how either treatment compares with placebo (no placebo group), what happens beyond 6 weeks or with a full course of escitalopram, or how much expectancy contributed (patients were told they would receive psilocybin, many preferred it, and blinding was not assessed).

sample.recruitment: Formally through trial networks and informally through social media and other sources directing people to a recruitment website; information about the trial and its eligibility criteria was posted online on the Centre for Psychedelic Research website, ClinicalTrials.gov, the MQ recruitment platform and the ISRCTN registry; volunteers made contact by e-mail after hearing about the trial, and most of those recruited referred themselves (pp. 1403–1404). About 1000 people were screened by telephone (103 also attended a screening visit); 891 did not meet inclusion criteria (19 because of a coexisting psychiatric condition) and 50 declined (p. 1406).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 18 to 80; HAM-D-17 of at least 17 at screening, assessed by video call; diagnosis of depression and medical history confirmed by the general practitioner (p. 1404). Main exclusions: immediate family or personal history of psychosis; medically significant conditions; history of serious suicide attempts; positive pregnancy test; contraindications to SSRIs or MRI; previous use of escitalopram (previous psilocybin use was allowed); suspected or known psychiatric conditions, such as borderline personality disorder, that could jeopardize rapport with the two caregivers; further criteria in the protocol, which was not read (p. 1403). Psychiatric medication fully stopped at least 2 weeks, and psychotherapy at least 3 weeks, before the first trial medication (p. 1404).
sample.demographics: Mean age 41 years (psilocybin 43.3, SD 11.7, range 21–64; escitalopram 39.1, SD 9.7, range 22–60); 20 (34%) women; White 28 (93%) and 24 (83%); university education 22 (73%) and 23 (79%); no previous psilocybin use 22 (73%) and 21 (72%); weekly alcohol 36.8 g (SD 43.1) and 67.7 g (SD 66.6); duration of illness 22.1 (SD 10.7) and 15.1 (SD 11.0) years; psychiatric medications previously used 2.2 and 1.8; previous psychotherapy 28 (93%) and 26 (90%); pretreatment QIDS-SR-16 14.5 (SD 3.9, range 7–23) and 16.4 (SD 4.1, range 6–22); HAM-D-17 19.2 and 18.4; BDI-1A 29.1 and 28.7 (Table 1, p. 1407; Results › Patients, p. 1406).
sample.attrition: All 59 randomized patients were in the intention-to-treat analysis (p. 1405). Escitalopram group: 5 of 29 did not complete the protocol requirements (4 stopped the escitalopram capsules because of adverse events; 1 missed the second dosing day and later visits because of Covid-19 restrictions), and 1 more, who had guessed the capsule content, halved the dose from 20 to 10 mg because of perceived adverse events, as the protocol allowed. Psilocybin group: 3 of 30 did not complete all dosing procedures (2 missed the second dosing day and later visits because of Covid-19 restrictions; 1 stopped the daily placebo capsules after guessing their content) (p. 1406). The number of patients with a week-6 primary outcome value is not stated in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: Self-referred volunteers who sought out a psilocybin trial, many of whom expressed a preference for psilocybin over escitalopram (p. 1410); not ethnically or socioeconomically diverse; mostly university-educated (Table 1). People with conditions judged incompatible with the limited psychological support available were excluded, which the authors say may have biased the sample towards people who could take psilocybin without unacceptable side effects (p. 1409). Baseline severity was in the moderate range on average (p. 1410). About a quarter of each group had used psilocybin before (Table 1). Chance baseline imbalances: longer illness (22 vs 15 years), lower QIDS-SR-16 (14.5 vs 16.4) and less alcohol in the psilocybin group (Table 1).

exposure.measurement: Dosing days at the NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility, each supervised by the patient's two assigned mental health professionals (one a clinical psychologist, psychotherapist or psychiatrist), who cared for the patient's physical and psychological well-being; a trial psychiatrist judged when the patient could be discharged. Preparatory session at baseline, psychological debriefing the day after the first dosing day and by telephone or video a week later, an integration session the day after the second dosing day (p. 1404). Daily capsules were taken at home from a screw-top bottle; medications and placebos were prepackaged with nondisclosing labels (p. 1404). Adherence to the daily capsules is reported only through the deviations listed under attrition.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: psilocybin group, 25 mg psilocybin on dosing-day 1 and dosing-day 2 (3 weeks apart) plus daily placebo capsules (microcrystalline cellulose) for 6 weeks; escitalopram group, 1 mg psilocybin on both dosing days plus escitalopram capsules, 10 mg daily for 3 weeks and then 20 mg daily (two capsules) for 3 weeks, with reduction to 10 mg allowed (pp. 1402, 1404, 1406). Psilocybin was ingested on the dosing days (the form is not described in the main text); the daily medication or placebo was in capsules.
exposure.polysubstance: Weekly alcohol use was recorded and was higher in the escitalopram group (67.7 vs 36.8 g; editors' conversion with the table's factor of 8 g per UK unit: about 8.5 vs 4.6 units); a post hoc analysis for this imbalance gave results in the same direction (p. 1407; Section S12, not read). Previous psilocybin use was allowed (editors' calculation from Table 1: 8 of 30 and 8 of 29 had used it). Other drug use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Psychiatric medication fully stopped at least 2 weeks, and psychotherapy at least 3 weeks, before the first trial medication (p. 1404); 23 of 59 (39%) had stopped a psychiatric medication to enter and 4 (7%) had stopped psychotherapy (p. 1406). How this was verified is not described.

comparison.controls: Escitalopram group (n=29): daily escitalopram for 6 weeks, 1 mg psilocybin on both dosing days (a dose the authors presumed to have negligible activity) and the same psychological support (p. 1404). There was no placebo-only group: an arm receiving 1 mg psilocybin and placebo capsules was in the initial design but was dropped because three groups were judged too complex and expensive to conduct and power with the resources available (p. 1405).
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1 with a random-number generator, implemented by staff outside the research team (details in Section S2.6, not read); size- and colour-matched placebo capsules; all patients told they would receive psilocybin, without the dose (p. 1404).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomized, so baseline factors are expected to balance on average in a large trial; with 59 patients, imbalances in illness duration, baseline severity and alcohol use occurred (Table 1). Preference for psilocybin and expectancy, which the authors say many patients expressed (p. 1410), are not reported as measured variables in the main text.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The escitalopram group drank more alcohol (Table 1); both groups had the same medication and psychotherapy washout (p. 1404).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: QIDS-SR-16 (self-report, 0 to 27), collected weekly. Secondary (16): QIDS-SR-16 response and remission at week 6; QIDS-SR-14 change between the day before and the day after the first dosing day; changes to week 6 in BDI-1A, HAM-D-17 and MADRS, the Flourishing Scale, STAI trait anxiety, BEAQ, WSAS, SHAPS, WEMWBS (every 2 weeks) and SIDAS; at week 6, PRSexDQ, LEIS and the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (p. 1405; Figure 1 legend, p. 1408). Safety: adverse events from dosing-day 1 to week 6, elicited by asking how patients had been since the last visit or observed on site, coded with MedDRA 23.0; the investigator-constructed Post-Treatment Changes Scale (PTCS) (p. 1405).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated depression, anxiety and well-being scales; the PTCS was constructed by the investigators (p. 1405).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: change from baseline in QIDS-SR-16 at week 6. Response: a fall of at least 50% according to Methods (p. 1405) but of more than 50% according to the abstract and Table 2 (pp. 1402, 1409); remission: QIDS-SR-16 of 5 or less at week 6. Acute subjective effects of psilocybin were not counted as adverse events, because earlier studies suggested they may mediate benefit (p. 1408). Related adverse events: those judged probably or definitely related by the study clinician in dialogue with the patient (Table 3 footnote, p. 1410).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the 16 secondary outcomes: with no prespecified plan for multiplicity, P values were not reported for them and the authors state that no clinical conclusions can be drawn from them (p. 1406; Table 2 footnote, p. 1409). The count is the primary outcome plus the 16 secondary outcomes named in the abstract; 15 secondary outcomes are in Table 2 and the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory is in the supplement.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Investigators and medication-administering staff were unaware of group assignment (p. 1404). The primary outcome is self-rated by patients who were told they would receive psilocybin. Who administered the clinician-rated scales (HAM-D-17, MADRS) is not stated in the main text. Blinding effectiveness was not assessed; patients given 25 mg rated the acute subjective effects as more intense than those given 1 mg (Figure S7, not read) (p. 1410).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary, QIDS-SR-16 change at week 6 (means adjusted for baseline, ± SE): −8.0 ± 1.0 with psilocybin vs −6.0 ± 1.0 with escitalopram; difference −2.0 points (95% CI −5.0 to 0.9; P=0.17) (Table 2, p. 1409). Secondary, uncorrected: response 21/30 (70%) vs 14/29 (48%), difference 22 percentage points (−3 to 48); remission 17/30 (57%) vs 8/29 (28%), 28 points (2 to 54; 28.1, 2.3 to 53.8, in the text); HAM-D-17 −10.5 vs −5.1 (difference −5.3, −8.2 to −2.4); MADRS −14.4 vs −7.2 (−7.2, −12.1 to −2.4); BDI-1A −18.4 vs −10.8 (−7.6, −13.3 to −1.8); WEMWBS +15.4 vs +7.3 (8.1, 2.6 to 13.5); QIDS-SR-14 between the day before and the day after the first dosing day −5.7 vs −2.8 (−3.0, −5.5 to −0.4) (Table 2). Editors' calculation for the primary outcome: standardized difference about 0.35 in favour of psilocybin, with an interval from about 0.87 in favour of psilocybin to about 0.16 in favour of escitalopram (SD of change back-calculated from the CI, about 5.8).
analysis.covariates: Baseline score of each outcome: repeated-measures ANCOVA for the primary outcome; logistic regression adjusted for baseline for response and remission; permutation tests stratified by baseline for BDI-1A and SIDAS; Wilcoxon test for PRSexDQ; Jonckheere–Terpstra test for the PTCS (pp. 1405–1406). A post hoc analysis for the alcohol imbalance is in Section S12 (not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03429075 (p. 1402); the protocol is said to be available with the full text at NEJM.org (p. 1403). Neither the registry record nor the protocol was among the files read, so registered and reported outcomes could not be compared. The paper states that prespecified hypotheses existed for the QIDS-SR-16 and WEMWBS (Figure 1 legend, p. 1408).
analysis.selective_reporting: All secondary outcomes named in Methods are reported, without P values (Table 2; Emotional Breakthrough Inventory in Figure S7). Per-protocol results (Table S1), unadjusted values (Table S12), the alcohol analysis (Section S12), PTCS results (Table S2) and the full adverse-event list (Table S5) are only in the supplement (not read). Imaging and cognitive-task data were not yet analysed and the 6-month follow-up not yet fully collected (pp. 1404–1405).
analysis.power: Powered on data from previous trials, assuming equal variance for the two drugs, at two-sided P<0.05 with 80% power: 20 patients per group were required and at least 30 per group were planned (p. 1405); the assumed difference is not stated in the main text. Editors' calculation: with 20 per group and 80% power, the detectable standardized difference is about 0.9, so the trial could show only a large difference between two active treatments; a non-significant result does not show that the two are equivalent.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over 6 weeks, in 59 mostly self-referred patients with, on average, moderate depression, the self-rated primary outcome did not differ significantly between two psilocybin sessions and daily escitalopram: a difference of 2.0 QIDS-SR-16 points in favour of psilocybin, with a 95% interval from 5.0 points in favour of psilocybin to 0.9 points in favour of escitalopram. The interval is wide enough to include a moderate advantage for psilocybin and a small advantage for escitalopram. Remission (57% vs 28%) and most other secondary scales favoured psilocybin, without correction for 16 comparisons. Similar proportions reported adverse events (87% vs 83%), with different profiles.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract conclusion matches the primary result and flags the missing multiplicity correction (p. 1402). Points where the paper overstates or could be overstated: the abstract prints the primary difference as 2.0 with an interval (−5.0 to 0.9) that excludes it (p. 1402); the abstract states that secondary outcomes generally favoured psilocybin, which, though caveated, puts uncorrected results in the summary; the population is called moderate-to-severe in the abstract (p. 1402) and mild-to-severe in the Discussion (p. 1408), while its baseline severity was moderate on average (p. 1410); the PTCS findings on crying, compassion and pleasure are reported without statistics (p. 1408); the Discussion links psychedelic effects to neuronal plasticity using a rat study (p. 1410). A headline version (psilocybin works as well as, or better than, a standard antidepressant) would overstate: the trial was neither designed nor powered to show equivalence, had no placebo arm, gave escitalopram for only 6 weeks, which the authors call a limitation (p. 1409), compared psilocybin with escitalopram given within the same support programme rather than as usually prescribed (the authors say the support may have improved the escitalopram group's outcomes, p. 1409), used a self-rated primary outcome in patients who were told they would receive psilocybin and largely preferred it, and did not test blinding (p. 1410).
