replication.where_it_stands: No other head-to-head randomized comparison of psilocybin with an SSRI was among the papers read. The two later trials read for these cards compared a single 25-mg dose with a control condition, not with an antidepressant (Goodwin et al., 2022; Raison et al., 2023). Critiques, a reanalysis and a 6-month follow-up of this trial are listed in the project's psilocybin list but were not among the files read, so their findings are not stated here.

funding.funder: A private donation from the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust and the founding partners of Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research; infrastructure support from the NIHR Imperial Biomedical Research Centre and the NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility (p. 1411). Psilocybin was provided by COMPASS Pathways, and escitalopram and placebo by the Pharmacy Manufacturing Unit at Guy's and St Thomas' Hospital (p. 1403). An investigator-initiated, university-sponsored trial; the authors state there was no industry involvement in data collection or analysis and no agreements between the authors and any commercial entity (p. 1403).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 1411): Carhart-Harris, consulting fees from COMPASS Pathways, Entheon Biomedical, Mydecine, Synthesis Institute, Tryp Therapeutics and Usona Institute; Giribaldi, consulting fees from SmallPharma; Watts, advisory board fees from Usona Institute and employment by Synthesis Institute; Baker-Jones, fees for facilitating meetings from Synthesis Institute; Erritzoe, consulting fees from Field Trip and Mydecine; Nutt, consulting fees from Awakn, H. Lundbeck and Psyched Wellness, advisory board fees from COMPASS Pathways, lecture fees from Takeda Medical Research Foundation, and stock in Alcarelle. No other potential conflicts were reported; the disclosure forms at NEJM.org were not read.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors were at the Centre for Psychedelic Research, Imperial College London (p. 1402). The supplier of the psilocybin, COMPASS Pathways, paid consulting fees to the first author and advisory board fees to the last author (p. 1411). The first author designed the trial and wrote the first draft with the second author; the eighth author analysed the data (p. 1403). The first author is also a co-author of the COMPASS Pathfinder-sponsored trial by Goodwin et al. (2022). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: An adequately powered non-inferiority trial of psilocybin with psychological support against an SSRI given for a full course (12 weeks or more) with the same support, with a clinician-rated primary outcome assessed blind, expectancy measured before treatment and allocation guesses recorded, recruitment not limited to people seeking a psilocybin study, and ideally a placebo arm so that each treatment's own effect can be estimated.

domains.note: Random-number generator, implemented by staff outside the research team, with prepackaged nondisclosing labels (p. 1404; details in Section S2.6, not read). Baseline imbalances in illness duration, QIDS-SR-16 and alcohol use are compatible with chance in 59 patients, and the primary analysis adjusts for baseline score.

Double-dummy design, but patients given 25 mg rated the acute effects as more intense and blinding was not assessed (p. 1410); one patient in each group guessed the capsule content and changed adherence, and 4 of 29 stopped escitalopram because of adverse events (p. 1406), reducing exposure to the comparator. Analysis by intention to treat.

Few patients missed visits (3 after the first dosing day, for Covid-19 restrictions, a reason unrelated to the outcome). The number with a week-6 score is not stated, and how these patients were counted for response and remission is not described.

The primary outcome is self-rated by patients who were told they would receive psilocybin, could probably tell 25 mg from 1 mg, mostly referred themselves and in many cases preferred psilocybin (pp. 1404, 1410). The authors state they cannot be confident that guessing or biased expectations in favour of psilocybin did not influence the results. Influence of beliefs about allocation on reported symptoms is likely.

The primary outcome and analysis are as stated in the paper, and all secondary outcomes are reported, without P values. The registry record and protocol were not read, so this rests on the paper's own statements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomization and allocation concealment appear adequate and few data were missing, but the primary outcome is a self-rated scale completed by patients who could probably tell which dose they had received, who were told they would receive psilocybin and of whom many preferred it, with no blinding check; bias in the measurement of the outcome, in favour of psilocybin, is likely. Deviations reduced exposure to escitalopram (4 of 29 stopped it, 1 halved it). Because this bias would favour psilocybin, the true difference on the primary outcome is, if anything, smaller than the observed 2.0 points, and the secondary results favouring psilocybin are the ones most exposed to it. The card may be cited for the primary difference and its interval, the adverse-event profiles and the design's limits; the secondary outcomes only as uncorrected, exploratory comparisons; and not for equivalence or superiority of psilocybin over escitalopram.

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, QIDS-SR-16 change at week 6: −8.0 (SE 1.0) with psilocybin (n=30) vs −6.0 (SE 1.0) with escitalopram (n=29); difference −2.0 points (95% CI −5.0 to 0.9; P=0.17), not significant; a per-protocol analysis gave similar results (Table S1, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (p. 1409)

key_findings.finding: QIDS-SR-16 response at week 6: 21 of 30 (70%) with psilocybin vs 14 of 29 (48%) with escitalopram, difference 22 percentage points (95% CI −3 to 48); remission (score 5 or less): 17 of 30 (57%) vs 8 of 29 (28%), difference 28.1 points (2.3 to 53.8). Both are secondary outcomes without correction for multiplicity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (p. 1409)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: raw differences 21.7 and 29.1 percentage points, with raw Wald 95% intervals −2.8 to 46.2 and 5.0 to 53.1. Table 2 states that all values are adjusted for baseline, and Methods name logistic regression adjusted for baseline scores for response and remission (pp. 1405–1406); how the percentage-point differences and their intervals were derived is not described (reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Other secondary outcomes, change to week 6 (psilocybin vs escitalopram; difference with uncorrected 95% CI): HAM-D-17 −10.5 vs −5.1 (−5.3; −8.2 to −2.4); MADRS −14.4 vs −7.2 (−7.2; −12.1 to −2.4); BDI-1A −18.4 vs −10.8 (−7.6; −13.3 to −1.8); WEMWBS +15.4 vs +7.3 (8.1; 2.6 to 13.5). The authors state no clinical conclusions can be drawn from the secondary outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnote dagger

key_findings.finding: QIDS-SR-14 change from the day before to the day after the first dosing day: −5.7 with psilocybin vs −2.8 with escitalopram (difference −3.0, uncorrected 95% CI −5.5 to −0.4). In Figure 1A the psilocybin group's mean change was larger at every weekly point; the gap was about 2.7 points at the first weekly point and about 1.4 to 2.3 points from then to week 6 (editors' reading).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 1409); Figure 1A (p. 1408)
key_findings.note: Weekly values in Figure 1 are not printed; no P values are shown for intermediate time points. The gaps are the editors' approximate reading of a 300-dpi crop (marker positions measured against the axis ticks).

key_findings.finding: Both groups had two dosing days 3 weeks apart: the psilocybin group received 25 mg each time plus daily placebo capsules; the escitalopram group received 1 mg psilocybin each time, presumed by the authors to have negligible activity, plus escitalopram 10 mg daily for 3 weeks and 20 mg daily for the next 3 weeks. To standardize expectations, all patients were told they would receive psilocybin, without the dose.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Design, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Blinding was not assessed; patients given 25 mg rated the acute subjective effects as more intense than those given 1 mg; most volunteers referred themselves and many expressed a preference for psilocybin over escitalopram; the authors state they cannot be confident that guessing of allocation or biased expectations did not influence the results.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1409, continued on p. 1410)

key_findings.finding: In the escitalopram group, 4 of 29 stopped escitalopram because of adverse events, 1 missed the second dosing day and later visits because of Covid-19 restrictions, and 1, who had guessed the capsule content, halved the dose from 20 to 10 mg because of perceived adverse events (permitted by the protocol); in the psilocybin group, 2 of 30 missed the second dosing day and later visits because of Covid-19 restrictions and 1 stopped the placebo capsules after guessing their content.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Participants: 59 randomized (30 and 29) after about 1000 telephone screenings; mean age 41 years; 20 (34%) women; depression present for a mean of 22 years (psilocybin) and 15 years (escitalopram); baseline QIDS-SR-16 14.5 and 16.4; 23 (39%) had stopped a psychiatric medication to enter; no previous psilocybin use in 22 of 30 and 21 of 29.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1406); Table 1 (p. 1407)

key_findings.finding: Adverse events over 6 weeks: 26 of 30 (87%) with psilocybin vs 24 of 29 (83%) with escitalopram; no serious adverse events; events judged related 22 (73%) vs 23 (79%). On the first dosing day, any adverse event 15 (50%) vs 8 (28%), events judged related 15 (50%) vs 6 (21%), headache 13 (43%) vs 5 (17%) and nausea 4 (13%) vs 0. Over 6 weeks, headache 20 (67%) vs 15 (52%), fatigue 2 (7%) vs 7 (24%), anxiety 0 vs 4 (14%), dry mouth 0 vs 4 (14%). Acute psychedelic effects were not counted as adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph (p. 1407); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1408); Table 3 (p. 1410)

key_findings.finding: Sexual function and emotional responsiveness at week 6 (secondary, uncorrected): PRSexDQ 0 (0 to 0) with psilocybin vs 3 (0 to 7) with escitalopram, difference −2 (−4 to 0), higher scores meaning more dysfunction; LEIS 4.1 vs −2.2, difference 6.3 (3.6 to 9.0), positive scores meaning more intense emotional responsiveness.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: The table footnote describes the PRSexDQ as mean ± SE and the LEIS as mean (95% CI), the reverse of the printed formats; the PRSexDQ figures look like medians with ranges or interquartile ranges (analysed with a Wilcoxon test, p. 1406).

key_findings.finding: On the investigator-constructed PTCS, patients in the psilocybin group reported greater perceived improvements in the ability to cry and to feel compassion, in intense emotion and in pleasure, and less drowsiness, than those in the escitalopram group (no statistics in the main text; Table S2 not read). No visual perceptual changes, psychotic symptoms or dependency-related behaviours were observed or reported in either group at 6 weeks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Power: 20 patients per group were required for 80% power at two-sided P<0.05 (assumed difference not stated), and at least 30 per group were planned. An initial placebo group (1 mg psilocybin with placebo capsules) was dropped from the final protocol as too complex and expensive to conduct and power.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 1405); Methods › Trial Design, 5th paragraph (p. 1404, continued on p. 1405)

key_findings.finding: SIDAS (suicidal ideation) change at week 6: −2.0 (95% CI −4.3 to 0.0) with psilocybin vs −0.8 (−3.4 to 2.0) with escitalopram; printed difference −1.3 (−6.5 to −0.3), uncorrected.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: See reporting issues: the printed difference interval cannot be reconciled with the group intervals; not to be cited as showing less suicidal ideation with psilocybin.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that psychological support was given to both groups and that it may have improved outcomes in the escitalopram group.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1408, continued on p. 1409)
key_findings.note: Editors' note: the comparator was therefore escitalopram given with the trial's psychological support and two 1-mg psilocybin sessions, not escitalopram as usually prescribed; the authors also call the 6-week course of escitalopram a limitation (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 1409).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the primary between-group difference as 2.0 points with a 95% CI of −5.0 to 0.9, an interval that does not contain 2.0; the Results and Table 2 give −2.0 (−5.0 to 0.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sign was dropped in the abstract; the difference is −2.0, that is, 2 points more improvement with psilocybin, not significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Response is defined as a reduction of more than 50% in the abstract and the Table 2 footnote, but as a decrease of at least 50% in Methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: A patient with exactly a 50% reduction would be classified differently under the two rules; which rule produced the 21 and 14 responders cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The remission difference is printed as 28.1 percentage points (95% CI 2.3 to 53.8) in the text and as 28 (2 to 54) in Table 2 and the abstract, whereas the printed counts, 17 of 30 and 8 of 29, give a raw difference of 29.1 points (Wald 95% CI 5.0 to 53.1). The response difference (22) matches the raw 21.7 after rounding, but its interval (−3 to 48) is not the raw Wald interval (−2.8 to 46.2). Neither printed interval matches a continuity-corrected Wald or a Newcombe interval from the counts either (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably baseline-adjusted figures (Table 2 footnote: all values adjusted for baseline; Methods: logistic regression adjusted for baseline scores, pp. 1405–1406), but how adjusted percentage-point differences and their intervals were derived is not described; the discrepancies are small.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 2 footnote states that the PRSexDQ is reported as mean ± SE and the LEIS as mean (95% CI), but the table prints the PRSexDQ as 0 (0 to 0) and 3 (0 to 7) and the LEIS as 4.1 ± 0.9 and −2.2 ± 1.0.
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels are swapped or wrong; the PRSexDQ values look like medians with ranges or interquartile ranges, so the size of the sexual-function difference cannot be read reliably.

reporting_issues.issue: SIDAS: the printed difference, −1.3 (95% CI −6.5 to −0.3), excludes zero, although the group changes, −2.0 (−4.3 to 0.0) and −0.8 (−3.4 to 2.0), overlap widely. Editors' calculation: the group means differ by 1.2, and a normal approximation from the two group intervals gives a difference interval of about −4.7 to 2.3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval may come from the stratified permutation method, but as printed it cannot be checked; the SIDAS result should not be cited as showing less suicidal ideation with psilocybin.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample is described as having moderate-to-severe depression (abstract, introduction), mild-to-severe depression (Discussion, 1st paragraph) and baseline severity in the moderate range (Discussion, 4th paragraph). At pretreatment baseline, QIDS-SR-16 ranged from 6 to 23 and HAM-D-17 from 11 to 26, although all had HAM-D-17 of 17 or more at screening.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample should be described as moderately depressed on average, with some patients only mildly depressed at baseline.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor inconsistencies: the HAM-D-17 range is given as 0 to 52 in Methods and 0 to 50 in the Table 1 footnote; Methods describe the second dosing day as a second dose of psilocybin or placebo, whereas the abstract says the escitalopram group received 1 mg psilocybin on both dosing days.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the results; the escitalopram group's second dose is taken here to be 1 mg psilocybin, as the abstract states.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of patients with a week-6 primary outcome value is not given; Methods state there was no imputation except for the WSAS, yet response and remission use all randomized patients (30 and 29) as denominators, and how the 3 patients who missed visits after the first dosing day were counted is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The effect on the percentages is probably small, but the handling of missing week-6 data is unstated.

reporting_issues.issue: The power calculation does not state the difference or the variance assumed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot see what size of difference the trial was designed to detect; the editors' calculation (analysis, power) suggests only a large one.

design_detail: Phase 2, double-blind, dose-finding, parallel-group randomized trial (1:1:1) at 22 sites in 10 countries in Europe and North America, March 2019 to September 2021. Outpatients with a treatment-resistant major depressive episode (no response to 2 to 4 adequate treatments in the current episode) stopped their antidepressants during a 3-to-6-week run-in and then received one dose of COMP360, a proprietary synthetic psilocybin, at 25 mg, 10 mg or 1 mg (the 1-mg group was the control), with preparation, a 6-to-8-hour session attended by two therapists, and two integration sessions. Primary end point: change in MADRS total score from baseline to week 3, rated by blinded remote raters; follow-up to week 12. Designed and funded by COMPASS Pathfinder, which supplied its own proprietary formulation.
can_establish: Whether, in this selected group of outpatients with treatment-resistant depression who had stopped their antidepressants, one 25-mg or 10-mg dose of this psilocybin formulation given with psychological support changed clinician-rated depression scores at 3 weeks more than a 1-mg dose given with the same support, and which adverse events followed each dose over 12 weeks.
cannot_establish: How psilocybin compares with existing treatments or with no drug (there was no active comparator and no inert placebo), how much of the difference reflects participants recognizing a strong dose (blinding was not assessed), whether the effect lasts beyond 3 weeks (the 12-week sustained-response difference was not significant and a third of the 25-mg group started another treatment after week 3), or how the findings apply to people at clinically significant suicide risk, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Outpatients recruited through referrals from primary care and specialist psychiatric services, online advertisements and word of mouth (p. 1638), at 22 sites in the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, the United Kingdom, Canada and the United States (p. 1639). Of 428 people assessed, 195 were excluded (156 not meeting entry criteria, 1 lost to follow-up, 38 for other reasons) (Figure 1, p. 1641).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults aged 18 or older with a DSM-5 single or recurrent major depressive episode without psychotic features (clinical assessment, medical records and MINI 7.0.2), whose current episode had not responded to 2 to 4 adequate treatments (adequate dose and at least 8 weeks) on the MGH ATRQ; augmentation agents or other locally approved antidepressants could count as failed treatments (p. 1638). Other selection criteria are only in the protocol, which was not among the files read (p. 1639). The Discussion lists the exclusion of people judged to be at clinically significant suicide risk as a limitation (p. 1645). Antidepressants and other prohibited CNS medications were tapered during a 3-to-6-week run-in and stopped at least 2 weeks before baseline (p. 1639).
sample.demographics: Mean age 39.8 years (SD 12.2); 121 of 233 (52%) female; 215 (92%) White (self-reported); 14 (6%) had used psilocybin before; 222 (95%) had recurrent depression, mean 6.9 lifetime episodes (median 5.0); current episode 1 to under 2 years in 94 (40%) and 2 years or longer in 107 (46%); 191 (82%) had 2 failed treatments in the current episode and 37 (16%) had 3 or 4; 156 (67%) were withdrawn from an antidepressant at entry; mean MADRS 32.5 (SD 6.0), severe (31 or more) in 159 (68%); mean HAM-D-17 22.2 (SD 2.9) (Table 1, p. 1642).
sample.attrition: All 233 randomized participants received their dose and were in the modified intention-to-treat and safety sets. By week 12, 5 of 79 (6%) in the 25-mg group, 9 of 75 (12%) in the 10-mg group and 10 of 79 (13%) in the 1-mg group had withdrawn; withdrawals for adverse events were 2, 2 and 0 and for lack of efficacy 0, 1 and 1 (Figure 1 and Results › Participants, pp. 1640–1641). Per-protocol sets: 77, 65 and 68. Before week 3, new treatment for depression was started by 4 (5%), 9 (12%) and 14 (18%); between weeks 3 and 12 by 26 (33%), 18 (24%) and 16 (20%) (p. 1641).
sample.selection_effects: Outpatients with treatment-resistant depression who were willing to stop their antidepressants for at least 2 weeks and to take a psychedelic, recruited partly through advertisements and word of mouth; 92% White, which the authors name as a limitation; people at clinically significant suicide risk excluded; more than 90% had no previous psilocybin experience. The authors state that the sample resembled population studies of treatment-resistant depression (Table S11, not read) (p. 1641). Chance baseline differences: MADRS in the moderate range (20 to 30) in 42% of the 25-mg group vs 25% and 23% of the 10-mg and 1-mg groups; female 56%, 55% and 46% (Table 1, p. 1642).

exposure.measurement: Assigned by central randomization and given in a supervised administration session on day 1 lasting 6 to 8 hours, attended by the lead therapist who had prepared the participant and an assisting therapist, in rooms designed to feel calm and non-clinical, with a music playlist and eyeshades; participants went home after at least 6 hours once the acute effects had resolved. Preparation: at least three therapist meetings during the run-in. Integration: sessions on day 2 and at week 1, non-directive (p. 1639). Urine drug screening at screening, day 2 and week 3 (p. 1640).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: a single dose of COMP360 synthetic psilocybin, 25 mg, 10 mg or 1 mg, on day 1 only (pp. 1637, 1639); the route is not stated in the main text.
exposure.polysubstance: Antidepressants and other prohibited CNS medications were stopped at least 2 weeks before baseline, and participants were asked to stay off antidepressants for the first 3 weeks, although a physician investigator could start them at any time if clinically necessary (p. 1639). Urine drug screens were part of the laboratory tests (results not reported in the main text). Rules on alcohol and other drug use are not given in the main text. One serious adverse event after week 3 was codeine withdrawal syndrome (Table 3, p. 1647); one 25-mg participant received lorazepam for acute anxiety on day 1 (p. 1644).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Antidepressant washout of at least 2 weeks before the baseline visit (day −1), after a 3-to-6-week taper (p. 1639); 156 of 233 (67%) were withdrawn from an antidepressant at entry (Table 1). How the washout was verified is not stated.

comparison.controls: The 1-mg psilocybin group (n=79), which had the same preparation, session setting and integration support. There was no inert placebo and no active comparator; the authors list the lack of an active comparator as a limitation (p. 1645).
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1:1 at a central location, stratified by country and previous psilocybin experience (p. 1639); baseline characteristics similar across groups apart from the chance differences noted under selection effects (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomized, so measured and unmeasured baseline factors are expected to balance on average. Not measured: expectancy before dosing, preference for a group, and participants' guesses of their dose (the authors did not assess dose guessing, p. 1645). Psychedelic experience was recorded only as previous psilocybin use (6%).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same washout, antidepressant rule and urine screening in all groups. New depression treatment before week 3 was more frequent in the 1-mg group (14 of 79, 18%) than in the 25-mg group (4 of 79, 5%) (p. 1641).

outcomes.instruments: MADRS (0 to 60) administered by telephone by experienced clinician raters from an independent contract research organization (MedAvante-ProPhase), using the Structured Interview Guide for the MADRS, at baseline (day −1), day 2 and weeks 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 (pp. 1638–1639). Safety: adverse events at every visit coded with MedDRA 23.0 (weeks 6 and 9 remote), the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale, vital signs, laboratory tests including urine drug screens, and 12-lead ECG (p. 1640). HAM-D-17 at baseline (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated depression scales; the response (at least 50% decrease) and remission (MADRS 10 or less) thresholds are conventional (pp. 1639–1640).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: change in MADRS total from baseline to week 3. Key secondary: response at week 3, remission at week 3, and sustained response (a week-3 response kept at every visit through week 12) (pp. 1639–1640). Suicidal ideation with intent, or any item of the C-SSRS suicidal-behaviour section including non-suicidal self-injury, was recorded as a serious adverse event (p. 1640). Estimands: for participants who started a new antidepressant, later MADRS scores were imputed under a missing-not-at-random rule that progressively worsened them, and the same was done after withdrawal for lack of efficacy or adverse events; other missing scores were imputed as missing at random; for response, remission and sustained response such participants counted as non-responders (p. 1640).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Hierarchical fixed-sequence testing at two-sided 0.05: for each end point, 25 mg and then 10 mg against 1 mg, before moving to the next end point (p. 1640). Because the 10-mg comparison on the primary end point was not significant (P=0.18), testing stopped there, and every key secondary result, including those for 25 mg, counts as not significantly different (Table 2 footnote, p. 1643; Results › Efficacy, p. 1644). The count of 8 is the comparisons in Table 2 (4 end points × 2 doses); further efficacy outcomes are in Supplementary Tables S3–S6 (not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: MADRS raters were remote, worked for an independent contract research organization and were unaware of the trial details and group assignments (p. 1638). Therapists were unaware of assignments, collected no efficacy data and were discouraged from speculating about doses (p. 1639). Participants were not asked to guess their dose; the authors state that the intensity of the acute effects of 25 mg and 10 mg reduces the effectiveness of the double blind (p. 1645).

analysis.effect_sizes: Week-3 MADRS least-squares mean change: 25 mg −12.0 (SE 1.3; 95% CI −14.6 to −9.3), 10 mg −7.9 (SE 1.4; −10.6 to −5.2), 1 mg −5.4 (SE 1.4; −8.1 to −2.7). Difference vs 1 mg: 25 mg −6.6 (95% CI −10.2 to −2.9; P<0.001); 10 mg −2.5 (−6.2 to 1.2; P=0.18) (Table 2, p. 1643). Response at week 3: 29/79 (37%), 14/75 (19%), 14/79 (18%); odds ratio vs 1 mg 2.9 (1.2 to 6.6) for 25 mg and 1.2 (0.5 to 3.0) for 10 mg. Remission at week 3: 23/79 (29%), 7/75 (9%), 6/79 (8%); odds ratios 4.8 (1.8 to 12.8) and 1.2 (0.4 to 3.9). Sustained response to week 12: 16/79 (20%), 4/75 (5%), 8/79 (10%); odds ratios 2.2 (0.9 to 5.4) and 0.7 (0.2 to 2.0) (Table 2). Editors' calculations: standardized difference about 0.55 for 25 mg vs 1 mg (SD back-calculated from the SE of the difference, about 11.9; 0.60 with the planning SD of 11.0) and about 0.2 for 10 mg; absolute differences, 25 vs 1 mg, with Wald 95% intervals: response 19.0 percentage points (5.4 to 32.5; about 5 people treated for each additional responder), remission 21.5 (9.9 to 33.1), sustained response 10.1 (−1.0 to 21.2). These secondary contrasts are descriptive, because formal testing had stopped.
analysis.covariates: MMRM with treatment, visit, pooled trial site, treatment-by-visit interaction and baseline MADRS, unstructured correlation matrix; multiply imputed estimates combined with Rubin's rules (p. 1640). Post hoc models adding sex or the number of lifetime episodes gave similar results (p. 1644).
analysis.preregistration_detail: EudraCT 2017-003288-36; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03775200 (p. 1637). The protocol and the Supplementary Appendix are said to be available with the full text at NEJM.org; neither they nor the registry record were among the files read, so registered and reported end points could not be compared. The paper describes the primary analysis and the hierarchical test procedure as prespecified (pp. 1640, 1643).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four hierarchical end points are reported for both doses, including the non-significant ones. Alternative data-handling analyses (Figure S2), further efficacy results (Tables S3–S6), severe adverse events by organ class (Table S7), worsening of suicidal state (Table S8) and representativeness (Table S11) are only in the supplement (not read). MADRS changes after week 3 appear only in Figure 2, without between-group tests. The interpretation and the post hoc analyses were done by the sponsor (p. 1638).
analysis.power: 216 participants (72 per group) for 90% power to detect a 6-point MADRS difference at two-sided 0.05, assuming SD 11.0 (p. 1640); 233 were randomized. The observed 25-mg difference (6.6) was close to the planned difference; differences smaller than 6 points, such as the 2.5 points for 10 mg, were not what the trial was powered to detect.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At 3 weeks, one 25-mg dose given with psychological support lowered clinician-rated depression scores 6.6 MADRS points more than a 1-mg dose given with the same support (95% CI 2.9 to 10.2 points), in outpatients with treatment-resistant depression who had stopped their antidepressants; 10 mg did not differ from 1 mg. 37% of the 25-mg group responded at 3 weeks (18% with 1 mg), so most did not; the higher response and remission rates are formally untested because hierarchical testing stopped. By week 12, sustained response was 20% vs 10% (not significant), the MADRS difference had narrowed in Figure 2, and a third of the 25-mg group had started another treatment after week 3. Serious adverse events of suicidal ideation, self-injury or suicidal behaviour occurred in the 25-mg and 10-mg groups; up to week 3 there were none in the 1-mg group, although 2 participants given 1 mg had suicidal ideation that was not rated serious (Table 3, p. 1646).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says response and remission at 3 weeks were "generally supportive of the primary results" (p. 1637), although the paper itself says no definite conclusions can be drawn from them after the hierarchical test failed (p. 1644). The closing paragraph of the Discussion repeats this, naming only 12-week sustained response as not statistically significant (p. 1645). The Discussion opens by saying the trial showed the "feasibility of psilocybin monotherapy for up to 12 weeks" (p. 1645), while 4 of 79 participants in the 25-mg group started another depression treatment before week 3 and 26 of 79 between weeks 3 and 12 (p. 1641). It says the manualized preparation, support and integration "ensured safety" (p. 1645), although 3 participants in the 25-mg group had suicidal behaviour after week 3 and worsening of suicidal state by week 3 was more frequent with 25 mg (14%) and 10 mg (17%) than with 1 mg (9%) (pp. 1644–1645). It compares the 37% response at 3 weeks with first-line trials and with later STAR*D steps (p. 1645), which differ in population, comparator and timing, and offers dose-dependent receptor occupancy from another study as a possible explanation for the dose difference. The abstract conclusion itself (25 mg but not 10 mg better than 1 mg over 3 weeks, with adverse effects; larger and longer trials needed) matches the results. A headline version (one dose of psilocybin treats resistant depression) would overstate: the comparison was with a 1-mg dose at 3 weeks, most people given 25 mg did not respond, the 12-week difference was not significant, blinding was not checked, and suicidality events were more frequent at the higher doses.

timeline.event: Open-label feasibility study of psilocybin with psychological support in treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016, Lancet Psychiatry), cited by this paper as the pilot work in treatment-resistant depression; not read for this card

Psilocybin (two sessions of 25 mg) versus escitalopram (with two 1-mg sessions) in 59 patients with mainly moderate major depression: no significant difference on the self-rated primary outcome at 6 weeks; cited by this paper among the pilot studies

Critique of this trial on blinding and suicide risk (Gukasyan et al., 2023, Med, doi 10.1016/j.medj.2022.12.003; the project list notes a published correction); not among the files read, so its arguments are not stated here

Single 25-mg dose versus niacin in 104 adults with major depressive disorder, 13% treatment-resistant: MADRS difference −12.3 at day 43; its discussion compares severe adverse event rates with this trial, notes that no suicidal behaviour occurred in its own trial, and describes the effect in this trial as waning over 12 weeks

replication.where_it_stands: Of the trials read for these cards, this one and Raison et al. (2023) both found lower depression scores after a single 25-mg dose with psychological support than after the control condition, with a smaller difference in treatment-resistant depression at 3 weeks (6.6 MADRS points against a 1-mg dose) than in less treatment-resistant major depression at 6 weeks (12.3 points against niacin). The dose finding (25 mg but not 10 mg) and the durability beyond 3 weeks have not been replicated in the papers read; phase 3 results from the same sponsor were not among the files (the project's psilocybin list names them as a gap). A published critique of this trial's blinding and suicidality findings (Gukasyan et al., 2023) was not read.

funding.funder: COMPASS Pathfinder (abstract, p. 1637; end matter, p. 1647). The sponsor designed and funded the trial and supplied COMP360; a contract research organization paid by the sponsor (Worldwide Clinical Trials) supervised the conduct of the trial; the statistical analysis was done by that organization and reviewed by the sponsor; the interpretation and the post hoc analyses were done by the sponsor; the sponsor paid for professional writing assistance for the first draft (Methods › Trial Oversight, p. 1638).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not printed in the PDF: the article states that the authors' disclosure forms are available with the full text at NEJM.org (p. 1647); they were not among the files read. The PDF states that confidentiality agreements were in place between the investigators and COMPASS Pathfinder (p. 1638).
funding.affiliations_note: Eight authors, including the first author (contact address at compasspathways.com) and the last author, are listed with a COMPASS Pathfinder affiliation (Appendix, p. 1647). R. Carhart-Harris, first author of the psilocybin versus escitalopram trial (carhart-harris_2021), is a co-author here (affiliation UCSF). The formulation tested is the sponsor's proprietary product (p. 1638). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A larger trial in treatment-resistant depression with an active comparator and a placebo condition, recording each participant's expectancy before dosing and guess of allocation afterwards, reporting outcomes to 12 weeks or longer with every new treatment recorded and analysed under a treatment-policy approach as well as the hypothetical one, and reporting suicidality per participant over the whole follow-up.

domains.note: Central randomization (1:1:1), stratified by country and previous psilocybin experience (p. 1639); baseline differences (more moderate MADRS scores in the 25-mg group, fewer women in the 1-mg group) are compatible with chance (Table 1). The method of sequence generation is not described in the main text.

Participants and therapists were described as unaware of assignment, but the authors concede the acute effects of 25 mg and 10 mg weaken the double blind and blinding was not assessed (p. 1645). Starting new depression treatment before week 3 was more frequent with 1 mg (18%) than 25 mg (5%) (p. 1641), consistent with participants recognizing a weak dose. The analysis set included all randomized participants (modified intention to treat).

Week-3 scores after a new antidepressant or after withdrawal for lack of efficacy or adverse events were replaced by imputations that progressively worsened them (p. 1640). This probably applied to more 1-mg than 25-mg participants: starts of treatment for depression before week 3 numbered 14 with 1 mg and 4 with 25 mg (p. 1641), although the paper does not say how many were new antidepressants, and withdrawals for adverse events or lack of efficacy by week 12 were 2, 3 and 1 in the 25-mg, 10-mg and 1-mg groups (Figure 1, p. 1641). The number with an observed week-3 MADRS is not given in the main text; the alternative data-handling analyses said to be consistent are in Figure S2 (not read).

MADRS raters were remote, independent and unaware of assignment (p. 1638), but the rating rests on what participants report, and participants could probably tell a strong dose from 1 mg; no blinding check.

The paper states the primary analysis and hierarchical procedure were prespecified and reports all four end points for both doses, including the failures; the registry record, protocol and analysis plan were not among the files read, so this rests on the paper's own statements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Central stratified randomization and remote raters unaware of assignment make the 25-mg versus 1-mg difference unlikely to be an artefact of allocation or rater bias. The concerns all point in the same direction, favouring the higher dose: participants could probably tell a strong dose from 1 mg and the MADRS rests on their reports; new treatment before week 3 was more frequent in the 1-mg group, and the later scores of those who started a new antidepressant were imputed under a progressively worsening rule (the paper does not say how many of the starts were antidepressants); the sensitivity analyses said to agree are only in the supplement. Judged some concerns rather than high because the difference is clear of zero and the paper reports consistent alternative analyses, but its size may be overstated. The card may be cited for the 3-week difference between 25 mg and 1 mg, the absence of a 10-mg effect, and the adverse-event and suicidality counts; not for durability beyond 3 weeks, for comparison with standard treatments, or for the secondary end points as confirmatory evidence.

key_findings.finding: At week 3, the least-squares mean MADRS change was −12.0 (95% CI −14.6 to −9.3) with 25 mg, −7.9 with 10 mg and −5.4 with 1 mg; the difference from 1 mg was −6.6 points (95% CI −10.2 to −2.9; P<0.001) for 25 mg and −2.5 (−6.2 to 1.2; P=0.18) for 10 mg (n=79, 75 and 79).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, primary efficacy end point; also Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph (p. 1642, continued on p. 1644)

key_findings.finding: Because the 10-mg comparison on the primary end point was not significant, the prespecified hierarchical testing stopped, and all key secondary end points, including those for 25 mg, are formally not significantly different from 1 mg; the authors state that no definite conclusions can be drawn from the secondary results.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, footnote dagger (p. 1643); Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph (p. 1642, continued on p. 1644) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1644)

key_findings.finding: Response at week 3 (MADRS down at least 50%): 29 of 79 (37%) with 25 mg, 14 of 75 (19%) with 10 mg, 14 of 79 (18%) with 1 mg; odds ratio vs 1 mg 2.9 (95% CI 1.2 to 6.6) and 1.2 (0.5 to 3.0). Remission at week 3 (MADRS 10 or less): 23 of 79 (29%), 7 of 75 (9%), 6 of 79 (8%); odds ratios 4.8 (1.8 to 12.8) and 1.2 (0.4 to 3.9).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, secondary efficacy end points
key_findings.note: Formally not significant because hierarchical testing had stopped. Editors' calculation for 25 vs 1 mg: response difference 19.0 percentage points (Wald 95% CI 5.4 to 32.5), remission 21.5 (9.9 to 33.1).

key_findings.finding: Sustained response (week-3 response kept through week 12): 16 of 79 (20%) with 25 mg, 4 of 75 (5%) with 10 mg, 8 of 79 (10%) with 1 mg; odds ratio vs 1 mg 2.2 (95% CI 0.9 to 5.4) for 25 mg and 0.7 (0.2 to 2.0) for 10 mg; both intervals include 1.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, sustained response at week 12; Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph (p. 1644)

key_findings.finding: All three groups improved sharply by day 2, including the 1-mg group, and the 25-mg group's mean improvement shrank over the following weeks while the 10-mg group converged with the 1-mg group by week 6 (editors' reading of Figure 2, approximate: day 2 about −15, −12 and −9 points for 25, 10 and 1 mg; week 12 about −9.5, −5.7 and −6.0).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 2; only the week-3 values are printed (Table 2). No between-group tests are reported for weeks 6 to 12, and later points include imputed scores for participants who started new treatment.

key_findings.finding: Before the week-3 assessment, new treatment for depression was started by 4 participants (5%) in the 25-mg group, 9 (12%) in the 10-mg group and 14 (18%) in the 1-mg group; between weeks 3 and 12 by 26 (33%), 18 (24%) and 16 (20%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Participants, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Participants: 233 randomized of 428 assessed; treatment resistance meant 2 to 4 failed adequate treatments in the current episode, and 191 (82%) had 2 failed treatments and 37 (16%) 3 or 4; 156 (67%) were withdrawn from an antidepressant at entry; current episode 2 years or longer in 107 (46%); mean MADRS 32.5 (SD 6.0), severe in 159 (68%); mean age 39.8; 52% female; 92% White.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph (p. 1638), for the definition of treatment resistance; Table 1 (p. 1642); Figure 1 and Results › Participants, 2nd paragraph (p. 1641)

key_findings.finding: Adverse events occurred in 66 of 79 (84%) with 25 mg, 56 of 75 (75%) with 10 mg and 57 of 79 (72%) with 1 mg (179 of 233, 77%, overall). On day 1, headache affected 19 (24%), 11 (15%) and 13 (16%), and nausea 17 (22%), 5 (7%) and 1 (1%); severe adverse events on day 1 were reported by 3 (4%), 6 (8%) and 1 (1%); there were no serious adverse events on day 1.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1637) for 179 of 233; Results › Safety, 1st paragraph (p. 1644); Table 3, day 1 (p. 1646)

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events from day 2 to week 3: 4 of 79 (5%) with 25 mg (suicidal ideation 2, intentional self-injury 2), 4 of 75 (5%) with 10 mg (suicidal ideation 2, intentional self-injury 1, hospitalization for severe depression 1), none with 1 mg. After week 3 to week 12: 4 of 79 (5%) with 25 mg (suicidal behaviour 3, codeine withdrawal syndrome 1, adjustment disorder 1), 3 of 75 (4%) with 10 mg, 1 of 79 (1%) with 1 mg (intentional self-injury).
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1644); Table 3 (pp. 1646–1647)
key_findings.note: Counts are per period; the number of distinct participants with any serious adverse event over the 12 weeks is not given in the main text.

key_findings.finding: Suicidal ideation without intent or plan was present at baseline in 21 (27%), 27 (36%) and 19 (24%) of the 25-mg, 10-mg and 1-mg groups; worsening of suicidal state from baseline to week 3 occurred in 11 (14%), 13 (17%) and 7 (9%). The 3 participants in the 25-mg group with suicidal behaviour after week 3 all had a history of suicidal behaviour or non-suicidal self-injury and had not responded at week 3.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 4th paragraph (p. 1644, continued on p. 1645)

key_findings.finding: Blinding was not tested: participants were not asked to guess their dose, and the authors state that the intensity of the acute effects of 25 mg and 10 mg, compared with 1 mg, reduces the effectiveness of the double blind.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The sponsor designed and funded the trial, supplied the formulation, paid the contract research organization that supervised it, reviewed the statistical analysis done by that organization, did the interpretation and post hoc analyses, and paid for writing assistance for the first draft.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Trial Oversight, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Suicidal ideation recorded as an adverse event of any seriousness from day 2 to week 3: 5 of 79 (6%) with 25 mg, 4 of 75 (5%) with 10 mg and 2 of 79 (3%) with 1 mg (serious suicidal ideation in that period: 2, 2 and 0). With intentional self-injury as a serious event in 1 participant given 1 mg after week 3, suicidal ideation, behaviour or self-injury was recorded in every dose group, as the abstract states.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, day 2 up to week 3, adverse events in at least 5% of participants and serious adverse events (p. 1646), and after week 3, serious adverse events (p. 1647); Abstract, Results (p. 1637)
key_findings.note: Table 3 lists events that emerged or worsened after dosing; key finding 8 gives the serious events only.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the number of failed treatments in the current episode as 2 for 66, 62 and 63 participants (191 overall) and as 3 or 4 for 12, 11 and 14 (37 overall), in groups of 79, 75 and 79. Five participants are in neither category, although eligibility required 2 to 4 failed treatments (Methods › Participants). Editors' calculation: the two categories sum to 78 of 79, 73 of 75 and 77 of 79, 228 of 233 overall.
reporting_issues.consequence: The treatment resistance of 5 participants cannot be confirmed from the paper; either data are missing or the criterion was not met. The footnote attributes non-summing percentages to rounding, which does not explain counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the week-3 response and remission results in the 25-mg group as generally supportive of the primary result, and the closing paragraph of the Discussion says the secondary results generally supported the primary analysis, naming only 12-week sustained response as not statistically significant (p. 1645), whereas the paper's own hierarchical rule makes all of them not significant and the Results and the Discussion's 1st paragraph state that no definite conclusions can be drawn from them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The secondary end points should be cited as descriptive, not as confirmation of the primary result.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the trial as showing the feasibility of psilocybin monotherapy for up to 12 weeks, but between weeks 3 and 12 a treatment for depression was started by 26 of 79 (33%) in the 25-mg group, 18 of 75 (24%) in the 10-mg group and 16 of 79 (20%) in the 1-mg group, besides 4, 9 and 14 participants before week 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Outcomes after week 3 are not those of psilocybin alone. Under the paper's estimands, participants who started a new antidepressant counted as non-responders for response, remission and sustained response, and their later MADRS scores were imputed under a rule that progressively worsened them (p. 1640), so a new antidepressant could not have raised sustained response; the 12-week results depend on these handling rules. The Results count starts of any treatment for depression (p. 1641) and do not say whether each start was a new antidepressant handled this way.

reporting_issues.issue: The main text does not give the number of participants with an observed week-3 MADRS score, nor the primary result without imputation. Scores after a new antidepressant, and after withdrawal for lack of efficacy or adverse events, were imputed under a progressively worsening rule (p. 1640). Before week 3, treatment for depression was started by 14 participants in the 1-mg group and 4 in the 25-mg group (p. 1641), but the paper does not say how many of these starts were new antidepressants that triggered the rule; withdrawals for adverse events or lack of efficacy by week 12, timing not given, were 2, 3 and 1 in the 25-mg, 10-mg and 1-mg groups (Figure 1, p. 1641).
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the 25-mg versus 1-mg difference may depend on the imputation rule, which probably applied to more 1-mg than 25-mg participants; the paper says alternative data-handling analyses agreed (Figure S2), but they are only in the supplement, which was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Severe and serious adverse events are reported only by period (day 1; day 2 to week 3; after week 3), so the number of distinct participants with any severe or serious event over the whole trial cannot be derived from the main text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whole-trial rates per person are not available for comparison with other trials; Raison et al. (2023, p. 849) cite a 10% severe adverse event rate for this trial that does not appear in its main text.

design_detail: Phase 2, randomized, two-group trial (1:1) at 11 US sites, December 2019 to June 2022, described as blinding participants, site staff, sponsor, outcome raters and statisticians. 104 adults aged 21 to 65 with DSM-5 major depressive disorder (current episode of at least 60 days; central-rater MADRS of 28 or more), after a medication taper where needed, received one oral dose of 25 mg synthetic psilocybin or 100 mg niacin (an active placebo that causes flushing) in identical-looking capsules, each within the same protocolized programme: 6 to 8 hours of preparation, a 7-to-10-hour dosing session with two facilitators, and 4 hours of integration. Primary outcome: change in central-rater MADRS from baseline to day 43; key secondary outcome: day 8. Designed, sponsored and funded by the Usona Institute, a non-profit medical research organization.
can_establish: Whether, in adults with moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder who were mostly not treatment-resistant and had little or no recent psychedelic experience, one 25-mg dose of psilocybin given within a protocol of psychological support lowered clinician-rated depression scores over 6 weeks more than niacin given within the same protocol, and how adverse events differed between the two.
cannot_establish: How much of the difference reflects participants knowing or guessing their allocation (blinding was not assessed and the authors consider functional unblinding likely), whether the effect lasts beyond 6 weeks, how psilocybin compares with established treatments, or how the findings apply to people with marked treatment resistance, recent psychedelic use, recent suicidal behaviour or substance use disorders, or to more diverse populations.

sample.recruitment: Study-specific website, clinical programmes at participating institutions, advertisements, and national clinician-focused and patient-advocate listservs (p. 844); 11 US sites (list in eTable 1, not read). 1529 people completed prescreening; 1182 were excluded at telephone screening; 347 signed consent; 240 were excluded at screening (195 did not meet eligibility criteria, 32 withdrew, 7 lost to follow-up, 3 withdrawn by the investigator, 3 other); 3 were excluded in the early preparation phase; 104 were randomized (p. 846; Figure 1, p. 847).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Medically healthy adults aged 21 to 65 meeting DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder with a current episode of at least 60 days (SCID-5 Clinical Version); central-rater MADRS of 28 or more at screening, with no more than 30% improvement over a 7-to-35-day lead-in that allowed a psychiatric medication taper (no antidepressants for at least 2 weeks or 5 half-lives, whichever was longer); moderate to severe depression at baseline. Exclusions: psychosis or mania in the person or a first-degree relative; moderate or severe alcohol or drug use disorder; inability or unwillingness to stop prohibited psychotropic medications; any psychedelic use within 5 years, or more than 10 uses in a lifetime; current suicidal ideation with intent or plan; suicidal behaviour within the last 12 months; previous deep brain or vagus nerve stimulation, used as a marker of severe treatment resistance. No limits on the number of previous episodes, length of the current episode, maximum severity or number of previous treatments (p. 844).
sample.demographics: Mean age 41.1 years (SD 11.3); 52 (50%) women (p. 843). By group, psilocybin vs niacin: age 40.4 (SD 10.9) vs 41.8 (SD 11.7); White 44 of 51 (86%) vs 49 of 51 with data (96%); Hispanic or Latino 4 of 50 (8%) vs 12 of 53 (23%); annual income of 100 000 US dollars or more 23 of 45 (51%) vs 19 of 44 (43%); treatment-resistant depression on the MGH ATRQ 7 (14%) vs 6 (11%); medication taper before randomization 15 (29%) vs 8 (15%); baseline MADRS 35.5 (SD 5.7) vs 35.0 (SD 4.5); SDS 6.69 vs 7.14; median current episode 53 (IQR 25–135) vs 81 (26–145) weeks; first episode 4 (8%) vs 10 (19%); median previous pharmacological treatments in the current episode 1 (0–2) in both; previous lifetime psychedelic use 10 (19.6%) vs 13 (24.5%) (Table 1, p. 848; Results › Participants, p. 846).
sample.attrition: All 104 randomized participants received a study drug; one randomized to psilocybin received niacin and was analysed as psilocybin for efficacy and as niacin for safety (p. 846; Figure 1, p. 847). Withdrawal or loss to follow-up by week 6: 1 participant in the psilocybin group and 9 in the niacin group (as randomized); MADRS was missing for 1 and 9 participants at day 43 and for 0 and 3 at day 8 (pp. 846–847). Three participants in each group started antidepressant medication before day 43, of whom 2 and 1 also started psychotherapy; no one withdrew because of an adverse event (p. 846). Per-protocol population 45 and 36 (Figure 1).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers recruited partly through websites, advertisements and listservs, willing to stop psychotropic medication and to take a psychedelic, with little or no recent psychedelic experience (none in 5 years, at most 10 lifetime uses); mostly not treatment-resistant (12.5% met the TRD definition; median one previous treatment in the current episode); people with recent suicidal behaviour, active suicidal intent, a personal or family history of psychosis or mania, or moderate-to-severe substance use disorders were excluded (p. 844). Predominantly White, non-Hispanic and of higher income, which the authors call a major limitation (p. 850). Chance baseline differences: more first episodes (19% vs 8%) and longer current episodes (median 81 vs 53 weeks) in the niacin group, and more medication tapers in the psilocybin group (29% vs 15%) (Table 1).

exposure.measurement: One supervised administration on the day of randomization (day 1), within a protocolized programme identical for both groups: preparation sessions with two facilitators, totalling 6 to 8 hours, between baseline and dosing; a 7-to-10-hour dosing session in a comfortable room supervised by the same facilitators, with eyeshades and a curated music playlist on headphones encouraged; and 4 hours of integration sessions. Lead facilitators were doctoral-level psychologists or physicians with experience treating depression; co-facilitators held at least a bachelor's degree in a mental health field; all completed study-specific training (p. 845). Fidelity to the support protocol was not assessed (p. 850).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one oral dose of 25 mg synthetic psilocybin, or 100 mg niacin, in identical-appearing capsules, on day 1 only (pp. 843–844).
exposure.polysubstance: Moderate or severe alcohol or drug use disorder, psychedelic use in the past 5 years and more than 10 lifetime psychedelic uses were exclusions (p. 844); previous lifetime psychedelic use was reported by 19.6% and 24.5% (p. 846). Psychiatric concomitant medication (psycholeptics or psychoanaleptics) was reported by 8 (16%) and 7 (13%) between enrollment and day 43 (Table 3, p. 851). Substance use during the trial is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Prohibited psychotropic medications were tapered during the 7-to-35-day lead-in; antidepressants stopped for at least 2 weeks or 5 half-lives, whichever was longer (p. 844); 15 (29%) and 8 (15%) completed a taper (Table 1). Verification is not described.

comparison.controls: Niacin 100 mg (53 randomized; 54 received it), chosen as an active placebo because it produces an acute physiological response, flushing, thought to aid blinding (p. 845), given within the same support programme. The paper describes niacin's acute effect only as flushing; it attributes likely functional unblinding to the acute psychoactive effects of psilocybin and suggests comparators with acute psychoactive effects, such as ketamine, for future trials (p. 849).
comparison.matching: Randomization 1:1 on the day of dosing, permuted blocks of random size (2, 4 or 6) stratified by site, administered centrally through the contract research organization's data system with blinded bottle numbers (pp. 844–845).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomized, so baseline factors are expected to balance on average. Expectancy before dosing and participants' beliefs about their allocation were not measured, and the success of blinding was not assessed (p. 849).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same exclusions and taper rules in both groups; antidepressants were started before day 43 by 3 participants in each group (p. 846).

outcomes.instruments: MADRS (0 to 60) by telephone at screening, baseline and days 2, 8, 15, 29 and 43, administered by trained remote central raters blinded to treatment, visit and the specifics of the protocol (pp. 843, 845). Sheehan Disability Scale (self-rated, overseen by blinded site raters). Exploratory: Clinical Global Impressions, Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, Quality of Life Enjoyment and Satisfaction Questionnaire, Symptoms of Major Depressive Disorder Scale, Oxford Depression Questionnaire for emotional blunting (p. 845). Safety: adverse events from enrollment to the end of the study, graded by site principal investigators; solicited events were active suicidal ideation (C-SSRS or MADRS item 10, confirmed clinically), blood pressure or heart rate needing medication, overdose with suicidal intent, headache, nausea and visual perceptual effects (p. 845).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated scales. No minimal clinically important difference was prespecified; the authors cite literature values of 2 to 9 points for a placebo-adjusted change and of 6 (meaningful) or 12 (substantial) points for absolute change on the MADRS (p. 845).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: between-group difference in mean MADRS change from baseline to day 43. Key secondary: the same at day 8. Secondary: SDS change to day 43; sustained response (at least 50% reduction from baseline at each of days 8, 15, 29 and 43) and sustained remission (MADRS 10 or less at each of those visits), both defined a priori (p. 845). Treatment-emergent adverse events: any occurring after drug administration; related: a reasonable possibility that the study drug caused the event, as judged by the site principal investigator (p. 845).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Sequential fixed-sequence testing at two-sided 0.05, stopping at the first non-significant result, in this order: MADRS day 43, MADRS day 8, SDS day 43, sustained response, sustained remission (p. 846). The first four were significant; sustained remission (P=.05) was not. MADRS at days 2, 15 and 29 and SDS at days 8, 15 and 29 are exploratory (Table 2 footnote b, p. 849), and P values for the exploratory scales in eTables 4–8 are nominal (p. 846). The count of 11 is the comparisons in Table 2.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: MADRS by remote central raters blinded to treatment, visit and protocol specifics, a choice made to reduce functional unblinding of raters (p. 845); participants, sponsor and site staff were blinded until data lock (p. 845). The success of blinding was not assessed, and the authors consider some functional unblinding of participants likely (p. 849).

analysis.effect_sizes: MADRS change, mixed model adjusted (Table 2, p. 849): day 43, −19.1 (95% CI −22.7 to −15.5) with psilocybin vs −6.8 (−10.5 to −3.1) with niacin, difference −12.3 (−17.5 to −7.2), P<.001; day 8, −17.8 vs −5.8, difference −12.0 (−16.6 to −7.4), P<.001; day 15, −11.1 (−15.8 to −6.3); day 29, −13.7 (−18.6 to −8.8); day 2, −2.7 in both groups, difference −0.1 (−2.1 to 1.9), P=.95. SDS at day 43: −4.07 vs −1.76, difference −2.31 (−3.50 to −1.11), P<.001. Sustained response 20/48 (41.7%) vs 5/44 (11.4%), difference 30.3 percentage points (13.5 to 47.1), OR 5.60 (1.87 to 16.74), P=.002; sustained remission 12/48 (25.0%) vs 4/44 (9.1%), difference 15.9 (1.0 to 30.8), OR 3.37 (0.99 to 11.47), P=.05; both restricted to participants with MADRS at baseline and on days 8, 15, 29 and 43. Editors' calculations: standardized difference at day 43 about 1.0 (SD back-calculated from the CI with 50 and 44 participants assessed, about 12.7; 1.2 with the planning SD of 10); about 3 participants treated per additional sustained responder among those assessed at every visit.
analysis.covariates: Mixed model for repeated measures with unstructured covariance and with baseline score, site, sex and TRD status as covariates, time as a categorical variable with a treatment-by-time term, no imputation; multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses for the primary and key secondary outcomes; logistic regression for sustained response and remission adjusted for sex and TRD, with site dropped because of convergence problems (p. 846).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03866174 (p. 843). The protocol (Supplement 1), statistical analysis plan (Supplement 2), eAppendix (Supplement 3) and registry record were not among the files read. The paper itself reports that the FDA first recommended day 8 as the primary end point, on which the power calculation was based, and later recommended day 43; the primary end point was changed accordingly and the sample size raised from 80 to 100 (p. 845). When this happened relative to enrolment is not stated; sponsor and site staff were blinded until data lock (p. 845), and both day-8 and day-43 results are reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results for all five hierarchical end points are reported, including the non-significant sustained remission. Response and remission at each visit (eTable 3), exploratory end points (eTables 4–8), suicidal ideation scores (eTables 10–11), multiple-imputation details (eTable 2) and the per-protocol analysis (eTable 9) are only in the supplement (not read). The sponsor interpreted the data and wrote the manuscript (p. 853).
analysis.power: Assumptions: MADRS change of 18 points at day 8 and 17 at day 43 with psilocybin and 10 with niacin, SD 10, dropout of 5% by day 8 and a further 7.5% by day 43; 100 participants gave 92% power for day 43 and 98% for day 8 (p. 845). The observed niacin change (about 6 to 7 points) was smaller, and the observed difference (12.3 points) larger, than assumed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six weeks after one 25-mg dose given with a protocol of psychological support, clinician-rated depression scores had fallen 12.3 MADRS points more than after niacin given with the same support (95% CI 7.2 to 17.5), in adults with moderate-to-severe major depression, most of them not treatment-resistant and without recent psychedelic experience. The difference was present by day 8 and similar at days 15, 29 and 43, but not at day 2, whose 7-day recall period mostly covered the days before dosing. Sustained response was 42% vs 11% among participants assessed at every visit; sustained remission (25% vs 9%) was not significant. Dropout was 1 of 51 with psilocybin vs 9 of 53 with niacin. No serious adverse events followed dosing, but drug-related adverse events in the first 9 days were more frequent with psilocybin (82% vs 44%), including severe ones (8% vs 0).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion speaks of a "clinically significant sustained reduction" of symptoms and of functional disability with psilocybin, and stresses the absence of serious adverse events (p. 843), and the Key Points call the dose well tolerated (p. 844). No minimal clinically important difference was prespecified (p. 845); clinical significance is argued afterwards from literature thresholds, comparing the 12.3-point difference with an upper active-placebo difference of 9 points and the 19.1-point change with a 12-point threshold for substantial improvement in treatment-resistant depression (p. 848); the first comparison rests on the point estimate, since the lower 95% confidence limit of the difference, 7.2 points (Table 2, p. 849), is below 9. For functional disability there is no such argument: the Methods state that no MCID is defined for active versus control comparisons on the Sheehan Disability Scale (p. 845), the Discussion argues clinical significance only for the MADRS (p. 848), and the only SDS threshold printed is a within-group change of 1.33 points (Table 1 footnote c, p. 848), which the niacin group's day-43 change (−1.76, Table 2, p. 849) also exceeds; yet the abstract calls the reduction in functional disability clinically significant (p. 843), and the Conclusions' sentence on clinical significance covers both outcomes (p. 851). The Discussion also claims higher point-prevalence response and remission rates than recent psilocybin studies of treatment-resistant depression (p. 848), a cross-trial comparison with a six-month follow-up study in treatment-resistant depression and with Goodwin et al. (its references 10 and 14), which differ in population, design and comparator; the rates by visit are only in eTable 3 (not read). Sustained here means through day 43, and the authors state that the study cannot show whether the effect would have waned later (p. 850). The authors themselves say blinding was not assessed, that functional unblinding probably contributed to the effect and to the higher niacin dropout, and that the low placebo response with a single niacin dose may have inflated the effect compared with daily-pill antidepressant trials, although in the same paragraph they also argue that niacin may have made the comparator more believable and enhanced the placebo response (p. 849). The Discussion compares its 8% severe adverse-event rate with a 10% rate attributed to Goodwin et al. (p. 849), although its own figure counts drug-related severe events only and the 10% figure does not appear in the main text of Goodwin et al. A headline version (one dose of psilocybin relieves depression for weeks) would overstate: the comparison was with niacin over 6 weeks in a selected, mostly non-treatment-resistant sample, blinding was unassessed, dropout was unequal, and the remission difference was not significant.

timeline.event: Psilocybin versus escitalopram in 59 patients with mainly moderate depression: no significant difference on the self-rated primary outcome at 6 weeks; cited by this paper

Single 25-mg, 10-mg or 1-mg dose in 233 patients with treatment-resistant depression: 25 mg vs 1 mg −6.6 MADRS points at the 3-week primary end point; sustained response at 12 weeks not significant; this paper cites it for a waning effect and contrasts its suicidality findings
Single-dose psilocybin in major depressive disorder with a 2-week primary end point (von Rotz et al., 2022, EClinicalMedicine), described by this paper as having an inactive placebo; not read
Accompanying editorial (JAMA 2023;330:813, named on p. 843; DOI not printed); not read
Correction of 26 January 2024: an author added to the byline and minor typographical errors corrected; the PDF read is the corrected version (p. 851)

replication.where_it_stands: Consistent in direction with Goodwin et al. (2022), in which a single 25-mg dose lowered depression scores more than a 1-mg dose at 3 weeks in treatment-resistant depression, though by less (6.6 MADRS points) and without a significant sustained response at 12 weeks; Carhart-Harris et al. (2021) compared psilocybin with escitalopram rather than a placebo. The single-dose trial by von Rotz et al. (2022) and the accompanying editorial were not read. Durability beyond 6 weeks, the contribution of expectancy and unblinding, and effects in more treatment-resistant and more diverse samples remain open.

The sponsor designed the study and oversaw a contract research organization (Emmes Company) that supervised the study, managed data collection and analysis and provided an initial draft of the Methods and Results; the sponsor interpreted the data, wrote the manuscript and decided to submit it (p. 853).
