William A. Linton is the sponsor's executive director, is listed as a donor to it, and is credited with obtaining funding (p. 852). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Replication in a larger and more diverse sample that includes people with marked treatment resistance, using a control condition with noticeable psychoactive effects or a dose comparison, measuring expectancy before dosing and allocation guesses afterwards, following participants for 6 months or more with all new treatments recorded, and analysing how much of the difference depends on what participants believed they had received.

domains.note: Central randomization through the contract research organization's data system, permuted blocks of random size stratified by site, blinded bottle numbers (pp. 844–845). Baseline differences (first episodes, episode length, tapers) are compatible with chance. One participant randomized to psilocybin received niacin, an administration error analysed by intention to treat.

Identical capsules and an active placebo whose described effect is flushing (p. 845); blinding was not assessed and the authors consider functional unblinding by the acute psychoactive effects of psilocybin likely (p. 849). Few deviations: 3 per group started antidepressants before day 43 (p. 846). Analysis by intention to treat.

Day-43 MADRS missing for 1 of 51 vs 9 of 53 (pp. 846–847); the authors link the higher niacin dropout to unblinding (p. 849), so missingness may relate to the outcome. The mixed model assumes data missing at random; multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses were similar (details in eTable 2, not read). Sustained response and remission were analysed only in participants with every assessment (48 and 44).

Remote central raters blinded to treatment, visit and protocol specifics (p. 845), but the MADRS rests on participants' reports, and participants could probably tell psilocybin from niacin; no blinding check.

The change of primary end point from day 8 to day 43 is reported, with its reason (FDA recommendation), and both results are given; all hierarchical end points are reported, including the non-significant one. The registry record and analysis plan were not read, so this rests on the paper's own statements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Central concealed randomization, identical capsules and remote central raters blinded to treatment and visit make allocation and rater bias unlikely. The concerns all favour psilocybin: blinding was not assessed and the authors consider functional unblinding likely, with a placebo whose described acute effect is flushing; dropout was 2% vs 17%, plausibly related to perceived allocation; and the MADRS rests on participants' reports. They could inflate the 12.3-point difference but are unlikely to remove a difference whose interval ends at 7.2 points; judged some concerns, close to high. The card may be cited for the 6-week MADRS and SDS differences, the sustained-response figures with their completer denominators, and the adverse-event counts; not for durability beyond 6 weeks, nor for people with marked treatment resistance, recent psychedelic use or recent suicidal behaviour.

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, MADRS change from baseline to day 43: −19.1 (95% CI −22.7 to −15.5) with psilocybin (n=51) vs −6.8 (−10.5 to −3.1) with niacin (n=53); difference −12.3 points (95% CI −17.5 to −7.2), P<.001.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MADRS day 43; also Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph (p. 846)

key_findings.finding: Time course of the MADRS difference (psilocybin minus niacin): day 2, −0.1 (95% CI −2.1 to 1.9), P=.95; day 8 (key secondary), −12.0 (−16.6 to −7.4), P<.001, with changes of −17.8 vs −5.8; day 15, −11.1 (−15.8 to −6.3); day 29, −13.7 (−18.6 to −8.8).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MADRS total score rows
key_findings.note: Days 2, 15 and 29 are exploratory. The authors suggest that the absent day-2 difference may reflect the 7-day recall period, kept at day 2 to maintain central-rater blinding, which mostly covered the days before dosing (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 848).

key_findings.finding: Sustained response (at least 50% MADRS reduction at days 8, 15, 29 and 43): 20 of 48 (41.7%) with psilocybin vs 5 of 44 (11.4%) with niacin, difference 30.3 percentage points (13.5 to 47.1), odds ratio 5.60 (1.87 to 16.74), P=.002. Sustained remission (MADRS 10 or less at all four visits): 12 of 48 (25.0%) vs 4 of 44 (9.1%), difference 15.9 (1.0 to 30.8), odds ratio 3.37 (0.99 to 11.47), P=.05, not significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, other secondary outcomes, footnotes d to i; also Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph (p. 846)
key_findings.note: Denominators are participants with MADRS at baseline and every follow-up visit (48 of 51 and 44 of 53), not all randomized.

key_findings.finding: In the per-protocol population of 81 (45 psilocybin, 36 niacin; 5 (10%) and 8 (15%) excluded for major protocol deviations), results were similar, except that sustained remission became significant: 12 of 44 (27%) vs 3 of 36 (8%), difference 18.9% (3.0% to 34.9%), odds ratio 4.0 (1.0 to 15.7), P=.04.
key_findings.locator: Results › Efficacy, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sheehan Disability Scale change at day 43: −4.07 (95% CI −4.88 to −3.26) with psilocybin vs −1.76 (−2.62 to −0.91) with niacin; difference −2.31 (−3.50 to −1.11), P<.001.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, SDS day 43

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal or loss to follow-up by week 6: 1 participant in the psilocybin group and 9 in the niacin group (as randomized); day-43 MADRS was missing for 1 and 9, and day-8 MADRS for 0 and 3. Three participants in each group started antidepressants before day 43 (2 and 1 of them also psychotherapy); no one withdrew because of an adverse event; one participant randomized to psilocybin received niacin.
key_findings.locator: Results › Participants, 2nd paragraph, and Results › Efficacy, 1st paragraph (p. 846); Figure 1 (p. 847)

key_findings.finding: Participants: 104 randomized of 1529 prescreened; mean age 40.4 and 41.8 years; half men; treatment-resistant depression in 7 of 51 (14%) and 6 of 53 (11%), 12.5% overall; median previous pharmacological treatments in the current episode 1 (IQR 0 to 2); baseline MADRS 35.5 and 35.0; previous lifetime psychedelic use 19.6% and 24.5%; first episode 4 (8%) and 10 (19%); White 44 of 51 (86%) and 49 of 51 with data (96%); annual income of 100 000 US dollars or more 23 (51%) and 19 (43%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 846); Table 1 (p. 848)

key_findings.finding: Eligibility required a central-rater MADRS of 28 or more and no more than 30% improvement during a 7-to-35-day lead-in; exclusions included any psychedelic use within 5 years or more than 10 uses in a lifetime, current suicidal ideation with intent or plan, suicidal behaviour within the last 12 months, moderate or severe substance use disorder, psychosis or mania in the person or a first-degree relative, and previous deep brain or vagus nerve stimulation.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adverse events between enrollment and day 43: 44 of 50 (88%) given psilocybin vs 33 of 54 (61%) given niacin. From dosing through day 9, drug-related adverse events affected 41 of 50 (82%) vs 24 of 54 (44%), and severe related events 4 of 50 (8%) vs 0 (migraine, headache, illusion, and panic attack with paranoia, one participant each). No serious adverse events followed dosing; three occurred before randomization (nephrolithiasis, obstructive incisional hernia, appendicitis). From day 10 to day 43, related events affected 2 of 50 (4%) vs 1 of 53 (2%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph (p. 847); Table 3 (p. 851)

key_findings.finding: Solicited adverse events: 38 of 50 (76%) with psilocybin vs 16 of 54 (30%) with niacin; headache 33 of 50 (66%) vs 13 of 54 (24%); nausea 24 of 50 (48%) vs 3 of 54 (6%); visual perceptual effects, assessed after the acute drug effects had resolved, on the dosing day 22 of 50 (44%) vs 3 of 54 (6%), and after the dosing day 3 of 50 (6%) with psilocybin, all resolved by the end of the study. Most solicited events were mild: 73 of 91 events (80%) with psilocybin and 22 of 23 (96%) with niacin.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph (p. 847, continued on p. 848); Table 3 (p. 851)

key_findings.finding: Based on the C-SSRS or MADRS item 10 and confirmed clinically, no suicidal or self-injurious behaviour occurred and all instances of suicidal ideation were considered passive; C-SSRS suicidal ideation scores rose from baseline to the end of the trial in 1 participant receiving psilocybin and 5 receiving niacin (eTables 10–11, not read). No clinically significant changes in vital signs or laboratory tests were observed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph (p. 847, continued on p. 848)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the success of blinding was not assessed and that the acute effects of psilocybin probably caused some functional unblinding that may have contributed to the observed effect and to the higher dropout with niacin (1st paragraph). On the placebo response they argue both ways (2nd paragraph): niacin may have made the comparator more believable and enhanced the placebo response, which matched that to a low-dose psilocybin comparator in treatment-resistant depression and exceeded that to an inactive placebo in a recent trial in major depression; yet the placebo response, smaller than with daily placebo pills, may have inflated the placebo-adjusted effect compared with studies of standard antidepressants.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: No minimal clinically important difference was prespecified; the Discussion argues clinical significance afterwards, noting that the 12.3-point difference exceeds an upper active-placebo difference of 9 points in the literature and that the 19.1-point change in the psilocybin group exceeds a 12-point threshold for substantial improvement in treatment-resistant depression.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Efficacy Assessments, 1st paragraph (p. 845); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 848)
key_findings.note: Editors' note: the lower 95% confidence limit of the difference, 7.2 points (Table 2, p. 849), is below the 9-point value, so the comparison rests on the point estimate. No such argument is made for the Sheehan Disability Scale, for which the Methods state that no MCID is defined for active versus control comparisons (p. 845).

key_findings.finding: The FDA first recommended day 8 as the primary end point, and the study was powered on assumed MADRS changes of 18 points (day 8) and 17 points (day 43) with psilocybin and 10 with niacin, SD 10, giving 92% power for day 43 and 98% for day 8 with 100 participants; after the FDA recommended day 43, the primary end point was changed and the sample size increased from 80 to 100.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Individual changes overlapped between groups: in Figure 2B some participants given psilocybin changed little and some given niacin improved markedly (editors' reading of a 300-dpi crop, approximate: median change about −19 with psilocybin, interquartile range about −30 to −9; about −5 with niacin, interquartile range about −15 to +1).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2B, box plots and individual-participant panel
key_findings.note: Raw changes in participants with a day-43 assessment; values not printed in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the difference in drug-related adverse events from dosing to day 9 as 38% with a 95% CI of 20.6% to 41.3%, whereas Table 3 gives 38 (20.6 to 54.6); 41.3 is the upper limit printed in Table 3 for any adverse event.
reporting_issues.consequence: Transcription error in the text; Table 3 is correct (an editors' Wald calculation from 41 of 50 and 24 of 54 gives 20.6 to 54.6).

reporting_issues.issue: The relative incidences printed in the text for drug-related adverse events from dosing to day 9 do not fit the counts: any related event 1.8 (95% CI 1.3 to 1.8), mild 1.8 (1.1 to 1.8) and moderate 2.3 (1.0 to 5.7). Upper limits equal to the point estimate are impossible for a Wald interval on the ratio scale, and 11 of 50 vs 2 of 54 is not a ratio of 2.3. Editors' Wald calculation from the counts: 1.84 (1.33 to 2.55), 1.83 (1.30 to 2.58) and 5.94 (1.38 to 25.5); the printed relative incidences for solicited events, headache and nausea do match their counts.
reporting_issues.consequence: The relative incidences for related, mild and moderate events should not be cited as printed; the counts and percentage differences, which are consistent with Table 3, can be.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CIs of the differences for headache and nausea are interchanged, in the text and in Table 3: headache 42% (27.3% to 57.6%) and nausea 42% (24.5% to 59.3%). Editors' Wald calculation from 33 of 50 vs 13 of 54 gives 24.5 to 59.3 for headache, and from 24 of 50 vs 3 of 54 gives 27.3 to 57.6 for nausea.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both differences remain clearly above zero.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the differences in sustained response (30.3) and remission (15.9) adjusted absolute differences, but they equal the raw differences of the printed counts, and the Table 2 footnote describes them as Wald intervals. For remission, the interval of the difference (1.0 to 30.8) excludes zero while the adjusted odds ratio interval (0.99 to 11.47) includes 1, with P=.05. The per-protocol remission difference, also called adjusted (18.9%, 95% CI 3.0% to 34.9%; p. 847), likewise equals the raw Wald difference from 12 of 44 vs 3 of 36.
reporting_issues.consequence: The remission result is borderline and was correctly treated as not significant in the testing sequence; the percentage-point differences are unadjusted (editors' recalculation from 20 of 48 vs 5 of 44, 12 of 48 vs 4 of 44 and 12 of 44 vs 3 of 36 reproduces all three intervals).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 footnote c refers to a median MADRS (a total-sample median of 35.5), but the row reports group means (35.5 and 35.0). The same footnote states minimal clinically important differences from baseline, that is, within-group improvements of 6 MADRS points and 1.33 SDS points, whereas the Methods say no MCID was prespecified for the MADRS, citing 6 points only as a literature value for change from pretreatment, and that none is defined for active versus control comparisons on the SDS. The values agree; the footnote presents them as if defined for the trial.
reporting_issues.consequence: The thresholds are within-group literature values applied after the fact, not prespecified criteria, and cannot show that a difference between groups is clinically important (the niacin group's day-43 SDS change, −1.76, also exceeds 1.33; Table 2, p. 849); the total-sample median is not otherwise reported.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 1, the box for the 17 niacin participants excluded from the per-protocol analysis carries footnote b (the misallocated participant) instead of footnote c (reasons for exclusion). The text gives 5 (10%) and 8 (15%) excluded for major protocol deviations, whereas Figure 1 shows 6 and 17 excluded in total; the remainder are presumably those with missing day-8 or day-43 MADRS, as footnote c implies, but this is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling issue; the per-protocol population is 45 and 36 in both places.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion compares the 8% rate of severe adverse events with psilocybin with a 10% rate attributed to Goodwin et al. for a single 25-mg dose. The 8% here counts drug-related severe events: 4 of 50 from dosing to day 9, the same count as from enrollment to day 43 (Table 3, which gives severity only for drug-related events).
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a like-for-like comparison: the main text of Goodwin et al. reports severe adverse events of any relation by period (3 of 79, 4%, on day 1; 7 of 79, 9%, from day 2 to week 3; 2 of 79, 3%, after week 3; Goodwin et al., pp. 1644 and 1646) and gives no whole-trial 10% figure.

design_detail: Double-blind, randomized, parallel-group trial at two US academic centres (University of New Mexico, recruiting March 2014 to May 2015; New York University, July 2015 to March 2020), registered as ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02061293. 95 adults with DSM-IV alcohol dependence and at least 4 heavy drinking days in the 30 days before screening were randomized 1:1 to psilocybin (n=49) or diphenhydramine as an active placebo (n=46), given in two 8-hour sessions at weeks 4 and 8 within 12 sessions of manualized psychotherapy (motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy) from a team of two therapists including a licensed psychiatrist. Primary outcome: percentage of heavy drinking days by timeline follow-back over the 32 weeks after the first dose (weeks 5–36), analysed by multivariate repeated-measures ANOVA with multiple imputation in the 93 who received medication. Planned for up to 180 participants; enrolment stopped at 95 when COVID-19 suspended recruitment. Only the double-blind phase is reported; an open-label psilocybin session offered at week 38 is not (pp. 953–955).
can_establish: That, among 93 adults with alcohol dependence who all received the same psychotherapy, those randomized to psilocybin reported fewer heavy drinking days over the following 32 weeks than those randomized to diphenhydramine, and that there were no serious adverse events in the psilocybin group.
cannot_establish: How much of the difference is due to the drug rather than to expectation, since about 94% of participants and 92–97% of therapists correctly identified the medication; whether the effect lasts beyond week 36; whether it holds for more severe alcohol use disorder, psychiatric comorbidity or settings without careful screening and two therapists; or what the psychotherapy itself contributes (both groups received it).

sample.recruitment: Community volunteers recruited through advertisements in local media; 569 screened by telephone, 172 in person, 110 qualified, 15 withdrew before randomization, 95 randomized (Figure 1, p. 956; Participants, p. 954). Participants were paid up to $560 for completing assessments but not for attending therapy or medication sessions (p. 954).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 25 to 65; DSM-IV alcohol dependence by structured clinical interview; at least 4 heavy drinking days (5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) in the 30 days before screening. Excluded: major psychiatric and drug use disorders, any hallucinogen use in the past year or more than 25 lifetime uses, medical contraindications to either medication, exclusionary medications, and current treatment for alcohol use disorder (p. 954).
sample.demographics: Mean age 45.8 (SD 11.6); 42 women (44.2%); 75 non-Hispanic White (78.9%), 14 Hispanic (14.7%), 4 Black (4.2%), 3 Asian (3.2%), 1 American Indian or Alaska Native (1.1%); median household income $100,000. A mean of 5.3 of 7 dependence criteria, 14.2 years of dependence; in the 12 weeks before screening, drinking on 74.9% of days, heavy drinking on 52.7% and 7.1 drinks per drinking day (Table 1, p. 957; p. 956).
sample.attrition: 93 of 95 received medication (one per group did not, for elevated blood pressure) and were analysed. Second medication session: 43 of 48 given psilocybin vs 35 of 45 given diphenhydramine (declined by personal preference: 4 vs 10; one more psilocybin session prevented by COVID-19 restrictions). 46 of 48 psilocybin and 42 of 45 diphenhydramine participants completed 8 months of follow-up; valid drinking data for 717 of 744 participant-months (96.4%) (Figure 1, p. 956; p. 957).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers willing to take psilocybin, without major psychiatric comorbidity or other drug use disorders, mostly White and with relatively high incomes; the authors note they drank less intensely at screening than participants in most alcohol-medication trials (p. 960). By chance the psilocybin group drank more at baseline (heavy drinking days 57.20% vs 47.93%; very high WHO risk 36.7% vs 26.1%) (Table 1, p. 957); the analysis adjusted for drinking in weeks 1–4.

exposure.measurement: Study medication in a single opaque capsule of unvarying appearance and weight, randomized and assigned by a site pharmacist (p. 955); psilocybin provided by the Usona Institute, Nicholas Cozzi and David Nichols (p. 954).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: at week 4, psilocybin 25 mg/70 kg or diphenhydramine 50 mg by mouth; at week 8, if there were no dose-limiting adverse events and the participant agreed, psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg (if the first session's Mystical Experience Questionnaire total was at least 0.6) or 40 mg/70 kg (if below 0.6), or diphenhydramine 100 mg (p. 955). Actual second-session doses: psilocybin 25 mg/70 kg (n=1), 30 (n=27), 40 (n=15); diphenhydramine 50 mg (n=11), 100 mg (n=24); mean absolute psilocybin dose 28.3 mg (range 19.3–40.0) in session 1 and 37.7 mg (range 24.1–64.5) in session 2 (p. 957). Sessions: medication at about 9 am, at least 8 hours in the session room with the therapists, lying on a couch with eyeshades and headphones playing a standardized playlist; medications for hypertension, severe anxiety or psychotic symptoms were available (p. 955).
exposure.polysubstance: Major drug use disorders and recent or frequent hallucinogen use were exclusions (p. 954); use of other substances during the trial is not reported in the main text.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants tried to stop drinking in preparation for the first medication session (p. 958); drinking during follow-up is the outcome.

comparison.controls: Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine, as active placebo, with the same 12 psychotherapy sessions and the same session procedures (pp. 954–955).
comparison.matching: Randomization stratified by site in balanced blocks of varying size; sequence generated and treatment assigned by a study pharmacist at each site (p. 955).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations about psilocybin were not measured at baseline; prior hallucinogen use was limited by the exclusion criteria (p. 954).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same exclusion criteria as the psilocybin group.

outcomes.instruments: Timeline follow-back interview at weeks 8, 12, 24 and 36 (one standard drink = 14 g of ethanol); ethyl glucuronide (EtG) in hair or fingernail samples at week 24 to check self-reported abstinence; Short Index of Problems (SIP-2R) at baseline and weeks 12, 24 and 36; States of Consciousness Questionnaire, including the 43-item Mystical Experience Questionnaire, after each session; blood pressure and heart rate every 30–60 minutes for 6 hours; adverse events solicited at each assessment and coded with MedDRA; participants' and therapists' guesses of the medication with a 0–100 certainty scale (p. 955).
outcomes.validity_norms: The timeline follow-back is described as a reliable, valid calendar method and the standard outcome measure in alcohol trials (p. 955); EtG was used only as a check on reported abstinence (p. 957).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: percentage of heavy drinking days (5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) during weeks 5–36. Secondary: percentage of drinking days, drinks per day, and dichotomous outcomes: abstinence (WHO risk level 0), no heavy drinking days, and a fall of 1, 2 or 3 WHO risk levels relative to the 12 weeks before screening (pp. 954–955; Table 3 notes, p. 959).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors say analyses of secondary outcomes should be considered exploratory (p. 955). Main text: 3 continuous drinking outcomes, 5 dichotomous outcomes each in two periods, and the total problems score; further problem categories and adverse-event tables are in Supplement 2, not read.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: By design all staff except the pharmacists, and all participants, were blind (p. 955). In practice participants guessed their medication correctly after 93.6% of first and 94.7% of second sessions, and therapists after 92.4% and 97.4% (p. 957). The outcome is the participant's own report of drinking.

analysis.effect_sizes: Weeks 5–36, psilocybin vs diphenhydramine (48 vs 45): heavy drinking days 9.71% vs 23.57%, difference 13.86 percentage points (95% CI 3.00–24.72), Hedges g 0.52 (0.11–0.94), p=0.01; drinking days 29.39% vs 42.83%, difference 13.44 (−0.18 to 27.05), g 0.40, p=0.05; drinks per day 1.17 vs 2.26, difference 1.09 (0.27–1.92), g 0.54, p=0.01 (Table 2, p. 958). Dichotomous outcomes: numbers needed to treat 4.0 to 8.2, odds ratios 2.03 to 4.74 (Table 3, p. 959). Problems at week 36: 6.59 vs 13.00, difference 6.4 (2.22–10.60), g 0.67 (p. 958).
analysis.covariates: Site, site-by-treatment and treatment-by-assessment terms, and each outcome's value in weeks 1–4 (the 4 weeks before the first dose); missing monthly values imputed by multivariate imputation by chained equations (p. 955).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02061293 (p. 953); protocol and statistical analysis plan in Supplement 1, not among the files. The registry record was not read, so registered and reported outcomes were not compared. The paper itself gives the primary outcome window as weeks 5 to 32 in the Methods (p. 955) and weeks 5–36 everywhere else.
analysis.selective_reporting: Primary and secondary outcomes are all reported with intervals. The primary test is a multivariate test across three drinking outcomes (F1,86=6.18, p=0.02), from which the heavy-drinking-day contrast was decomposed (p. 958); the abstract reports a univariate F (6.43) that does not appear in the Results.
analysis.power: Designed for up to 180 participants, with an interim sample-size re-estimation planned at 100 to give power 0.8 for a small to moderate effect (f² = 0.16); enrolment stopped at 95 when COVID-19 suspended recruitment on 19 March 2020 (p. 955).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 93 people with alcohol dependence who were all offered 12 psychotherapy sessions (attending a mean of 11.75 and 11.47), those given psilocybin reported heavy drinking on 9.7% of days over 32 weeks against 23.6% with diphenhydramine (difference 13.9 percentage points, 95% CI 3.0 to 24.7). Both groups had already cut their heavy drinking days by more than half before any medication, and about 94% of participants and nearly all therapists knew which drug had been given.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Key Points say psilocybin with psychotherapy “produced robust decreases in percentage of heavy drinking days” beyond active placebo and psychotherapy (pp. 953–954) and describe a double-blind trial without mentioning that the blind failed. The Discussion is more careful, saying psilocybin was associated with improved drinking, listing the failure of diphenhydramine to maintain the blind as the first limitation and noting that biased expectancies could have influenced the results (p. 960). The lower end of the interval, 3 percentage points, is compatible with a small effect, so “robust” is stronger than the estimate. A headline such as “psilocybin cut heavy drinking by 83%” overstates it: that is the psilocybin group's change from screening, most of which also happened with placebo and much of it before any medication was given (editors' calculation from Table 2: heavy drinking days 56.48% to 9.71% with psilocybin, 48.57% to 23.57% with diphenhydramine).

timeline.event: Meta-analysis of 6 randomized trials of LSD for alcohol dependence published 1966–1971 (Krebs and Johansen, 2012), described by the authors as showing remission nearly twice as often as with comparators (odds ratio 1.96, 95% CI 1.36–2.84) (p. 954); not read.
Single-arm psilocybin pilot for smoking cessation from another group, cited among earlier work.

Open-label proof-of-concept study of psilocybin in alcohol dependence (Bogenschutz et al., 2015), described by the authors as showing doses of 21 to 28 mg/70 kg were well tolerated, with large reductions in drinking over 32 weeks (p. 954); not read.
A feasibility randomized trial of psilocybin in alcohol use disorder with depressive symptoms (Luquiens et al., 2025) is on the project's psilocybin list; not read in this round.

replication.where_it_stands: The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first controlled trial of psilocybin for alcohol use disorder (p. 960). No independent replication was among the sources read in this round. The open questions are blinding and expectancy, durability beyond 36 weeks, objective confirmation of drinking, and effects in more severe or comorbid alcohol use disorder.

what_would_settle_it: A larger trial run by an independent group, with an active comparator that participants cannot easily tell from psilocybin (or a design that measures and adjusts for expectancy), blinding checked in participants and raters, drinking verified objectively in every participant at repeated time points, follow-up beyond a year, and a psychotherapy-only arm to separate the drug from the therapy.

domains.note: Site-stratified randomization in balanced blocks of varying size, generated and assigned by a pharmacist. Baseline differences (the psilocybin group drank more) are compatible with chance, and the analysis adjusted for drinking in the 4 weeks before the first dose.

Participants and therapists were functionally unblinded (about 94% and 92–97% correct guesses). More participants given diphenhydramine declined the second session (10 of 45 vs 4 of 48, by personal preference), which may reflect knowing they had placebo; psychotherapy attendance was similar (11.75 vs 11.47 of 12 sessions). Analysing all who received medication (93 of 95) is appropriate.

Valid drinking data for 96.4% of participant-months, with multiple imputation for the rest; the 2 randomized participants not analysed (one per group) never received medication. The diphenhydramine group's count of missing months does not reconcile with Figure 1; the psilocybin group's is compatible (see reporting issues).

The primary outcome is self-reported drinking from participants who almost all knew their allocation and had volunteered for a psilocybin trial. EtG was available for only 50 of 93 at a single time point and could check only reported abstinence (14 of 14 negative).

Registered, with protocol and analysis plan in a supplement not read; the primary outcome window is stated inconsistently (weeks 5 to 32 in the Methods, 5–36 elsewhere), and the primary test is a multivariate test across three outcomes, with the heavy-drinking-day contrast decomposed from it.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomization, retention and analysis are strong, and the difference in reported heavy drinking days is of a size that would matter clinically, but the primary outcome is self-reported by participants who overwhelmingly knew whether they had received psilocybin, with only partial biochemical corroboration. The card may be cited for the observed between-group difference in self-reported drinking with its interval, for the blinding-failure figures, for the large improvement in both groups before any medication, and for the adverse events in a screened trial population; it may not be cited for a blinded estimate of psilocybin's pharmacological effect, for effects beyond 36 weeks, or for more severe or comorbid alcohol use disorder.

key_findings.finding: Over the 32 weeks after the first dose, heavy drinking days made up 9.71% of days in the psilocybin group and 23.57% in the diphenhydramine group (48 vs 45 participants): a difference of 13.86 percentage points (95% CI 3.00–24.72; Hedges g 0.52, 95% CI 0.11–0.94; p=0.01). The authors express this as the psilocybin group's rate being 41% of the placebo group's.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and Results › Efficacy › Continuous Drinking Outcomes (p. 958); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 960)
key_findings.note: Figure 2A's weeks 5–36 inset reads about 21.9% vs 9.2% rather than Table 2's 23.57% vs 9.71%, and the paper does not say whether Table 2's follow-up means are observed or model-estimated (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Before any medication, from screening to weeks 1–4, while attending four therapy sessions and trying to stop drinking, both groups cut heavy drinking days sharply: by 32.37 percentage points in those later given psilocybin (from 56.48% to 24.11%; g 1.08) and by 27.26 points in those later given diphenhydramine (from 48.57% to 21.31%; g 1.02). The paper reports this fall under the heading Changes in Drinking Prior to Randomization, and Figure 1 lists 4 people who began therapy but withdrew before randomization, so allocation apparently followed these weeks of therapy; when randomization took place is not stated.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 956); Table 2 and Results › Changes in Drinking Prior to Randomization (p. 958)

key_findings.finding: Secondary, exploratory and uncorrected: drinking days 29.39% vs 42.83% (difference 13.44, 95% CI −0.18 to 27.05; p=0.05); drinks per day 1.17 vs 2.26 (difference 1.09, 95% CI 0.27–1.92; g 0.54; p=0.01); total drinking-related problems at week 36, using all available data, 6.59 vs 13.00 (difference 6.4, 95% CI 2.22–10.60; g 0.67; p=0.003).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Efficacy › Dichotomous Drinking Outcomes and Problems Related To Drinking

key_findings.finding: No heavy drinking days at all during weeks 5–36: 16 of 48 (33.3%) with psilocybin vs 5 of 45 (11.1%) with diphenhydramine (odds ratio 4.0, 95% CI 1.32–12.10; number needed to treat 4.5). No drinking at all in weeks 5–36: 11 of 48 (22.9%) vs 4 of 45 (8.9%) (odds ratio 3.05, 0.89–10.40; p=0.06). In the final month (weeks 33–36): abstinent 23 of 48 (47.9%) vs 11 of 45 (24.4%) (odds ratio 2.84, 1.17–6.89); no heavy drinking 30 of 48 (62.5%) vs 18 of 45 (40.0%) (odds ratio 2.5, 1.08–5.76). Nominal p values, no correction for multiple comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: The between-group gap in heavy drinking days stayed at roughly 16 to 18 percentage points from weeks 5–8 through weeks 17–20 and narrowed afterwards, to about 9 points in the last two months; no monthly numbers are printed (editors' reading of Figure 2A–B, approximate: heavy drinking days about 4% vs 20% in weeks 5–8, about 11% vs 29% in weeks 17–20, about 17% vs 29% in weeks 25–28 and about 9% vs 18% in weeks 33–36; drinking days about 40% vs 46% in weeks 25–28).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2A–B
key_findings.note: Values read from 300-dpi crops of Figure 2 (estimated monthly means with SE). Marker positions measured at 300 dpi give gaps of about 16, 16, 16, 18, 14, 12, 9 and 9 points from weeks 5–8 to weeks 33–36, so the gap was not widest just after dosing; the screening markers reproduce Table 2 within 0.1 point.

key_findings.finding: Blinding failed: participants guessed their medication correctly after 93.6% of first sessions (mean certainty 88.5%) and 94.7% of second sessions (90.6%); therapists guessed correctly after 92.4% and 97.4% (mean certainty 92.8% and 95.4%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinding Integrity
key_findings.note: Percentages as printed; the paper gives no counts or denominators, and three of the four fit no whole count of the 93 first or 78 second sessions (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Mean Mystical Experience Questionnaire scores (0–1 scale) were 0.59 with psilocybin vs 0.10 with diphenhydramine after session 1, and 0.64 vs 0.11 after session 2 (both p<0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute Effects › Subjective Effects

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events: none in the psilocybin group; three in the diphenhydramine group, all during binge drinking (one participant admitted to hospital twice for suicidal ideation reported during binges; one hospitalized for a Mallory-Weiss tear from severe vomiting). Total adverse events over 32 weeks: 119 in the psilocybin group and 85 in the diphenhydramine group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within 48 hours of dosing, headache occurred in 21 of 48 participants given psilocybin (43.8%) vs 2 of 45 given diphenhydramine (4.4%); anxiety and nausea were also reported more frequently during psilocybin sessions. Two participants given psilocybin received oral diazepam for anxiety during their second session (resolved within 45 and 210 minutes); one participant assigned to psilocybin reported passive suicidal ideation for 15 minutes during a session, which resolved without sequelae; no persistent disturbances suggesting psychosis or hallucinogen persisting perception disorder.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Psilocybin raised systolic and diastolic blood pressure relative to diphenhydramine, but no participant reported symptoms or was treated for hypertension; blood pressure was no longer significantly raised by 360 minutes, and heart rate was higher until about 300 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute Effects › Cardiovascular Effects

key_findings.finding: Objective checks of drinking were limited: EtG results were available for 50 of 93 participants (53.8%), missing mainly because of telephone visits (24) or insufficient hair (12); the 14 of these 50 who reported total abstinence on the week-24 timeline all tested negative (below 8 pg/ng). 63 of 337 follow-up timeline interviews (18.7%) were done by phone. By the authors' report, participants missing EtG data did not differ from the others on baseline drinking measures, age, race, ethnicity or sex (no values shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Exposure and Retention, 2nd paragraph; Convergent Validity of Self-report and EtG

key_findings.finding: 43 of 48 given psilocybin (89.6%) and 35 of 45 given diphenhydramine (77.8%) had the second medication session (F1,91=2.40, p=0.13); 10 in the diphenhydramine group and 4 in the psilocybin group declined it by personal preference. Psychotherapy attendance was similar: 11.75 vs 11.47 of 12 sessions.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 956); Results › Treatment Exposure and Retention, 1st paragraph (begins p. 956, continues p. 957)

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give the prespecified primary outcome as heavy drinking days during weeks 5 to 32 and list the last monthly bin as weeks 32 to 36 (p. 955), while the abstract, analysis, tables and Figure 2 use weeks 5–36 and a last bin of weeks 33–36 (pp. 953, 958–959).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably typographical, but the registered outcome window cannot be confirmed without the registry record or protocol, which were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text prints the heavy-drinking-day SD as 26.21 for both groups (p. 958), while Table 2 gives 26.21 for psilocybin and 26.67 for diphenhydramine (p. 958).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 2 is presumably right, but the printed Hedges g does not settle it, since 0.52 is reproduced with either SD (editors' calculation: 0.520 with Table 2's SDs, 0.524 with 26.21 for both groups).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives F1,86 = 6.43 for the heavy-drinking-day contrast (p. 953); this statistic does not appear in the Results, which report the multivariate F1,86 = 6.18, P = .02 and only P = .01 for the univariate contrast (p. 958).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's F cannot be checked against the body of the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The diphenhydramine group's missing participant-months do not reconcile with Figure 1. The text reports 351 of 360 valid months in the diphenhydramine group (9 missing) and 366 of 384 in the psilocybin group (18 missing) (p. 957); Figure 1 shows two diphenhydramine participants followed for 5 months and one for 1 month, at least 13 missing months (editors' calculation), more than the 9 reported. In the psilocybin group one participant followed for 5 months and one with no drinking data account for at least 11 missing months, which is compatible with the 18 reported (p. 956).
reporting_issues.consequence: The discrepancy is a few months out of 744 and missing values were imputed, so the effect on the estimate is probably small, but it is unexplained.

reporting_issues.issue: The blinding results are printed as percentages only, with no counts or denominators (p. 957). Three of the four fit no whole count of the 93 first or 78 second sessions: participants' 93.6% (first sessions) and 94.7% (second) and therapists' 92.4% (first); only the therapists' 97.4% (second sessions) fits a whole count (editors' calculation; the same holds if each of the two therapists guessed separately).
reporting_issues.consequence: Some guesses were apparently not collected, or the figures are misprinted; how many guesses were assessed is unknown, so the percentages are recorded as printed and no counts are derived from them.

reporting_issues.issue: How participants with missing months were classified for the dichotomous outcomes is not described; Table 3 uses all 45 and 48 treated participants as denominators, including one psilocybin participant who provided no drinking data (pp. 956, 959).
reporting_issues.consequence: The odds ratios and numbers needed to treat may depend on an imputation or classification rule that is not stated in the main text.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints identical results for a fall of 2 WHO risk levels in weeks 5–36 and in weeks 33–36 (18 of 45 vs 29 of 48, odds ratio 2.29, P = .049) (p. 959).
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly correct, but it may be a duplicated row; it cannot be checked without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 2B the bar chart for weeks 5–36 is labelled heavy drinking days although the panel shows the percentage of drinking days (p. 959).
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling error only; the values correspond to drinking days (Table 2).

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2A's weeks 5–36 inset bars, which the caption does not describe separately (it calls the figure's values mean (SE) estimates), read about 21.9% heavy drinking days with diphenhydramine and 9.2% with psilocybin (editors' reading at 300 dpi), below Table 2's 23.57% and 9.71%, a difference of about 12.7 against 13.86 points; the panel B and C insets lie within 1 percentage point and 0.04 drinks of Table 2. The paper does not say whether Table 2's follow-up means are observed or model-estimated (pp. 958–959).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two presentations of the primary outcome differ by up to 1.7 points, and it is not stated whether Table 2's means and their 13.86-point difference are observed or model-estimated; the discrepancy is small beside the interval (3.00 to 24.72).

design_detail: Double-blind randomized crossover trial with an active comparator at Johns Hopkins, Baltimore. 36 hallucinogen-naive adults who took part regularly in religious or spiritual activities were randomly assigned to two sessions (n=30) or three sessions (n=6). The 30 received psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg and methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg by mouth in counterbalanced random order (15 per order), in individual 8-hour sessions 2 months apart. The other 6 received methylphenidate twice and then open-label psilocybin: a decoy arm meant to obscure the design, whose data were left out of the statistical analyses. Monitor ratings, blood pressure and heart rate during sessions; questionnaires on drug effects and mystical experience about 7 hours after the capsule; questionnaires and ratings by three community observers about 2 months after each session (pp. 269–274).
can_establish: That in 30 carefully screened, hallucinogen-naive, religiously or spiritually active volunteers, psilocybin given in a supportive one-person setting produced much higher scores on mystical-experience questionnaires than an active stimulant comparator, and that 2 months later these volunteers rated the psilocybin session as more personally meaningful and spiritually significant and attributed more positive change to it.
cannot_establish: Whether these effects occur in people not selected for spiritual practice, health and education, or outside this preparation and setting; how much is due to expectancy (participants knew psilocybin would come in at least one session, and their own blinding was never assessed); whether self-attributed lasting change is real change in behaviour (standardized personality and affect measures showed no difference); or how safe the dose is in general (36 screened volunteers).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: flyers in the local community announcing a study of states of consciousness brought about by a naturally occurring psychoactive substance used sacramentally in some cultures. 135 people screened by telephone, 54 in person, 36 enrolled; no monetary compensation; motivation described as curiosity about psilocybin and the chance for self-reflection (p. 269).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Hallucinogen-naive adults, medically and psychiatrically healthy, without family history of schizophrenia, other psychotic disorders or bipolar I or II disorder, all reporting at least intermittent participation in religious or spiritual activities such as services, prayer or meditation (p. 269).
sample.demographics: 14 men (22 women by subtraction); mean age 46 (range 24–64); 35 (97%) college graduates and 20 (56%) with postgraduate degrees; 30 (83%) employed full time; 19 (53%) affiliated with a religious or spiritual community; 20 (56%) reported daily and 14 (39%) at least monthly religious or spiritual activities (p. 269).
sample.attrition: No withdrawals are reported. Analyses used the 30 crossover participants. The 2-month Persisting Effects Questionnaire, which carries the meaningfulness ratings, exists for only 24 of the 30 (12 per order) because it was introduced after the study had begun; community-observer data were analysed for 26 of the 30 (pp. 273–274).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers answered an advertisement framed around sacramental use; all were religiously or spiritually active, highly educated, middle-aged and unpaid (p. 269). The authors note that their religious or spiritual interest may have made a spiritual and meaningful reading of the experience more likely, and that the effect of being hallucinogen-naive is unknown (p. 281). The results describe this group, not the general population or people who use psilocybin outside research.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered drugs: psilocybin synthesized by David Nichols (Acknowledgements, p. 282) and methylphenidate, in identical opaque size-0 gelatin capsules taken with about 180 ml water (p. 270). A urine sample was taken on each session morning to verify drug-free status (p. 270).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg and methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg by mouth, one drug per session, sessions 2 months apart. The authors chose the psilocybin dose as a high dose they judged safe from 1950s–1960s studies, and the methylphenidate dose as a high, discriminable dose with a similar time course and some overlapping effects (p. 270). Setting: 8-hour individual sessions in a living-room-like room with two monitors; participants were encouraged to lie on a couch with an eye mask and headphones playing the same classical music programme, and to attend to their inner experience; monitors gave verbal or physical reassurance (such as a touch on the hand) when a participant reported fear or anxiety. Preparation: four meetings with the primary monitor (8 hours in total) before the first session and four (4 hours) after each session (p. 270).
exposure.polysubstance: No personal history of hallucinogen use (p. 269); urine checked for drug-free status on session mornings (p. 270); other alcohol, tobacco or drug use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Urine sample on the morning of each session to verify drug-free status (p. 270); results not reported.

comparison.controls: Within-person comparison with methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg, an active stimulant chosen because its onset and duration resemble psilocybin's and some of its effects (excitability, nervousness, raised mood) overlap (p. 270). Same participants, room, monitors and preparation.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with drug order assigned at random (15 per order). For the lifetime and personality measures the two order groups did not differ significantly at screening (values not shown) (p. 278).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations and beliefs about psilocybin were not measured. Participants and monitors were told that at least one session would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin (p. 270), and the monitors' preparation conveyed their expectation that sessions could increase personal awareness and insight (p. 270).

outcomes.instruments: During sessions (10 minutes before and 30–360 minutes after the capsule): blood pressure, heart rate and a 20-item monitor rating questionnaire (mean of the two monitors). About 7 hours after the capsule: Hallucinogen Rating Scale (99 items), APZ (72 items), Addiction Research Center Inventory short form (49 items), States of Consciousness Questionnaire (100 items, 43 of which form the Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire) and the 32-item Hood Mysticism Scale. At 2 months: Persisting Effects Questionnaire (89 items, including three questions on personal meaning, spiritual significance and change in well-being or life satisfaction), Mysticism Scale–Lifetime, Spiritual Transcendence Scale, NEO PI-R, PANAS-X, and ratings by three adults nominated by each participant (structured telephone interview, 11 dimensions on 1–10 scales) (pp. 271–273).
outcomes.validity_norms: The mystical-experience questionnaires come from the psychology of religion and rest on Stace's descriptive account of mystical experience (pp. 271–272). The Mysticism Scale had not previously been used to measure change after a drug experience (p. 272). The Persisting Effects Questionnaire was written for this study and introduced after it had started (p. 273).
outcomes.operationalization: “Mystical” means questionnaire scores. A “complete” mystical experience was defined in advance, after Pahnke, as a score of at least 0.6 of the maximum on each of six States of Consciousness scales: unity (internal or external, whichever higher), transcendence of time and space, ineffability, sacredness, noetic quality and positive mood (p. 272). Personal meaning was rated from 1 (no more than routine, everyday experiences) to 8 (the single most meaningful experience of my life); spiritual significance from 1 (not at all) to 6 (the single most spiritually significant experience of my life); change in well-being from −3 to +3 (pp. 272–273).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. At least 57 psilocybin–methylphenidate comparisons in Tables 1–4 (20 monitor ratings, 14 drug-effect subscales, 11 mysticism scales, 12 two-month ratings), plus the cardiovascular time courses, NEO PI-R, PANAS-X and the two lifetime scales, all by paired or unpaired t tests without adjustment (p. 274).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and monitors were blind by design, and the decoy arm and instructions (sessions without a moderate or high psilocybin dose might bring placebo, a low psilocybin dose or one of 11 other drugs) were used to obscure the design (pp. 270–271). Participants were not asked to guess what they had received; the monitors guessed after each session and misclassified 23% of sessions, mostly calling methylphenidate psilocybin (pp. 271, 274). Community raters were told nothing about the participant by the interviewer, and 60% of interviews were done by an assistant who had never met the participant, but raters were told their own previous ratings (p. 273).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes, confidence intervals, test statistics or exact p values are reported; tables give means with SEM and p thresholds only. Editors' calculation (between-condition standardized difference with SD = SEM × √n, ignoring the within-person pairing, so approximate): Mysticism Scale total about 1.41 (N=30); personal meaningfulness about 2.18 (N=24); community-observer positive change about 0.70 (N=26).
analysis.covariates: None. Paired t tests for the within-person contrasts; for the lifetime, personality and affect measures, planned t tests between the order groups at screening and 2 months after session 1, and a paired t test within the methylphenidate-first group (p. 274).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned in the paper; registries were not searched in this round.
analysis.selective_reporting: The study-design paragraph lists measures of psychiatric symptoms and quality of life before and 2 months after each session (p. 270), but no such results are reported. The Persisting Effects Questionnaire was added after the study had started, with its scoring categories fixed before data analysis (pp. 272–273). Null results for the NEO PI-R and PANAS-X are reported in the Results (p. 278) but not in the abstract.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 30 selected volunteers, psilocybin produced much higher mystical-experience questionnaire scores than methylphenidate (in the blinded sessions 19 of 30 met the a priori “complete” criteria, editors' sum); at 2 months, 16 of 24 rated it among the five most meaningful experiences of their lives (2 of 24 said so of methylphenidate) and attributed positive changes to it; community observers rated small positive changes; personality and affect inventories did not change; 11 of 36 reported strong or extreme fear.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says volunteers attributed sustained positive changes in attitudes and behaviour to the experience, consistent with changes rated by community observers, and concludes that under supportive conditions psilocybin occasioned experiences similar to spontaneous mystical experiences (p. 268). These statements are worded as the volunteers' ratings and attributions and match the Results, but the abstract does not mention that the NEO PI-R and PANAS-X showed no difference (p. 278), that 11 of 36 rated their fear strong or extreme (p. 278), or that only the monitors, never the participants, were asked to guess the drug. The Results conclude that “the blinding procedures overall were adequately maintained” (p. 274), resting on the monitors' beliefs about the design, although monitors recognized most psilocybin sessions. The Discussion says a high dose can be given safely with careful screening, preparation and supervision (p. 281) and also warns that 31% had significant fear and 17% transient ideas of reference or paranoia (p. 282). A headline version overstates the paper if it says psilocybin gives most people a mystical experience, changes personality, or is safe: the sample was chosen for spiritual practice, “mystical” is a questionnaire score, the lasting changes are self-attributions plus a small observer-rated change, the personality inventory did not move, and safety rests on 36 screened, prepared and closely supervised volunteers.

timeline.event: Good Friday Experiment (Pahnke, 1963; long-term follow-up by Doblin, 1991), as described by the authors: 10 theology students received psilocybin 30 mg and 10 nicotinic acid during a group religious service; the psilocybin group scored higher on the Pahnke Mystical Experience Questionnaire, but participants knew some would be controls and the blind broke quickly (pp. 280–281). Not read.
Four commentaries published with this paper (Nichols; Snyder; Kleber; Schuster, 2006), listed in the project's psilocybin PDF list as critiques of it; not among this reader's files and not read.

14-month follow-up (Griffiths et al., 2008), described by Johnson et al. (2014, p. 983) as showing that 61% of volunteers associated these experiences with moderate to extreme positive behaviour change; primary paper not read.

Same group's dose–effect study (Griffiths et al., 2011), cited by Johnson et al. (2014, p. 984) for a greater prevalence of mystical experience at 20 and 30 mg/70 kg than at lower doses; primary paper not read.
The same group used these session procedures in a single-arm psilocybin pilot for smoking cessation (Johnson et al., 2014).

Bogenschutz et al. used the 0.6 Mystical Experience Questionnaire threshold to set the second psilocybin dose in an alcohol use disorder trial and cite this study's methylphenidate among control drugs that did not adequately maintain blinding in past psilocybin trials (Bogenschutz et al., 2022, pp. 955, 960).

replication.where_it_stands: High mystical-experience questionnaire scores after psilocybin in prepared volunteers were reported again by the same group (as cited by Johnson et al., 2014); independent replications and the four published commentaries were not read in this round. The open questions are expectancy and functional unblinding, generalization beyond spiritually engaged volunteers, and whether self-attributed lasting change corresponds to change measured by blind observers or standard instruments.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01 DA03889 and the Council on Spiritual Practices (Acknowledgements, p. 282).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: W. A. Richards and R. Jesse list the Council on Spiritual Practices, one of the two funders, as an affiliation (p. 268). The primary session monitor, a clinical psychologist experienced in monitoring hallucinogen sessions, is identified by the initials W.R. (p. 270), which match co-author W. A. Richards. The psilocybin was synthesized by David Nichols (p. 282). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered trial in a broader sample, including people with no religious or spiritual practice, using an active comparator that participants cannot readily tell from psilocybin, with blinding assessed in participants as well as staff, prespecified lasting outcomes measured by standard instruments and by observers blind to condition, and follow-up beyond a year.

domains.note: Random assignment to the two- or three-session arm and to drug order is stated without the method of sequence generation or allocation concealment; the order groups did not differ at screening on the lifetime and personality measures (values not shown).

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: Two months between sessions removes drug carryover, but psychological carryover is plausible (the authors analyse the lifetime measures separately for this reason). The paired analyses of the 7-hour and 2-month ratings do not model period or order, and the psilocybin-first group rated its methylphenidate session after a psilocybin experience.

No deviations are reported and all 30 were analysed for the acute measures, but the large difference in effects makes functional unblinding likely, and the monitors' preparation conveyed an expectation that sessions could increase awareness and insight.

Acute data complete for 30. The 2-month questionnaire is missing for 6 because it was introduced after the start, and observer data for 4 because rater interviews were incomplete; neither reason is likely to depend on the outcome. The observer exclusion rule is ambiguously worded (see reporting issues).

Apart from blood pressure and heart rate, every outcome is a rating by the participant or by monitors who were present. Participants were told psilocybin would come in at least one session and were never asked to guess; monitors recognized most psilocybin sessions; the 2-month outcomes are participants' attributions of change to the experience.

No registration is mentioned; psychiatric-symptom and quality-of-life measures announced in the design are not reported; the 2-month questionnaire was added after the start. Null personality and affect results are reported, which lowers the concern.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The acute contrast, much higher mystical-experience questionnaire scores after psilocybin than after methylphenidate, is large and unlikely to be produced by bias alone, but every outcome that carries the paper's message is a self-rating or monitor rating made without effective blinding, in volunteers selected for spiritual practice and told to expect psilocybin. The card may be cited for what these volunteers reported acutely and at 2 months, with the right denominators (30, 24, 26 or 36), for the rates of fear and anxiety, and for the null personality and affect results; it may not be cited for a blinded estimate of psilocybin's effect, for generalization beyond this sample, or for the safety of the dose in general.

key_findings.finding: Within the same 30 volunteers, mystical-experience questionnaire scores were much higher after psilocybin than after methylphenidate on every scale: Mysticism Scale total 252.1 vs 174.7 (SEM 8.5 and 11.3); the seven States of Consciousness scales 0.66 to 0.81 of the maximum after psilocybin vs 0.21 to 0.38 after methylphenidate (all p<0.001), measured about 7 hours after the capsule.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug effect and mysticism measures assessed 7 h after drug administration › Measures of mystical experience (p. 276); Table 3 (p. 277)

key_findings.finding: By criteria set in advance (at least 0.6 of the maximum on each of six scales), 22 of 36 volunteers had a “complete” mystical experience after psilocybin and 4 of 36 after methylphenidate. By session, ten, nine and three participants in sessions 1, 2 and 3, that is 67%, 60% and 50% of those given psilocybin in each; the third session was the open-label one. The authors read this as no sign that longer preparation raised the rate (editors' calculation for the blinded crossover alone: 10 + 9 = 19 of 30, 63%).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › States of consciousness questionnaire (continued on p. 272); Results › Measures of mystical experience (p. 276); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 281)
key_findings.note: The 22 of 36 and 4 of 36 counts pool the 30 crossover participants with the 6 decoy-arm participants, whose psilocybin session was open-label and whose data were otherwise excluded; 4 of 36 counts people, six of whom had two methylphenidate sessions.

key_findings.finding: Two months after the session, 67% of the volunteers who completed this rating called the psilocybin session the single most meaningful experience of their lives or among the top five, and in written comments likened it, for example, to the birth of a first child or the death of a parent. Figure 3 gives the denominator, N=24 (editors' count from Figure 3 bar lengths, each matching a whole count out of 24: single most meaningful 3 of 24 and top five 13 of 24, together 16 of 24; after methylphenidate, top five 2 of 24, single most none, and 15 of 24 likened it to experiences that occur monthly, weekly or every day).
key_findings.locator: Results › Measures assessed 2 months post-sessions › Persisting Effects Questionnaire, 1st paragraph (begins p. 276, continues p. 277); Figure 3 (p. 279)
key_findings.note: Figure 3 bars measured on a 300-dpi rendering: psilocybin single most 12.5%, top five 54.2%, top ten 12.5%, once every 5 years 16.7%, once a year 4.2%; methylphenidate top five 8.3%, top ten 4.2%, once every 5 years 12.5%, once a year 12.5%, once a month 29.2%, once a week 25.0%, everyday 8.3%; each equals k/24.

key_findings.finding: 33% of the volunteers rated the psilocybin session the single most spiritually significant experience of their lives and another 38% placed it among the top five; after methylphenidate, 8% placed it in the top five and none rated it the single most. 79% said the psilocybin experience had increased their well-being or life satisfaction moderately (50%) or very much (29%), against 17% and 4% after methylphenidate; no one reported a decrease after either drug. N=24 (editors' counts out of 24: 8 and 9; 2; 19, 12 and 7; 4 and 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Persisting Effects Questionnaire, 1st paragraph (begins p. 276; these figures on p. 277); Table 4, footnote a (N=24, p. 278)
key_findings.note: 33% and 79% are printed in words on p. 277 (thirty-three, seventy-nine percent).

key_findings.finding: Mean 2-month ratings, psilocybin vs methylphenidate (N=24): personal meaningfulness 6.54 vs 3.42 on the 1–8 scale; spiritual significance 4.79 vs 2.63 on the 1–6 scale; change in well-being or life satisfaction +2.04 vs +0.79 on the −3 to +3 scale (all p<0.001). As percentages of the maximum score: positive attitudes about life or self 55.0% vs 22.8%, positive mood changes 39.2% vs 16.0%, altruistic or positive social effects 46.6% vs 17.3% and positive behaviour changes 60.0% vs 29.2% (all p<0.001); the negative categories stayed between 0% and 1.7% and did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 4

key_findings.finding: Three adults nominated by each participant, interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session (N=26), rated a mean positive change of 2.42 (SEM 0.70) after psilocybin sessions against −0.03 (SEM 0.68) after methylphenidate (p<0.01); the authors call this a small but significant positive change (editors' calculation: standardized difference about 0.70, from SD = SEM × √26, ignoring the pairing).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Community observer ratings of changes in participants’ and behavior and attitudes (heading as printed)

key_findings.finding: No factor of the NEO PI-R personality inventory and neither the positive nor the negative affect scale of the PANAS-X was differentially affected by psilocybin: the two order groups (15 each) did not differ at screening or 2 months after session 1, and the methylphenidate-first group did not change from post-session 1 to post-session 2. No values are shown.
key_findings.locator: Results › Personality and affect

key_findings.finding: Two months after the first session, lifetime mystical experience (Mysticism Scale) and Spiritual Transcendence Scale scores were significantly higher in the psilocybin-first group than in the methylphenidate-first group (15 each), and both rose significantly in the methylphenidate-first group after its psilocybin session; no test statistics are given, and the y-axes of Figure 4 start at 190 and 90 (editors' reading of Figure 4, approximate: about 255 vs 208 and about 106 vs 97 after the first session).
key_findings.locator: Results › Lifetime assessment of mystical experience and spirituality (p. 278); Figure 4 (p. 280)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 4.

key_findings.finding: In post-session ratings, 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session as strong or extreme, against none after methylphenidate. Four said anxiety or psychological struggle dominated the whole session and four more that it filled a significant part of it; six of these eight had mild, transient ideas of reference or paranoid thinking, which were readily managed with reassurance and did not persist beyond the session; two compared the experience to being in a war and three said they would never want to repeat it. Most of the eight still rated the experience as having personal meaning and spiritual significance, and no volunteer reported reduced well-being or life satisfaction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fear, anxiety/dysphoria, and ideas of reference/paranoia (begins p. 278, continues p. 279)
key_findings.note: On p. 279 the statement that these effects did not persist beyond the session follows, and refers to, the ideas of reference or paranoid thinking; the paper does not say so of the anxiety or dysphoria episodes. The Discussion says the psychological effects were readily managed with reassurance (p. 281).

key_findings.finding: The authors' summary: despite 8 to 24 hours of contact with the monitors before the psilocybin session, 22% (8 of 36) had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria; no one needed drug treatment and no one used the 24-hour on-call contact before the next-day meeting. They add that 31% had significant fear and 17% transient ideas of reference or paranoia, and warn that without monitoring such reactions could escalate to panic and dangerous behaviour.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 281) and 7th paragraph (p. 282)

key_findings.finding: Monitors' peak ratings (0–4 scale, N=30), psilocybin vs methylphenidate: anxiety or fearfulness 1.05 vs 0.42, tearing or crying 1.38 vs 0.77, joy or intense happiness 2.03 vs 0.63, peace or harmony 1.90 vs 0.92; monitor-rated minutes of strong anxiety averaged 5.6 vs 0.7 (of 360; not significant). Volunteers spent less time talking with the monitors (50.9 vs 72.0 minutes) and more time in physical contact such as reassuring touch (57.6 vs 23.7 minutes). The ARCI euphoria scale did not differ (8.60 vs 6.77), while its hallucinogen/dysphoria scale (7.33 vs 4.33) and the APZ dread-of-ego-dissolution scale (5.03 vs 1.03; units unclear, see reporting issues) were higher (p<0.001); the Discussion cites the monitor anxiety ratings and these two scales as measures of anxiety and dysphoria (p. 281).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 275); Table 2 (p. 276); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 281)

key_findings.finding: Participants and monitors were told that at least one session would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin, and that the other sessions might bring an inactive placebo, a low dose of psilocybin or one of 11 other drugs. Participants were never asked to guess what they had received. One or both monitors misclassified 23% of sessions (the primary monitor 17%), mostly by calling methylphenidate sessions psilocybin; the authors judged the blinding adequately maintained because both monitors still believed a range of drugs, doses and placebo had been given.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Instructions to participants and monitors (begins p. 270, continues p. 271); Results › Integrity of blinding procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 274)

key_findings.finding: Heart rate rose by about 10 beats per minute with both drugs; effects began at the 30- or 60-minute assessment and peaked between 90 and 180 minutes; psilocybin raised blood pressure modestly more than methylphenidate.
key_findings.locator: Results › Blood pressure, heart rate, and monitor ratings throughout the session (begins p. 274, continues p. 275); Figure 1 (p. 276)

key_findings.finding: At the time of writing, the 1-year follow-up was still ongoing and had been completed by 30 of 36 volunteers; in its open-ended clinical interviews there had been no reports of persisting perceptual phenomena or of problematic recreational hallucinogen use (the paper's wording is narrower than no use: it does not say whether any volunteer used hallucinogens outside the study). This is the authors' summary of an ongoing follow-up, not a systematic measure.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say APZ scores were expressed as a proportion of the maximum possible score (p. 271), but Table 2 prints APZ means from 1.03 to 8.87 (p. 276), which cannot be proportions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The units of the APZ values are unclear; the direction of the psilocybin–methylphenidate difference is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The exclusion sentence is ambiguous: four of the 30 were eliminated because of “a failure to interview all three of the raters” after one of the sessions (p. 273). Read as fewer than three raters interviewed, it contradicts the data kept for the other 26, 17% of whose 52 rating occasions were conducted with two raters (editors' calculation from the printed 83%); read as none of the three interviewed, the two statements agree, which fits the Data analyses' description of the 26 as those with complete observer data (p. 274).
reporting_issues.consequence: The exact reason for the four exclusions is uncertain; either way, incomplete interviewing is unlikely to depend on the outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The most quoted counts pool blinded and unblinded sessions: 22 of 36 complete mystical experiences, 11 of 36 strong or extreme fear and 8 of 36 notable anxiety or dysphoria all include the 6 decoy-arm participants, whose psilocybin session was open-label and whose data were otherwise excluded from analysis (pp. 269, 276, 278, 281). The authors state that these six participants' data were generally consistent with the reported results (p. 269) but report them only within these pooled counts and the third-session counts (3 complete mystical experiences and 2 participants with notable anxiety or dysphoria among the 6 open-label sessions; pp. 276, 279).
reporting_issues.consequence: For the blinded crossover the complete-mystical-experience rate is 19 of 30 (editors' calculation from the per-session counts). The 4 of 36 after methylphenidate counts people, six of whom had two methylphenidate sessions, so it is not a per-session rate. The statement that the excluded data were consistent with the results cannot be checked beyond these counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The meaningfulness, spiritual-significance and well-being percentages in the Results text (pp. 276–277) do not state their denominator; the questionnaire was introduced after the study began and completed by 24 of the 30 crossover participants (p. 273), which only Table 4 and Figure 3 state.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 67% headline is 16 of 24 people (editors' calculation), not two-thirds of the 36 enrolled or of the 30 analysed.

reporting_issues.issue: The study-design paragraph lists measures of psychiatric symptoms and of quality of life among the measures taken before and 2 months after each session (p. 270), but neither instrument is named and no result is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible selective reporting; whether psilocybin affected these outcomes is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Only p-value thresholds are printed, without t statistics, degrees of freedom, effect sizes or confidence intervals; the misclassification rate of 23% is given without the number of sessions or monitor guesses it refers to (pp. 274–278).
reporting_issues.consequence: Degrees of freedom cannot be checked against sample sizes and precision cannot be judged; the editors' standardized differences ignore the within-person pairing and are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion counts the Mysticism Scale among “empirically validated measures of mystical experience” (p. 281), while the Methods say it had not previously been used to assess changes after a drug experience (p. 272).
reporting_issues.consequence: The scale's validity for drug-occasioned experiences rests largely on this study.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 4 presents the lifetime-measure comparisons as bars on y-axes starting at 190 and 90, with no numerical values or test statistics anywhere in the paper (p. 280).
reporting_issues.consequence: The truncated axes visually enlarge the differences, and their size cannot be judged from the paper.
