design_detail: Invited commentary, one of four published with Griffiths et al. (2006) in the same issue (Psychopharmacology 187:291–292; received 24 May, accepted 27 May 2006), by an author at Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons and the Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute, who writes of seeing casualties of unsupervised hallucinogen use in the 1960s (citing his own 1967 paper). No data of its own and no search; five references. The most specific of the four commentaries: it restates the trial's counts of complete mystical experiences, top-five ratings and sessions dominated by anxiety, sets out a research agenda, and weighs the concern that positive findings could encourage uncontrolled use by young people.
can_establish: How a commentator from an addiction research division read the trial: the counts he chose to restate, the risks he weighed and the research he called for.
cannot_establish: Anything beyond the trial's own data: its figures are restated from the trial without denominators, and its statements about trends in psychedelic use and about LSD studies in alcoholism have no sources.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). Notes that all the trial's volunteers were naive to hallucinogens (p. 291).
sample.selection_effects: The counts restated out of 36 pool the 30 crossover volunteers with 6 whose psilocybin session was open-label (companion card sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., pp. 269, 276); the commentary does not mention the volunteers' selection for religious or spiritual practice.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no data). Gives the trial's conditions as psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg and methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg as an active control, each volunteer receiving at least one session with each in counterbalanced order, with extensive time with the monitors before and after sessions (p. 291).

comparison.controls: None of its own; describes methylphenidate as the trial's active control (p. 291).

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. Refers to the trial's measures of mystical experience, its criterion for a complete mystical experience and its 2-month meaningfulness ratings (pp. 291–292).
outcomes.operationalization: As in the trial; not defined in the commentary.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Restated from the trial: 8 of 36 volunteers described all or most of their psilocybin session as dominated by anxiety or dysphoria, none after methylphenidate; 22 of 36 had a complete mystical experience after psilocybin against 4 of 36 after methylphenidate; at 2 months, 67% rated the psilocybin experience the single most meaningful or among the five most meaningful of their lives, against 8% placing the methylphenidate experience in the top five and none as the single most; monitors misidentified the drug about a quarter of the time (pp. 291–292).
analysis.selective_reporting: Reports the 8 of 36 with sessions dominated by anxiety but not the trial's figure of 11 of 36 who rated their fear strong or extreme, nor the transient ideas of reference and paranoid thinking reported (companion card sc_griffiths_2006).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The only one of the four commentaries to report the trial's anxiety figures and to weigh risks: it restates the trial's counts as far as they go, notes historical casualties of unsupervised use, and calls the concern about uncontrolled use by young people not unwarranted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: That the time spent with monitors kept adverse effects such as fear and panic to a minimum; that the anxiety did not outlast the session and apparently had no lasting negative consequence; that blinding was so careful that monitors misidentified the drug about a quarter of the time (p. 291); and that a scientific study is unlikely to change use much, psychedelic use having stayed roughly constant for three decades (p. 292). Gaps: (1) minimal fear sits beside 8 of 36 sessions dominated by anxiety and, by the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006), 11 of 36 volunteers with strong or extreme fear and transient paranoid thinking in 6 of the 8; (2) the percentages carry no denominators: per the companion card, 67% and 8% are of the 24 volunteers who completed the 2-month questionnaire (16 and 2 of 24), not of the 36 just mentioned, and the 22 and 4 of 36 include open-label sessions (19 of 30 in the blinded crossover); (3) blinding is inferred from the monitors only; (4) the statement about stable use is unsourced. The word apparently is appropriately hedged. A headline version giving two-thirds of 36 volunteers would misstate the denominator.

timeline.event: Kleber: prolonged adverse reactions from unsupervised use of hallucinogenic drugs (J Nerv Ment Dis), cited by the author for 1960s casualties (p. 291). Not read.
Griffiths et al.: the trial this commentary discusses (appraised on its own card).
Commentaries by Nichols, Snyder and Schuster in the same issue, all appreciative and without adverse-event figures.

replication.where_it_stands: One of four commentaries published with the trial (see sc_nichols_2006), and the one closest to a critical reading. The research it called for (dose effects, individual differences, antagonists, neuroimaging) and its point about preparation are questions for later trials, which have their own cards.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the commentary.
funding.affiliations_note: College of Physicians and Surgeons, Columbia University; Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute (p. 291). No link to the trial is stated.

what_would_settle_it: Full reporting of adverse psychological reactions with denominators by session type (blinded or open-label) and participants' guesses of their condition; for the concern about young people, population data on psychedelic use before and after widely publicized trial results.

domains.note: No search; five references chosen by the author.
Reports the trial's anxiety figures and notes limits of earlier LSD research (model psychosis limited, therapeutic data inadequate), but takes the monitors' errors as proof of careful blinding.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only source given for 1960s casualties is the author's own 1967 paper and clinical experience.
Concerns and possibilities are framed as such, but statements about constant psychedelic use over three decades and about LSD studies in alcoholism are presented as fact without sources.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on benefits and harms
domains.note: Gives both the trial's benefits and its anxiety figures, historical casualties and the risk of uncontrolled use; the strong-fear ratings are omitted.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The most balanced of the four commentaries, but still an opinion piece with no data or search. Its numbers are the trial's and must be cited to the trial with the denominators given on the trial's card; the commentary may be cited for the commentator's concerns and research agenda.

key_findings.finding: Describes the 1960s from the mental health front line: most young people who experimented with psychedelics did not suffer lasting damage, but a number of casualties were seen (the author's 1967 paper); Sandoz, the manufacturer of LSD, stopped supplying researchers around 1965, after which licit supply for research and research funding largely disappeared.
key_findings.locator: 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: Says earlier research with LSD and other psychedelics covered model psychosis (with significant limitations), the nature of hallucinations, treatment of trauma and of dying patients (inadequate data) and altered states; some was carefully done, but in most the researchers seemed carried away by the drugs' effects.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Describes the trial as double-blind, with psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg and methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg as an active control, each volunteer having at least one session with each in counterbalanced order, all volunteers hallucinogen-naive; says the blinding was so careful that even the experienced monitors misidentified the drug about one quarter of the time.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Per the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., p. 274), one or both monitors misclassified 23% of sessions, mostly by calling methylphenidate sessions psilocybin; participants were never asked to guess.

key_findings.finding: Reports that 8 of the 36 volunteers described all or most of their psilocybin session as dominated by anxiety or dysphoria, none after methylphenidate; these effects did not outlast the session, were handled with reassurance and apparently had no lasting negative consequence; the commentary credits the time spent with the monitors for keeping fear and panic to a minimum.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Per the companion card (from Griffiths et al., pp. 278–279, 281): four volunteers said anxiety dominated the whole session and four a significant part of it; separately, 11 of 36 rated their fear strong or extreme (none after methylphenidate), and 6 of the 8 had transient ideas of reference or paranoid thinking. The 36 include 6 volunteers whose psilocybin session was open-label.

key_findings.finding: Reports that 22 of the 36 volunteers had a complete mystical experience after psilocybin against 4 of 36 after methylphenidate, and that at the 2-month follow-up 67% rated the psilocybin experience the single most meaningful of their lives or among the five most meaningful, against 8% placing the methylphenidate experience among the top five and none as the single most.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (p. 291, right column, continuing at the top of p. 292)
key_findings.note: No denominator is given for the percentages. Per Griffiths et al. (p. 276; Figure 3, p. 279), 67% and 8% are 16 and 2 of the 24 volunteers who completed the 2-month questionnaire; the 22 of 36 include three open-label third sessions (19 of 30 in the blinded crossover), whereas the 4 of 36 after methylphenidate all came from blinded sessions (two each in the first and second sessions).

design_detail: Invited commentary, one of four published with Griffiths et al. (2006) in the same issue (Psychopharmacology 187:284–286; received 3 May, accepted 27 May 2006), by an author in the Department of Medicinal Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Purdue University. Argument and history only: no data of its own, no search, no appraisal of the studies cited; 12 references. It praises the trial's design, places it in a history of psychedelic research (Pahnke's Good Friday experiment; Kast's reports of LSD in gravely ill patients; LSD-assisted psychotherapy for terminal cancer at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center; Strassman's DMT studies) and offers a speculative 5-HT2A mechanism.
can_establish: What one pharmacologist writing beside the trial in 2006 took to be its strengths and its place in the history of psychedelic research, and which earlier studies he pointed to as evidence of clinical promise.
cannot_establish: Anything about psilocybin's effects beyond what Griffiths et al. report: the commentary has no data, gives its historical figures (such as improvement in 60–70% of patients given LSD) without denominators, comparison groups or appraisal, and does not discuss the trial's limits or harms.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). It describes the trial's volunteers as not theology students but ordinary people with an interest in spiritual things, studied outside a church or other religious venue (p. 285).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the author chose what to cite.
sample.selection_effects: Studies chosen by the author. The LSD-era studies are cited for benefit only, although the commentary itself says that research of that era produced little of clear significance, partly because of faulty design and analysis (pp. 284–285). Describing the trial's volunteers as ordinary people leaves out that all were selected for at least intermittent religious or spiritual practice (companion card sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., p. 269).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no data). The commentary does not give the trial's doses; it gives the conditions of Pahnke's experiment as psilocybin 30 mg or nicotinic acid 200 mg given as a placebo (p. 284).

comparison.controls: None of its own. It calls the trial placebo-controlled with proper controls (pp. 284–285); the trial's comparator was the active drug methylphenidate, as the other three commentaries state (Snyder, p. 288; Schuster, p. 289; Kleber, p. 291).

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. It says the trial analysed the experience with more modern instruments than Pahnke's and used ratings by community observers such as family members or friends (p. 285).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable. Mystical experience and beneficial effects are not defined in the commentary.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Second-hand figure: less need for analgesics and better mood and quality of life in 60–70% of patients with terminal cancer treated with LSD in the Maryland studies, attributed jointly to Grof et al. (1973) and Pahnke et al. (1969, 1970a, 1970b), with no denominators, comparison groups or indication of which paper reports it (p. 285).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. No limitation of the trial is mentioned, for example the fear and anxiety reported during psilocybin sessions (11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear strong or extreme, per the companion card sc_griffiths_2006).

interpretation_gap.results_show: An appreciative commentary without data. It lists the trial's advances over Pahnke's experiment (proper controls, better design and analysis, more modern instruments, a setting that was not religious, volunteers who were not theology students) and says some persisting positive changes the volunteers reported were confirmed by community observers (p. 285).
interpretation_gap.claimed: It calls the trial the first well-designed, placebo-controlled clinical study of psilocybin's psychological effects in more than four decades, says it "convincingly demonstrates" that psychedelics used appropriately can produce remarkable, possibly beneficial effects (p. 284), and calls it a possible watershed (p. 285). Gaps: (1) the comparator was an active drug, methylphenidate, not a placebo (Snyder, p. 288; Schuster, p. 289; Kleber, p. 291); (2) the observer confirmation rests on ratings by people the volunteers nominated, which showed a small mean positive change (companion card sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., p. 278); (3) calling the volunteers ordinary people leaves out their selection for religious or spiritual practice; (4) the 60–70% improvement figure from the LSD era comes without denominators or controls, from an era whose research the commentary itself calls often faulty; (5) harms go unmentioned. The commentary's own words for the effects are possibly beneficial and deserving further study; a headline version saying psilocybin was shown to be beneficial would overstate both the commentary and the trial.

timeline.event: Pahnke's Good Friday experiment (doctoral dissertation, 1963), as described here: 20 students from a Christian theological seminary given psilocybin 30 mg or nicotinic acid 200 mg during a Good Friday service (p. 284). Not read.
Griffiths et al.: double-blind crossover trial of psilocybin against methylphenidate in 36 hallucinogen-naive volunteers, the paper this commentary discusses (appraised on its own card).
Commentary by Snyder in the same issue: also appreciative; infers from the monitors' errors that expectancy did not contaminate the results.
Commentary by Schuster in the same issue, which refers to this commentary for the LSD studies in dying patients.
Commentary by Kleber in the same issue: the only one of the four to give the trial's anxiety figures and to weigh risks.

replication.where_it_stands: One of four invited commentaries published with the trial. The project's psilocybin list labels all four as critiques of the trial, but none is a methodological critique: all four praise it, and only Kleber's reports adverse reactions. The questions the trial's card leaves open (expectancy and functional unblinding, generalization beyond spiritually engaged volunteers, self-attributed lasting change) are not raised here.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the commentary.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Medicinal Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Purdue University School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences (p. 284). The trial's acknowledgements, as recorded on the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., p. 282), state that the psilocybin used was synthesized by David Nichols; the commentary does not mention this. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the commentary.

what_would_settle_it: For the benefit the commentary anticipates: trials in volunteers not selected for spiritual practice, with an inert placebo as well as an active comparator, participants asked to guess their condition, and persisting effects measured with standard instruments by raters blind to condition; for the LSD-era figures, the cited studies read in full.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria; the historical studies were chosen by the author.
No appraisal: the 60–70% figure from the LSD studies is given without design, comparison or denominators, and the trial's limits are not discussed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One review by the author (Nichols, 2004) is cited, for background history only.

The mechanism (5-HT2A depolarization making cortical cells more sensitive to weak signals) is labelled speculation (p. 285), but what the trial measured (questionnaire ratings) is not distinguished from benefit.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on benefits and harms (harms under-represented)
domains.note: Only benefits are discussed; adverse reactions in the trial and in the earlier LSD research are not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. This is an invited, appreciative commentary with no data, no search and no appraisal. It may be cited for the commentator's view and as a pointer to the historical studies it names, never for the size or certainty of any effect; the trial's own card is the source for its results.

key_findings.finding: Calls Griffiths et al. the first well-designed, placebo-controlled clinical study in more than four decades of the psychological effects of psilocybin, and says it convincingly demonstrates that psychedelics, used appropriately, can produce remarkable, possibly beneficial effects that deserve further study.
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: The comparator was methylphenidate, an active drug (Snyder, p. 288; Schuster, p. 289; Kleber, p. 291); placebo-controlled is this commentary's wording.

key_findings.finding: Describes Pahnke's Good Friday experiment (1963 doctoral dissertation): 20 volunteers from a Christian theological seminary received psilocybin 30 mg or nicotinic acid 200 mg as a placebo during a Good Friday service, and Pahnke concluded that those given psilocybin had experiences indistinguishable from categories in his typology of mysticism.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: The dissertation is quoted but not listed among the references (p. 286).

key_findings.finding: Says LSD was investigated in studies involving tens of thousands of patients until research was halted by laws passed over concern about recreational use, and that little of clear significance resulted, partly because of faulty design and data analysis.
key_findings.locator: 5th paragraph, beginning 'Clearly, these substances' (p. 284, right column, continuing on p. 285)
key_findings.note: No reference is given for these statements.

key_findings.finding: Says one indication for psychedelics, particularly LSD, was reasonably well documented: Kast reported in 1964 that some gravely ill patients given LSD had mood elevation and less need for pain medication lasting nearly 2 weeks (Kast & Collins, 1964), and later that some listless, depressed patients were moved to tears by an unexpected depth of feeling (Kast, 1966).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'All that being said' (left column)

key_findings.finding: Cites the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center studies of LSD in patients with terminal cancer (Grof et al., 1973; Pahnke et al., 1969, 1970a, 1970b) for significantly reduced need for analgesics and improved mood and quality of life in 60–70% of patients treated with LSD; the response appeared to be correlated with the extent of mystical or transcendental experience, those with the most profound states seeming to gain most, and the benefit appeared related to a reduced or abolished fear of death.' Note unchanged.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Kast's findings' (left column)
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure; the cited studies were not read. No denominators, comparison groups or study-by-study figures are given.

key_findings.finding: Lists the trial's advances over Pahnke's experiment: proper controls, better design and analysis with more modern instruments, a setting that was not a church or other religious venue, and volunteers who were not theology students; says psilocybin occasioned experiences similar to spontaneous mystical states and that some persisting positive changes reported by volunteers were confirmed by independent ratings from community observers such as family members or friends.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'What Griffiths et al. have done' (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Per the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., pp. 269, 278), all volunteers reported at least intermittent religious or spiritual activity, and the observers, nominated by the volunteers, rated a small mean positive change.

key_findings.note: No references are given for the mechanism.

key_findings.finding: Says that apart from Strassman's DMT studies in the mid-1990s no significant work on the clinical effects of psychedelics had appeared for more than a generation, and that the trial could be a watershed.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'With such a huge potential impact' (right column)

design_detail: Invited commentary, one of four published with Griffiths et al. (2006) in the same issue (Psychopharmacology 187:289–290; received 11 May, accepted 27 May 2006), by an author in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, Wayne State University School of Medicine. One reference (Kast, 1966); no data, no search. It argues that the trial's effects exceeded expectancy because the active control did not reproduce them, says set and setting may strongly shape the experience and any therapeutic effect, suggests uses in addiction and at the end of life, and argues that Schedule I control should not keep curtailing research.
can_establish: How one commentator read the trial in 2006, including his view that the preparatory sessions set expectations for a positive experience and that set and setting may determine both the experience and any therapeutic effect.
cannot_establish: That the trial's effects were free of expectancy or that psilocybin can be given safely: the commentary has no data, does not discuss whether participants could tell the drugs apart, and does not mention the fear and anxiety reported in the trial.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). Describes the trial's participants as healthy people without a history of hallucinogen use (p. 289).
sample.selection_effects: The commentary does not mention that the trial's volunteers were selected for religious or spiritual practice (companion card sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., p. 269).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no data). Gives the active control as methylphenidate 40 mg (p. 289), without the per-70-kg adjustment that Snyder (p. 288) and Kleber (p. 291) state; the psilocybin dose is not given.

comparison.controls: None of its own. Treats the trial's active control (methylphenidate) as the reason the effects cannot be expectancy effects (p. 289).

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. Refers to the trial's ratings of significance, spirituality, positive attitude and behaviour, and to ratings by friends and relatives (p. 289).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The commentary gives no numbers for the trial's results, only that a majority found the experience very meaningful and spiritually significant and that most placed it among the five most important experiences of their lives (p. 289).
analysis.selective_reporting: The trial's adverse psychological reactions are not mentioned, although the commentary says the study shows psilocybin can be safely studied.

interpretation_gap.results_show: An appreciative commentary without data. Its most useful point is a caveat: the preparatory sessions set expectations for a positive experience and the setting was designed to be introspective, and these may be important determinants of the experience and of any therapeutic effect (p. 289).
interpretation_gap.claimed: That the study demonstrates psilocybin can be safely studied in healthy people with no history of hallucinogen use, and that it is clear the effects were more than expectancy effects because the active control, methylphenidate, did not produce similar effects (p. 289). Gaps: (1) the active-control argument holds only if participants could not tell the two drugs apart; per the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006), participants were never asked to guess and the monitors identified most sessions; (2) by the commentary's own caveat about set and setting, expectations specific to psilocybin were part of the conditions, not excluded by them; (3) safety is not qualified by the fear and anxiety reported during psilocybin sessions (11 of 36 strong or extreme fear, per the companion card). A headline version saying the trial ruled out expectancy would overstate it.

timeline.event: Kast: LSD and the dying patient, the commentary's only reference, cited for easing distress at the end of life (p. 289). Not read.
Griffiths et al.: the trial this commentary discusses (appraised on its own card).
Nichols's commentary in the same issue, to which this one refers for the LSD studies in dying patients.

Bogenschutz et al. cite the trial's methylphenidate among control drugs that did not adequately maintain blinding in past psilocybin trials (as recorded on the companion card sc_griffiths_2006; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: One of four appreciative commentaries published with the trial (see sc_nichols_2006). Its expectancy argument rests on blinding that the trial did not test in participants; its set-and-setting caveat bears on the expectancy and context questions that the trial's card leaves open.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the commentary.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, Wayne State University School of Medicine, Detroit (p. 289). No link to the trial is stated.

what_would_settle_it: A trial that measures participants' expectations before dosing and asks them to guess their condition afterwards, compares psilocybin with an active control they cannot tell apart from it, and varies preparation and setting to test their contribution.

domains.note: No search; one reference.
The trial's blinding and safety are taken as given; Kast (1966) is cited for promise without design details.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the author's studies are cited.
Personal belief and possibilities are labelled as such (a personal belief; entirely conceivable), but the expectancy conclusion is stated as clear.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on benefits and harms (harms under-represented)
domains.note: Notes that LSD studies in alcoholism failed to show clear benefit and that misuse led to scheduling, but does not mention the trial's adverse reactions.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. An appreciative commentary with no data and one reference. It may be cited for the commentator's view, notably the caveat that preparation and setting may shape the experience and any therapeutic effect; it is not evidence that the trial's effects were free of expectancy or that psilocybin is safe.

key_findings.finding: Says the study shows psilocybin can be safely studied in healthy people without a history of hallucinogen use; during sessions participants had perceptual changes and labile mood; at 2 months a majority reported the experience as very meaningful and spiritually significant, most placing it among the five most important experiences of their lives; and participants' reports of lasting positive changes in attitudes and behaviour were consistent with ratings by friends and relatives.

key_findings.note: No numbers are given. Per the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006), the 2-month ratings come from 24 of the 30 crossover volunteers, and 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session strong or extreme.

Gives the trial's conditions as psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg or methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg in separate sessions, with preparation by monitors before and after each session (p. 288), and Pahnke's as psilocybin 30 mg or nicotinic acid 200 mg in a group religious service (pp. 287–288).

comparison.controls: None of its own. Describes the trial's comparator, methylphenidate (p. 288).

outcomes.instruments: None of its own; mentions the trial's extensive questionnaires on mystical experience and the in-depth follow-up 2 months later (p. 288).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; mystical experience and adverse events are not defined.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures given: the monitors mistook one drug for the other in about 25% of sessions; two-thirds of participants rated the psilocybin experience the single most meaningful or among the five most meaningful of their lives (p. 288). Neither figure has a denominator or a source in the commentary.
analysis.selective_reporting: Adverse reactions are summarized as very few, without the trial's figures for fear and anxiety.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A summary of the trial without data or references. Its headline figures match the trial as recorded on the companion card (two-thirds is 16 of 24 respondents; one or both monitors misclassified 23% of sessions).
interpretation_gap.claimed: That the blinding was effective, so the results are not likely to be contaminated by the expectations or biases of experimenters or participants; that psilocybin "reliably" elicits a transcendent, mystical state; that adverse events were very few acutely and absent at the 2-month and 1-year follow-ups; and that the trial confirms the mystical influences of psychedelics (p. 288). Gaps: (1) per the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006), participants were never asked to guess their drug and the monitors identified most sessions correctly, erring mostly by calling methylphenidate sessions psilocybin, so the monitors' errors say nothing about participants' expectations; (2) 22 of 36 volunteers met the trial's criteria for a complete mystical experience after psilocybin (Kleber, p. 291; 19 of 30 in the blinded crossover, per the companion card), which is common but not reliable; (3) per the companion card, 11 of 36 rated their fear during the psilocybin session strong or extreme and 8 of 36 had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria; (4) the 1-year information was the trial authors' summary of an ongoing follow-up in which 30 of 36 had been interviewed. A headline version saying the trial showed psilocybin to be safe, or its effects free of expectancy, would overstate it.

timeline.event: Griffiths et al.: the trial this commentary discusses (appraised on its own card).
Commentaries by Nichols, Schuster and Kleber in the same issue; Kleber gives the trial's anxiety figures (8 of 36), which this commentary does not.

Bogenschutz et al. cite the trial's methylphenidate among control drugs that did not adequately maintain blinding in past psilocybin trials (as recorded on the companion card sc_griffiths_2006; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: One of four appreciative commentaries published with the trial (see sc_nichols_2006). The blinding question it treats as settled remains open on the trial's own card: participants were not asked to guess what they had received.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement. In the text the author discloses, in the interests of full disclosure, that he had single sessions with LSD and with DMT more than 40 years earlier (p. 287).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Neuroscience, of Pharmacology and Molecular Sciences, and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (p. 287), the institution where the trial was run (companion card sc_griffiths_2006). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the commentary.

what_would_settle_it: A trial that asks participants as well as monitors to guess their condition, includes an inert placebo arm, and reports every adverse psychological reaction with its denominator, with follow-up of all participants.

domains.note: No search and no references at all.
The trial's blinding is judged from the monitors' errors alone, and its adverse reactions are not quantified.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the author's studies are cited.

The serotonin account of synaesthesia and ego dissolution is framed as conceivable, but the trial's results are restated more firmly than the trial reports them (reliably; very few adverse events; blinding effective).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on benefits and harms (harms under-represented)
domains.note: Adverse reactions are summarized as very few; the fear and anxiety reported in the trial are not described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The commentary has no data and no references and restates the trial's blinding and safety more strongly than the trial's own data allow. It may be cited for the commentator's view and his disclosure; claims about blinding, adverse reactions or rates of mystical experience must cite the trial.

key_findings.finding: Discloses that the author himself had single sessions with LSD and with DMT more than 40 years before writing.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph of the text (begins in the left column; the disclosure is in the right column)

key_findings.finding: States without references that pharmacological studies have established that phenethylamine psychedelics (mescaline, DOM and MDMA are named) and indole psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD, DMT) act primarily by mimicking serotonin at 5-HT2A/C receptors.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph of the text (right column)

key_findings.finding: Describes Pahnke's Good Friday study as groups of ten theological seminary students given psilocybin 30 mg or nicotinic acid 200 mg in a group setting during a religious service, with psilocybin consistently eliciting a mystical experience not seen with nicotinic acid.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph of the text (right column of p. 287, ending at the top of p. 288)

key_findings.finding: Says that widespread misuse of psychedelics in the late 1960s led to controls so strict that clinical and even laboratory research virtually vanished; then summarizes the trial: emotionally stable, generally middle-aged college graduates received psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg and methylphenidate 40 mg/70 kg in separate sessions, with careful preparation by monitors who met them several times before and after each session, extensive questionnaires and an in-depth follow-up 2 months later.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph of the text (left column, first full paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Calls the effectiveness of the blinding a striking result: even the monitors mistook one drug for the other in about 25% of sessions, so the results are not likely to be contaminated by the expectations and biases of experimenters or participants.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph of the text (left column)
key_findings.note: Per the companion card (sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., p. 274), one or both monitors misclassified 23% of sessions (the primary monitor 17%), mostly by calling methylphenidate sessions psilocybin, and participants were never asked to guess. The inference about participants' expectations has no data behind it.

key_findings.finding: Reports that psilocybin produced perceptual and visual distortions, feelings of transcendence and a high incidence of mystical experiences, substantially greater than in Pahnke's study (no figures), and that at 2 months two-thirds of participants rated it the single most meaningful experience of their lives or among the top five, reporting better attitudes to life, mood and relationships.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph of the text (left column, ending at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: Two-thirds corresponds to the trial's 67%, which the companion card gives as 16 of the 24 volunteers who completed the 2-month questionnaire (sc_griffiths_2006, from Griffiths et al., Figure 3).

key_findings.finding: States that there were very few adverse events acutely and none at the 2-month and 1-year follow-ups, and takes the trial to show that clinical research with psychedelics need not be so risky as to be off-limits to most investigators.
key_findings.locator: 5th paragraph of the text (right column)
key_findings.note: Per the companion card (from Griffiths et al., pp. 278–279, 281), 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session strong or extreme and 8 of 36 had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria; the 1-year information was the authors' summary of an ongoing follow-up in which 30 of 36 had been interviewed, with no persisting perceptual effects or recreational hallucinogen use reported.

key_findings.finding: Takes the trial to show that psilocybin reliably elicits a transcendent, mystical state, and proposes, as conceivable, that serotonin projections from the raphe nuclei, which receive sensory input, could mediate synaesthesia and the dissolution of ego boundaries; concludes that the trial may help revive psychedelics as tools for probing the molecular bases of consciousness.
key_findings.locator: 6th and 7th paragraphs of the text (right column)
key_findings.note: By Kleber's figures, 22 of 36 volunteers had a complete mystical experience after psilocybin (Kleber, p. 291).

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary has no reference list: the history, the 5-HT2A/C mechanism, Pahnke's results and the comparison with Pahnke's rate of mystical experience are all uncited.
reporting_issues.consequence: None of these statements can be traced or cited from this source.

reporting_issues.issue: The rate of mystical experience is called substantially greater than in Pahnke's study without a rate for either study.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Adverse events are described as very few acutely and none at 2 months and 1 year, without numbers; per the companion card the trial reported strong or extreme fear in 11 of 36 volunteers and, at the time of writing, 1-year interviews for 30 of 36.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the commentary alone would underestimate the trial's acute psychological reactions and overestimate the completeness of the 1-year follow-up.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Psychopharmacology 187:287–288, both pages (text checked on rendered pages; no references, tables, figures, funding or conflict statement). The trial itself (Griffiths et al., 2006) was not among this reader's files; statements about it come from the commentaries and from the companion card sc_griffiths_2006, as marked. Read by AI reader 551.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 603 (round-2 check), missed item: Minor locator: that participants were not asked to guess is stated on the trial's p. 271; the KF4 note cites p. 274, which reports only the monitors' guesses (the same in the Schuster KF1 and Kleber KF2 notes).
disagreements.resolution: Recorded by the AI co-editor (13 November 2026) for the next revision of this card; it changes no answer.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 603 (round-2 check); adjudicated by the AI co-editor

design_detail: Open-label, single-arm pilot trial with no control group, at Johns Hopkins, Baltimore. 15 adults who smoked daily (mean 19 cigarettes a day for 31 years, mean 6 previous quit attempts) received a 15-week manualized smoking-cessation programme: four weekly preparation meetings combining cognitive behavioural therapy with preparation for the sessions, psilocybin sessions in week 5 (the target quit date), week 7 and optionally week 13, weekly support meetings, 19 in-person meetings in all and brief daily calls for 2 weeks after the quit date. Main outcome: 7-day point-prevalence abstinence 6 months after the quit date, from self-report confirmed by breath carbon monoxide and urinary cotinine; also self-reported smoking, craving, self-efficacy, withdrawal, safety and persisting effects (pp. 984–986). The schema has no single-arm-trial design; case-series is the closest, appraised with ROBINS-I as for the other single-arm psychedelic-therapy pilots in the card set.
can_establish: That psilocybin sessions could be given within an intensive smoking-cessation programme to 15 screened, motivated volunteers without adverse events needing medical intervention, and how many of these 15 were biochemically confirmed not to be smoking 6 months after their quit date.
cannot_establish: Whether psilocybin added anything to the intensive counselling, contact, motivation and expectation (there is no comparison group); whether the abstinence rate is higher than with other treatments (the comparisons are with other trials in other people); rare or delayed harms; or results in people who have not sought out a psilocybin treatment.

sample.recruitment: Advertisements offering a novel smoking-cessation treatment involving psilocybin; 323 people screened by telephone, 27 in person, 15 enrolled. Those excluded by phone were mainly seeking payment, taking medications or not smoking enough; participants received no monetary compensation (p. 984).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: At least 10 cigarettes a day, multiple unsuccessful quit attempts, still wanting to quit, healthy on medical interview, electrocardiogram and blood and urine tests. Excluded after a structured clinical interview (DSM-IV-TR): personal or family history of psychotic or bipolar disorders, and drug dependence (including alcohol, excluding nicotine) within the past 5 years (p. 984).
sample.demographics: 10 men, 5 women; mean age 51 (SD 10.5, range 26–65); 14 White, 1 Asian; education: some college 4, bachelor's degree 7, graduate degree 4; Fagerström Test for Cigarette Dependence 5.3 (SD 1.3); 31 years of smoking (SD 9.9); 19 cigarettes a day at intake (SD 2.9, range 15–25); 6 previous quit attempts (SD 3.6). Ten reported minimal past hallucinogen use (mean 8 lifetime uses, range 1–17, the most recent a mean of 27 years before intake); five were hallucinogen-naive (Table 1 and Participants, p. 984).
sample.attrition: All 15 completed the study and the 6-month follow-up. Twelve had three psilocybin sessions; three did not have a third (one had to leave the country for business, two declined it) (pp. 984, 987–988, 991).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers who answered an advertisement for a psilocybin treatment (15 enrolled out of 323 screened), highly educated and almost all White, two-thirds with some earlier hallucinogen experience. The authors note the racial homogeneity and high education may have affected the outcomes (p. 990). Motivation to quit and expectations of psilocybin were probably higher than among people starting usual cessation treatment, but were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Psilocybin given by the study in sessions overseen by a team of two or three staff including a doctoral-level psychologist, with a physician on call and rescue medications available (pp. 984–985). The source and purity of the psilocybin are not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: psilocybin 20 mg/70 kg at the first session (week 5, the target quit date); by default 30 mg/70 kg at week 7 and optionally at week 13, with participants allowed to repeat the lower dose (p. 984). This paper does not state the route: it says sessions were conducted as previously described (Griffiths et al., 2006, 2011; p. 984), and in Griffiths et al. (2006, p. 270) psilocybin was given in capsules by mouth. In all, 42 sessions: 16 at 20 mg/70 kg and 26 at 30 mg/70 kg; one participant chose the lower dose for the second session (p. 987). Sessions followed the group's earlier method: lying on a couch with an eye mask and headphones playing music, non-directive support from staff, no smoking-cessation content during the session, a brief motivational statement repeated before each dose, a guided imagery exercise at the end of the first session, a written account afterwards and a meeting the next day (pp. 984–985).
exposure.polysubstance: Drug dependence in the past 5 years was an exclusion (p. 984). Participants were told not to use other cessation treatments; one used nicotine lozenges and gum during a relapse, and five took over-the-counter headache medicine after a session (p. 988). Alcohol and other drug use during the study are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: smoking abstinence is the outcome.

comparison.controls: None. Change is measured within person from intake to 6 months. The Discussion compares the abstinence rate with published trials of bupropion, varenicline, a CBT programme and extended combined treatment in other samples (p. 990).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Motivation and expectations about psilocybin, which brought participants to answer an advertisement for a psilocybin treatment, were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Timeline follow-back calendar of cigarettes per day at each meeting; breath carbon monoxide (Bedfont Micro III, about the past 24 hours) and urinary cotinine (independent laboratory, about the previous 6 days) at intake, weekly and at 6 months; Fagerström Test for Cigarette Dependence (intake); Questionnaire on Smoking Urges, Smoking Abstinence Self-Efficacy scale and Wisconsin Smoking Withdrawal Scale; Visual Effects Questionnaire (intake and 6 months); post-session headache interview (last 10 participants only); lifetime Mysticism Scale (intake and 1 week after sessions 2 and 3); States of Consciousness Questionnaire (end of each session); Persisting Effects Questionnaire with questions on how psilocybin had helped (1 week after each session) (pp. 985–986; Table 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard smoking-cessation measures with cited validation; biochemical cut-offs taken from the literature (pp. 985–986).
outcomes.operationalization: Abstinence: 7-day point prevalence 6 months after the quit date, from the timeline follow-back and confirmed by breath CO of 6 ppm or less and urinary cotinine below 200 ng/mL (pp. 985, 988). A lapse was any smoking after the quit date, even a puff; a relapse was smoking on 7 or more consecutive days (Note 1, p. 991).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eleven tests: paired t tests on self-reported smoking, breath CO and cotinine in all 15 and in the 3 who kept smoking, four repeated-measures ANOVAs with linear contrasts, and a paired t test on the lifetime Mysticism Scale; persisting effects, mechanisms and safety were described without tests (pp. 986–987).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open-label. The staff who treated participants collected the self-reports; cotinine was analysed by an independent laboratory (p. 985).

analysis.effect_sizes: 12 of 15 (80%) abstinent at 6 months; editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 52% to 96% (Clopper–Pearson). Self-reported smoking fell from intake to 6 months (t14=11.1, p<0.001), as did breath CO (t14=3.8, p<0.01) and cotinine (t14=2.3, p=0.04) (p. 988). No effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned in the paper; registries were not searched in this round.
analysis.selective_reporting: The headline outcome is 7-day point prevalence at 6 months, a standard measure; continuous abstinence is not reported as such, although the text shows that of the 12 abstinent at 6 months three reported lapses and one a 14-week relapse (p. 988), so at most 8 of 15 reported no smoking at all after the quit date (editors' count).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 self-selected, motivated volunteers given intensive counselling and two or three psilocybin sessions, 12 were biochemically confirmed abstinent at 6 months (7-day point prevalence), all 12 having quit after the first session; no adverse event needed medical intervention; there was no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the observed cessation rate “substantially exceeds rates commonly reported for other behavioral and/or pharmacological therapies” (typically under 35%) and that psilocybin may be an efficacious adjunct, while noting that the open-label design does not allow definitive conclusions (p. 983). The Discussion itself cites two trials of extended counselling with bupropion and nicotine replacement that reached 45% to 59% at about 6 months, and acknowledges that participants here had much more staff contact than usual (p. 990). With 15 people the interval around 80% runs from about 52% to 96% (editors' calculation), so the data cannot distinguish this package from intensive conventional treatment, let alone isolate psilocybin. A headline such as “psilocybin helped 80% of people quit smoking” overstates it: the 80% belongs to a package of counselling, contact, motivation and psilocybin in volunteers who sought out a psilocybin treatment, and it is point-prevalence abstinence, not continuous abstinence.

timeline.event: A secondary analysis of mystical experiences in this sample (Garcia-Romeu, Griffiths and Johnson, Current Drug Abuse Reviews) is cited by Bogenschutz et al. (2022, reference 28) and dated 2015 in the project's psilocybin list; not read.
Open-label psilocybin pilot in alcohol dependence (Bogenschutz et al., 2015), described by Bogenschutz et al. (2022, p. 954) as the proof-of-concept for their randomized trial; not read.
Randomized, active-placebo-controlled trial of psilocybin in alcohol use disorder by another group, which cites this study among earlier work; a different drug of dependence, not a replication.

replication.where_it_stands: No controlled test of psilocybin for smoking cessation was among the sources read in this round; the authors call for a randomized controlled trial (p. 991). The randomized trial in alcohol use disorder (Bogenschutz et al., 2022) shows how difficult blinding is with psilocybin, which any controlled smoking trial would also face.

funding.funder: Amanda Feilding of the Beckley Foundation provided initial encouragement and funding, with continued funding from the Heffter Research Institute; Dr Garcia-Romeu was supported by National Institute on Drug Abuse grant T32DA07209 (p. 991).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr Griffiths is on the board of directors of the Heffter Research Institute, a funding sponsor of the study (p. 991).
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are at Johns Hopkins; the session method and the ascending dose sequence come from the same group's earlier studies (Griffiths et al., 2006, 2011) (p. 984). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial giving the same counselling programme with psilocybin or with an active control that participants cannot easily identify, with biochemically verified continuous abstinence at 6 and 12 months as the prespecified primary outcome, enough participants to estimate the difference precisely, and recruitment that does not select for people seeking a psychedelic treatment.

domains.note: No comparison group. The programme included cognitive behavioural therapy, 19 in-person meetings, daily calls after the quit date and other techniques, so any effect of psilocybin cannot be separated from counselling, contact, motivation, expectation or time.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers who answered an advertisement for a psilocybin treatment and still wanted to quit; 15 enrolled out of 323 screened by telephone; motivation and expectation probably higher than in usual treatment-seekers.
Everyone followed the same protocol; sessions and doses were recorded (42 sessions: 16 at the lower dose, 26 at the higher).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Three did not have the third session (one left the country, two declined); one used nicotine replacement during a relapse despite instructions; the dose at sessions 2 and 3 was partly the participant's choice.

All 15 completed and were assessed at 6 months; one participant lacks biochemical samples for weeks 6–10 after the quit date; one was excluded from the withdrawal analysis and one from the first-session persisting-effects ratings.

Abstinence at 6 months was confirmed by breath CO and urinary cotinine, which protects the main outcome, though these cover only about the last day and the last 6 days. Self-reported smoking, craving, self-efficacy, persisting effects and the mechanisms participants endorsed were reported to the unblinded staff who treated them (serious for those outcomes).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration is mentioned. The reported measure, 7-day point prevalence, is standard but more favourable than continuous abstinence, which the text implies was at most 8 of 15.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that psilocybin helps people stop smoking, the study is at critical risk of bias: there is no comparison group, and psilocybin came packaged with intensive counselling and contact in motivated volunteers who sought it out. The card may be cited for feasibility, for the absence of adverse events needing medical intervention in 15 screened people (with none in 15, a true rate of up to about 22% per person cannot be excluded, editors' calculation), and for the observed 12 of 15 biochemically confirmed abstinent at 6 months as a description; it may not be cited for psilocybin's effect or for comparisons with other treatments.

key_findings.finding: 12 of 15 participants (80%) were abstinent 6 months after their quit date by 7-day point prevalence, from self-report confirmed by breath CO and urinary cotinine. Eleven of the 12 reported quitting on the target quit date and were biochemically verified abstinent through the following 10 weeks of treatment; the twelfth reported quitting on the quit date and was verified abstinent at every meeting attended, but had to leave the country and missed samples for weeks 6–10 (editors' calculation: exact 95% interval for 12 of 15 is 52% to 96%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking cessation outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 12 were not all continuously abstinent: three reported self-corrected lapses of 1, 4 and 48 cigarettes in the 16 weeks between the end of treatment and the 6-month follow-up, and another relapsed after 13 weeks of abstinence, smoking an average of 5 cigarettes a day for 14 weeks (using nicotine lozenges and gum) before stopping again before follow-up, as biologically confirmed (editors' count: at most 8 of 15 reported no smoking at all after the quit date).
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking cessation outcomes, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: As printed, 13 weeks of abstinence plus 14 weeks of smoking exceed the 26 weeks between the quit date and the 6-month follow-up (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: All 12 who quit did so after their first session, at the lower dose (20 mg/70 kg); the 3 who did not quit did not manage to quit after their later higher-dose (30 mg/70 kg) sessions either.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 3 who did not quit reported 4, 11 and 22 days of abstinence after the quit date and then resumed daily smoking. Their self-reported smoking fell from an average of 20 to 14 cigarettes a day (t2=5.3, p=0.03), but their breath CO and cotinine did not change significantly from intake to 6 months (editors' reading of Figure 1A–B, approximate: their median cotinine was about 4700 ng/mL at 6 months against about 2300 at the first preparation meeting, and median CO about 49 against about 38 ppm).
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking cessation outcomes, 3rd paragraph (p. 988); Figure 1A–B (p. 989)
key_findings.note: Figure values read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1; medians of 3 people.

key_findings.finding: Across all 15, self-reported smoking fell from intake to 6 months (t14=11.1, p<0.001), and so did breath CO (t14=3.8, p<0.01) and urinary cotinine (t14=2.3, p=0.04) (editors' reading of Figure 2A: mean about 16.6 cigarettes a day at intake and about 3 at 6 months).
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking cessation outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 988); Figure 2A (p. 990)
key_findings.note: Figure 2A read on a 300-dpi crop. Its intake mean is lower than the 19 cigarettes a day of Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: From intake to 6 months, confidence to abstain rose and temptation to smoke and craving fell (repeated-measures ANOVAs F2,34=24.9, F3,43=18.5 and F3,39=12.7, all p<0.001); withdrawal peaked 1 week after the quit date and then fell (F4,46=4.0, p=0.009).
key_findings.locator: Results › Smoking cessation outcomes, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In 42 sessions (16 at 20 mg/70 kg, 26 at 30 mg/70 kg) no clinically significant adverse event needed a physician or medication. Six of 15 participants (40%) gave strong (five) or extreme (one) ratings of fear, fear of insanity or feeling trapped at some point, in five lower-dose and five higher-dose sessions; all were managed with interpersonal support and had resolved by the end of the session.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety data, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure and heart rate peaked on average 1.5 to 2.5 hours after psilocybin: systolic mean peak 153 mmHg (SD 11, range 134–173) against 125 at baseline; diastolic 87 (SD 11, range 72–105) against 71; heart rate 87 beats a minute (SD 11, range 66–120) against 68.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety data, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Eight of the 10 participants asked about headache reported at least one headache after a session, lasting a mean 5.8 hours (range 2.0–9.5) and starting a mean 6.2 hours after the dose (range 3.5–11.5), rated mild on average (2.6 on a scale from 1 to 6); five took over-the-counter medicine that evening. The Visual Effects Questionnaire showed no increase in clinically significant or bothersome visual effects between intake and 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety data, 3rd paragraph and 4th paragraph (begins p. 987, continues p. 988)

key_findings.finding: 13 of 15 (87%) rated at least one psilocybin session among the 10 most meaningful experiences of their lives, 11 (73%) among the five most spiritually significant, and 13 (87%) said a session had increased their well-being or life satisfaction very much. Lifetime Mysticism Scale scores rose from intake to 1 week after the last session (mean difference +54; t14=3.5, p=0.004). On the Persisting Effects Questionnaire, positive subscales averaged 55.8% (SD 12.1) of the maximum score and negative subscales 5.3% (SD 3.6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Persisting effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 988, continues p. 990) and 2nd paragraph (p. 990); Table 4 (p. 987)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 55.8% and 5.3% and their SDs are the mean and SD of the 18 positive and the 18 negative subscale-by-session means in Table 4 (6 subscales, 3 sessions), so the SDs describe spread across subscales and sessions, not across people; the session means rest on 14, 15 and 12 people (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Asked 3 weeks after the quit date how psilocybin had helped, participants most often endorsed a changed orientation toward the future (11 of 15, 73%), a stronger belief in their ability to quit (11, 73%) and changed life priorities (10, printed as 67.7% in Table 5 and 68% in the text); one participant, the one with the shortest abstinence (4 days), said it had not helped. These are participants' attributions, not measured mechanisms.
key_findings.locator: Table 5 (p. 988); Results › Persisting effects, 3rd paragraph (p. 990)

key_findings.finding: The Discussion compares the 80% with 24.9% to 26.3% (bupropion) and 33.5% to 35.2% (varenicline) at about 6 months in other trials, 17.2% at 6 months for the CBT programme the counselling was based on, and 45% to 59% in two trials of extended counselling combined with bupropion and nicotine replacement; it notes that participants here had substantially more staff contact.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 prints 10 of 15 endorsing changed life priorities as 67.7%, and the text rounds it to 68% (pp. 988, 990) (editors' calculation: 10 of 15 is 66.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Arithmetic slip; the correct figure is 67%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Persisting Effects Questionnaire is said to have 140 items rated in six categories (p. 986), but the category sizes given (26, 22, 18, 18, two and 43 items) do not add up to 140 (editors' calculation: they sum to 129).
reporting_issues.consequence: The questionnaire's structure cannot be reconstructed from the paper, so the percentage-of-maximum scores in Table 4 cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 states N=15 for all three sessions, but its own footnote excludes one participant from session 1 and only 12 participants had a third session (p. 987).
reporting_issues.consequence: The session means rest on 14, 15 and 12 people, not 15 each.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 19 cigarettes a day at intake (SD 2.9, range 15–25; p. 984), and the text compares a relapse with a mean of 19 a day at intake (p. 988), but the timeline follow-back intake bar in Figure 2A, the basis of the t test, is lower (editors' reading at 300 dpi: about 16.6 cigarettes a day, p. 990).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different intake figures, probably usual smoking at intake against the 30-day calendar, are not distinguished in the paper; the size of the reported reduction depends on which is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The four repeated-measures ANOVAs are reported with degrees of freedom of F2,34, F3,43, F3,39 and F4,46 (p. 988), smaller than 15 participants measured at 10 time points would give, so a sphericity correction must have been applied, but none is described (editors' calculation: uncorrected degrees of freedom would be 9 and 126).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the method should be stated so the tests can be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports significantly reduced self-reported smoking in the three participants who did not quit (p. 988), while their breath CO and cotinine did not change significantly from intake to 6 months (p. 988), and Figure 1 shows their median values higher at the 6-month follow-up than at the first preparation meeting, its earliest time point (Figure 1 has no intake point) (p. 989).
reporting_issues.consequence: In this subgroup the self-reported reduction is not supported by the objective measures, which suggests self-reports in this unblinded study may be optimistic.

reporting_issues.issue: The relapse timeline does not fit the follow-up: one of the 12 abstinent participants is reported to have relapsed after 13 weeks of continuous abstinence and smoked for 14 weeks before resuming abstinence prior to the 6-month follow-up (p. 988), but the follow-up came 16 weeks after the end of the 15-week programme, that is 26 weeks after the week-5 quit date (pp. 984, 988). The 27 weeks of abstinence and smoking exceed the time available even before the 7 days of renewed abstinence that 7-day point prevalence requires (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one printed duration is wrong, and the paper does not explain it. This participant's abstinence at follow-up rests on the biochemical confirmation, not on the reported timeline, so the 12 of 15 abstinent and the 8 of 15 reporting no smoking after the quit date are unaffected.
