design_detail: Observational 6-month follow-up, by the trial's own team, of the two randomized arms of the phase 2, double-blind trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram treatment (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021) in 59 adults with major depressive disorder at one site (the NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility, p. 4). Study conditions: psilocybin therapy, two oral 25-mg doses of COMP360 psilocybin 3 weeks apart with daily placebo capsules; escitalopram treatment, 1 mg psilocybin on the same two dosing days with escitalopram 10 mg daily for 3 weeks then 20 mg daily for 3 weeks; about 20 h of in-person psychological support in both arms. After the week-6 end point there was no study treatment and no restriction on psychiatric care, and escitalopram could be continued or stopped. Self-report questionnaires online every month (QIDS-SR-16) and every 3 months (WSAS, Watts Connectedness Scale, Flourishing Scale, Meaning in Life Questionnaire) for 6 months after the end of the trial (to week 30); at month 6, retrospective yes/no questions on medication, therapy and psychedelic use during follow-up. Safety was not assessed during follow-up. Per both protocol versions in the supplement (pre-trial V5 and V7 at trial completion), patients were to be told their allocation at the end of the week-6 visit, the 6-month follow-up was planned as unblinded, to assess safety and enduring effects, and at that visit the study psychiatrist was to discuss continuing or withdrawing escitalopram (escitalopram arm) or treatment options (psilocybin arm) (Protocol pp. 44, 48, 59, 79; 93, 97, 108, 129); the article mentions neither the unblinding nor these consultations, and it does not report the structured interviews planned at 6 months (V5) or at 1 and 6 months (V7).
can_establish: Whether, in this small and mostly self-referred group of patients with major depressive disorder, those randomized to two psilocybin sessions differed from those randomized to 6 weeks of escitalopram in self-rated depression, functioning, connectedness, meaning in life and flourishing during the 6 months after treatment ended, among those who returned questionnaires and whatever other treatment they then had.
cannot_establish: Whether either treatment caused the improvement still present at 6 months (no placebo or untreated comparison, patients had been told their allocation at week 6 according to the protocol, and about three-quarters of respondents had other treatment, including psychedelics, during follow-up), whether psilocybin's effects outlast those of an SSRI given for a full course (escitalopram stopped at 6 weeks unless patients chose to continue it), whether the two are equivalent on depression (not powered for small differences), or anything about harms after week 6 (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: The patients of the original trial; eligibility details are referred to the trial report (p. 3). Trial profile: about 1000 assessed for eligibility, about 941 excluded (about 891 not meeting inclusion criteria, about 50 declined), 59 randomized (Fig. 1, p. 6). The abstract says patients were recruited from a hospital in the UK (p. 1), whereas the original trial report describes mostly self-referral through websites and social media (per the companion card sc_carhart_harris_2021).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Abstract: DSM-IV major depressive disorder with HAM-D of 17 or more, no MRI or SSRI contraindications, diagnosis confirmed by a GP or mental health professional, aged 18–80, competent in English (p. 1). Methods: aged 18–85, physically healthy, unipolar major depressive disorder diagnosed by a physician, willing to stop antidepressants and/or psychological therapies before baseline (p. 3). The two age limits differ.
sample.demographics: Psilocybin vs escitalopram (Table 1, p. 5): age 43.3 (SD 11.7, range 21–64) vs 39.1 (SD 9.7, range 22–60) years; female sex 11 (37%) vs 9 (31%); White 28 (93%) vs 24 (83%); employed 21 (70%) vs 21 (72%); university education 22 (73%) vs 23 (79%); no previous psilocybin use 22 (73%) vs 21 (72%); weekly alcohol 36.8 (SD 43.1) vs 67.7 (SD 66.6) g; stopped a psychiatric medication for the trial 11 (37%) vs 12 (41%); illness duration 22.1 (SD 10.7) vs 15.1 (SD 11.0) years; psychiatric medications previously used 2.2 vs 1.8; previous psychotherapy 28 (93%) vs 26 (90%); pretreatment QIDS-SR-16 14.5 (SD 3.9, range 7–23) vs 16.4 (SD 4.1, range 6–22); HAM-D-17 19.2 (range 16–23) vs 18.4 (range 11–26). Only sex assigned at birth was recorded; gender was not (p. 5).
sample.attrition: None lost to the week-6 end point. Missing at each follow-up time point, psilocybin vs escitalopram, reasons unknown: month 1, 1 vs 4; month 2, 2 vs 4; month 3, 9 vs 11; month 4, 4 vs 10; month 5, 3 vs 8; month 6, 5 vs 8 (Fig. 1, p. 6); 25 of 30 and 21 of 29 completed the 6-month questionnaire (p. 1). Average missing QIDS-SR-16 data 13% (range 3–29%) vs 26% (range 14–38%); for the 3-monthly scales 19% (range 13–23%) vs 31% (range 24–38%) (pp. 5, 7). No significant demographic differences between completers and non-completers (Supplementary Table S2, not read). Supplement (pp. 179–181): 16 of 30 psilocybin and 12 of 29 escitalopram patients completed at least 85% of the QIDS-SR-16 follow-ups; no psilocybin patient and 2 escitalopram patients completed none (one of the two a remitter at week 6); Table 2B gives 15 and 13 patients with every follow-up completed, which cannot be reconciled with 12 escitalopram patients completing at least 85%. Different questionnaires at the same time point had different numbers missing (Supplementary Table 1). Completers and non-completers did not differ significantly on the variables tested (Tables 2A–B and 10A–B, pp. 180–181, 194–196), but those tables contain copying errors (reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Follow-up results come from those who answered online questionnaires; more data were missing in the escitalopram arm, which the authors suggest may reflect greater positive regard for psilocybin (p. 5). The trial sample was mostly self-referred volunteers seeking a psilocybin trial (per the companion card). Chance baseline imbalances: longer illness, lower QIDS-SR-16 and less alcohol in the psilocybin arm (Table 1, p. 5), although the Methods state there were no baseline differences (p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Randomized allocation in the trial, by members of Imperial College London outside the research team with a random-number generator, without stratification (p. 4). Treatments during follow-up recorded only at month 6 by three retrospective questions: any formal mental health treatment and what it was (for example antidepressants or psychotherapy), and whether psychedelics were taken (p. 4); the exact methods, timing and frequency of medication, psychedelic use and therapy were not collected (pp. 11, 13). According to both protocol versions, allocation was disclosed to every patient at the end of the week-6 visit, before the follow-up began (Protocol pp. 59, 79; 108, 129).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: psilocybin therapy, two oral 25-mg doses of COMP360 psilocybin at visits 2 and 4, 3 weeks apart, with daily placebo capsules for 6 weeks; escitalopram treatment, 1 mg psilocybin at visits 2 and 4 with escitalopram 10 mg daily for 3 weeks then 20 mg daily for 3 weeks (pp. 1, 4). In both arms about 20 h of in-person support (screening, preparation, dosing days of about 6–8 h with two therapists, integration) and up to six optional integration calls, taken up equally (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: During follow-up, 8 of 26 respondents in the psilocybin arm (30.8%) and 4 of 23 in the escitalopram arm (17.4%) reported taking psychedelics; which substance, how much and how often were not recorded (Table 2, p. 7). Baseline alcohol use in Table 1; other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to the follow-up. Pre-trial antidepressants and psychological therapies were stopped before the trial baseline (p. 3).

comparison.controls: The escitalopram arm (n=29): 6 weeks of escitalopram with 1 mg psilocybin on both dosing days and the same psychological support. Neither arm had study treatment after week 6. There was no placebo or untreated group.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomized, so balanced on average; with 59 patients, chance imbalances in illness duration, baseline severity and alcohol use (Table 1). What patients did after week 6 (other treatment, psychedelic use) was recorded only as yes/no. Blinding was not assessed during the trial (per the companion card), and according to both protocol versions patients were told their allocation at the end of the week-6 visit (Protocol pp. 59, 79; 108, 129), so the follow-up was open-label by design; the article does not say so.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: During follow-up, escitalopram vs psilocybin arm respondents: medication 10 of 23 (43.5%) vs 8 of 26 (30.7%), p=0.53; therapy 9 of 22 (40.9%) vs 12 of 26 (46.2%), p=0.94; psychedelics 4 of 23 (17.4%) vs 8 of 26 (30.8%), p=0.45 (chi-square; Table 2, p. 7). Editors' check: the printed p values match chi-square tests with continuity correction. In the imputation models that included them, none of the three yes/no covariates was significantly associated with any outcome (Supplementary Table 9, pp. 191–194); in one model of Supplementary Table 12B, follow-up therapy went with higher (worse) QIDS-SR-16 scores at month 3 (3.13, SE 1.35, p = 0.03; p. 200).

outcomes.instruments: QIDS-SR-16 every month, the only depression measure at follow-up; every 3 months the Work and Social Adjustment Scale (WSAS), Watts Connectedness Scale (WCS), Flourishing Scale (FS) and Meaning in Life Questionnaire (MLQ); all self-report questionnaires sent by e-mail through an online survey platform, to be completed within a week of receipt (pp. 3–4). Response (QIDS-SR-16 reduction of at least 50%) and remission (QIDS-SR-16 of 5 or less) (p. 7). Safety was not assessed during follow-up (pp. 1, 14).
outcomes.validity_norms: Published scales, described as having acceptable to very good internal consistency (p. 4). The authors cite their own team's analysis questioning the validity of the QIDS-SR-16 (Weiss et al., 2023) as a possible reason for the null depression results at 6 weeks and during follow-up (p. 13). Supplementary Materials 1 (pp. 178–179) gives Cronbach's alpha ranges across time points: QIDS-SR-16 0.82–0.84, WSAS 0.71–0.85, WCS 0.83–0.91, FS 0.75–0.98 and MLQ 0.61–0.71; the MLQ's lower bound is below the conventional 0.70, and the MLQ was scored as one total across its Presence and Search subscales.
outcomes.operationalization: Change from the pretreatment baseline to each follow-up time point; the between-arm difference is the Time × Condition coefficient of linear mixed models with a random intercept per participant (pp. 4–5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate applied to the omnibus tests and, in a second step, to the omnibus tests and pairwise comparisons together (pp. 4–5); single-arm analyses, the imputation and covariate analyses and the sensitivity analyses were not corrected (pp. 5, 9–10). Five outcomes, each at up to seven follow-up time points.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: All outcomes were rated by the participants themselves, with no assessor. Per the companion card, blinding was not assessed in the trial and participants given 25 mg rated the acute effects as more intense than those given 1 mg. According to both protocol versions, patients were told their allocation at the end of the week-6 visit (Protocol pp. 59, 79; 108, 129), so every follow-up rating was made by patients who knew their allocation; the article does not mention this.

analysis.effect_sizes: Between-arm difference in change from baseline, psilocybin minus escitalopram, B with 95% CI (Table 3, panel 1A, p. 9; negative favours psilocybin for QIDS-SR-16 and WSAS, positive favours psilocybin for WCS and MLQ): QIDS-SR-16 week 6 −1.28 (−3.93 to 1.36); month 1 −3.58 (−6.31 to −0.85); month 2 1.02 (−1.71 to 3.77); month 3 0.13 (−2.89 to 3.16); month 4 0.93 (−1.97 to 3.84); month 5 1.80 (−1.04 to 4.64); month 6 1.51 (−1.35 to 4.38; p=0.311). WSAS week 6 −7.53 (−12.1 to −2.94), month 3 −10.29 (−15.5 to −5.08), month 6 −7.46 (−12.4 to −2.47). WCS 19.35 (10.25 to 28.46), 14.18 (4.04 to 24.36), 11.02 (1.25 to 20.83). MLQ 5.01 (1.23 to 8.80), 5.90 (1.59 to 10.23), 4.86 (0.67 to 9.05). Flourishing: omnibus Time × Condition F(3,147)=1.79, p=0.15. Within-arm change from baseline at month 6, psilocybin vs escitalopram (Table 3, panels 1B–1C, pp. 9–10): QIDS-SR-16 −5.27 (d 1.33) vs −6.83 (d 1.35); WSAS −12.73 (d 1.69) vs −5.26 (d 0.66); WCS 21.99 (d 1.22) vs 10.95 (d 0.74); MLQ 6.98 (d 1.02) vs 2.12 (d 0.31); FS 12.72 (d 1.38) vs 8.89 (d 1.08). Response and remission (Supplementary Table 6, cited in the article as S7; percentages of all randomized patients, chi-square p): month 6 response 43% vs 48% (p = .70) and remission 37% vs 34% (p = .86), matching the editors' reading of Fig. 2B–C; significant differences only for remission at week 6 (57% vs 28%) and month 1 (53% vs 21%). Imputation and sensitivity analyses (the second Supplementary Table 7, Tables 9 and 12A–B): see key findings.
analysis.covariates: First and second sets of analyses: linear mixed models with Timepoint × Condition and a random intercept per participant, without imputation (p. 5). Third set: single imputation of missing follow-up values with each participant's worst follow-up score in the psilocybin arm and best follow-up score in the escitalopram arm. Fourth set: the same imputation plus three yes/no covariates for medication, non-drug therapy and psychedelic use during follow-up (p. 5). Results of the third and fourth sets are in the supplement's second Supplementary Table 7 and in Supplementary Table 9 (cited in the article as S8 and S9; pp. 189–194), and sensitivity analyses excluding patients with missing data or follow-up psychedelic use, or adding a missingness covariate to the imputation, are in Supplementary Table 12A–B (pp. 199–200); see key findings.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03429075 (pp. 1, 4), and the article states that all outcome measures reported were prespecified in the study protocol (p. 4). The supplement holds the protocol (V1, pre-trial V5, V7 at trial completion), the amendment summary and two statistical analysis plans (November and December 2020). The protocols list the MLQ, FS and WSAS among measures taken before and after treatment and a self-constructed connectedness questionnaire, without naming the WCS (Protocol pp. 61–62, 110–111), and plan monthly QIDS-SR-16 and more comprehensive assessments at 1, 3 and 6 months after the first dosing session without naming the scales (Protocol pp. 60, 109–110). Both analysis plans analyse only change to week 6; their secondary outcomes include the FS and WSAS but not the WCS or MLQ, and no follow-up analysis is planned (SAP pp. 146, 151–155, 163–171). Deviations: the follow-up was planned to assess safety (Protocol pp. 44, 93), but safety was not assessed (p. 1), and the planned structured interviews are not reported. The registry record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The supplement (read for this update) reports response and remission (Supplementary Table 6) as shares of all randomized patients without stating how missing data were handled; its imputation tables omit the Flourishing Scale although their captions list it, and the second Supplementary Table 7 repeats the unimputed WCS estimates (pp. 189–191; Supplementary Table 9, with follow-up covariates, gives different WCS values, pp. 193–194); the article does not report the results of the sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Table 12A–B), in which some connectedness and meaning-in-life differences lost significance; and Tables 2A, 2B, 10B and 12B contain copying errors (reporting issues). Pairwise flourishing comparisons were run after a null omnibus test to reconcile the result with the original trial (pp. 8, 10). The safety follow-up and structured interviews planned in the protocol are not reported. The abstract gives the 6-month depression difference (1.51) without its direction.
analysis.power: No power calculation for the follow-up; the authors state that the study was not optimally powered to detect small but meaningful differences (pp. 1, 13). Editors' note: with 25 and 21 respondents at month 6, only large differences could be detected; the 6-month QIDS-SR-16 interval runs from 1.35 points in favour of psilocybin to 4.38 points in favour of escitalopram.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six months after a 6-week trial, self-rated depression had improved from baseline by similar amounts in both arms (QIDS-SR-16 change −5.27 with psilocybin and −6.83 with escitalopram). The only significant between-arm depression difference was at month 1 (10 weeks after baseline), in favour of psilocybin; from month 2 the point estimates slightly favoured escitalopram, all intervals including zero. Work and social functioning, connectedness and meaning in life had improved more in the psilocybin arm at months 3 and 6; flourishing did not differ. Up to 38% of the escitalopram arm and 30% of the psilocybin arm were missing at a follow-up point, and among respondents most reported other treatment during follow-up, including psychedelics (31% vs 17%). Harms were not recorded. In the supplement's conservative imputation (worst follow-up score for psilocybin, best for escitalopram) the 6-month depression difference favoured escitalopram by 2.27 points (p = .09; 2.56, p = .10, with follow-up treatment covariates), while the functioning, connectedness and meaning-in-life differences favouring psilocybin stayed significant; in sensitivity analyses excluding patients with missing data or follow-up psychedelic use, the 3-month connectedness and meaning-in-life differences were not significant (p = .08 and .52), and with a missingness covariate the 6-month connectedness difference was not (p = .07). According to the protocol, patients had been told their allocation at week 6.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says both arms yielded sustained improvements and that psilocybin therapy had greater between-condition differences in functioning, connectedness and meaning in life, while calling the results descriptive and listing limitations (p. 1). The Discussion suggests that psilocybin therapy "might be linked to sustained higher levels of global mental health" (p. 11) and argues, from correlations in Supplementary Table 11A (Supplement p. 198), that the psilocybin arm's improvement was more stable (p. 14), although those correlations (escitalopram 0.13–0.73, psilocybin 0.33–0.70, the largest being the escitalopram arm's at month 3) come without sample sizes, intervals or a test of the difference between arms. For the escitalopram arm's lasting improvement it offers the trial's intensive support, an explanation it says applies equally to the psilocybin arm (p. 12), or non-specific factors such as post-trial treatment, spontaneous improvement and regression to the mean (p. 13); it concedes that adjunct treatments may have had a causal role in the between-arm differences (p. 11), but does not weigh spontaneous improvement or regression to the mean for the psilocybin arm, where they apply equally. The Research in context panel restates the original trial as having found psilocybin therapy as effective as escitalopram and significantly better in well-being, anhedonia, emotional acceptance, suicidality and functioning (p. 2), whereas the original trial was not designed for equivalence, drew no conclusions from its uncorrected secondary outcomes, and printed a suicidality interval that cannot be reconciled with its group intervals (per the companion card). A headline version (the antidepressant effect of psilocybin lasts longer than that of an SSRI) would overstate: at 6 months depression did not differ and numerically favoured escitalopram, escitalopram was given for only 6 weeks, most respondents had other treatment, data were missing for up to a third, and harms after week 6 were not assessed. The article also describes the imputation analyses as consistent with the uncorrected results for all measures (pp. 10–11), although the supplement's imputation tables omit the Flourishing Scale and one of them (the second Supplementary Table 7) repeats the unimputed WCS estimates, and it does not report the results of its sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Table 12A–B).

timeline.event: The original 6-week trial: no significant difference on the self-rated primary outcome (QIDS-SR-16 −2.0, 95% CI −5.0 to 0.9); secondary outcomes uncorrected
Same team's psychometric reanalysis of the week-6 data, cited here for problems with the QIDS-SR-16, the only depression measure used at follow-up
Same team's analysis of expectancy and suggestibility in the same trial: after adjustment for expectancy no between-arm difference at week 6 on any of six scales

12-month follow-up of a waiting-list-controlled trial of psilocybin therapy in major depressive disorder (Gukasyan et al., 2022, J Psychopharmacol), cited here for a 79% response rate at 6 months; not read
6-month follow-up of an open-label study of psilocybin with psychological support in treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018, Psychopharmacology), cited here; not read

replication.where_it_stands: Among the papers read, this is the only comparison of psilocybin therapy with an SSRI beyond the end of treatment; it is observational after week 6, written by the trial's own team, and based on self-report with substantial missing data. The longer follow-ups that the authors cite (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018; Gukasyan et al., 2022) had no SSRI comparison and were not read. The same team's paper on antidepressant discontinuation before the trial (Erritzoe et al., 2024, J Psychopharmacol, doi 10.1177/02698811241237870) was not among the files.

Davis-Jewish General Hospital Foundation (JGH Québec Network on Suicide, Mood Disorders and Related Disorders). None of the other authors reported conflicts. COMPASS Pathways delivered the study drug (COMP360) and, through a contract agreement with Imperial College (study sponsor and intellectual property holder), was granted access to the study's safety data.
funding.affiliations_note: A secondary report by the trial's own team: eleven of the twelve authors are at the Centre for Psychedelic Research, Imperial College London, including the original trial's first and last authors; B. Weiss (shared last author) is at Johns Hopkins and K. T. Greenway at McGill (p. 1). DE, TB, BW and KG had access to and verified the data (p. 14). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of psilocybin therapy against an SSRI continued for a full course (or with arms that continue and stop the SSRI), followed for 6 months or longer with outcomes rated by assessors unaware of allocation, every later treatment and every psychedelic use recorded prospectively, attrition kept low and its reasons recorded, and adverse events, including suicidality, collected throughout follow-up.

domains.note: Random-number generator, run by Imperial College staff outside the research team (p. 4). Baseline imbalances in illness duration, baseline QIDS-SR-16 and alcohol use (Table 1) are compatible with chance in 59 patients.

After week 6 there was no protocol, so the comparison is of assignment followed by uncontrolled care. Participants could probably tell 25 mg from 1 mg and blinding was never assessed; according to both protocol versions, patients were told their allocation at the week-6 visit, where the study psychiatrist was to discuss continuing or withdrawing escitalopram or other treatment options (Protocol pp. 48, 59, 97, 108), so follow-up treatment choices were made with knowledge of allocation. At month 6 about three-quarters of respondents reported other treatment, psychedelic use was more frequent in the psilocybin arm (31% vs 17%), and escitalopram was continued or stopped at the patient's choice (pp. 4, 7). Adjustment used only yes/no covariates, none of them significant in the imputation models (Supplementary Table 9).

Missing at follow-up points up to 9 of 30 and 11 of 29, more in the escitalopram arm, reasons unknown (Fig. 1); different questionnaires at the same time point had different numbers missing (Supplementary Table 1). Mixed models without imputation assume data missing at random. Under the conservative imputation the 6-month depression difference moved further towards escitalopram (2.27, p = .09) and the functioning, connectedness and meaning-in-life differences stayed significant, but the imputed WCS estimates in the second Supplementary Table 7 repeat the unimputed ones (Table 9, with follow-up covariates, gives different values) and the FS is not shown; with a missingness covariate the 6-month WCS difference was not significant (p = .07), and excluding patients with missing data or psychedelic use left the 3-month WCS and MLQ differences non-significant (p = .08 and .52; Supplementary Table 12A–B).

Every outcome is self-rated online by participants who, according to both protocol versions, had been told their allocation at the week-6 visit (Protocol pp. 59, 79, 108, 129), many of whom preferred psilocybin (per the companion card). Connectedness and meaning in life are outcomes close to what psilocybin therapy is expected to change, so reports are likely to be influenced by knowledge of allocation.

Five outcomes at up to seven time points, with false discovery rate control for the main analyses. The protocols list the MLQ, FS, WSAS and a self-constructed connectedness questionnaire but do not name the WCS or specify the follow-up measures, and both analysis plans cover only week 6, so no follow-up analysis was prespecified (Protocol pp. 61–62, 110–111; SAP pp. 146, 151–155). Pairwise flourishing comparisons were added after a null omnibus test (pp. 8, 10); all five outcomes are reported at every time point and the alternative analyses are in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized comparison is preserved at follow-up, but the outcomes are self-reported by participants who, according to the protocol, had been told their allocation at week 6; up to a third of the data are missing at some time points; and most respondents had other treatment, recorded only as yes/no. Measurement bias would favour psilocybin on the secondary outcomes (functioning, connectedness, meaning in life). The supplement's imputation and sensitivity analyses leave the depression comparison null, with point estimates favouring escitalopram, and leave most functioning, connectedness and meaning-in-life differences significant, with exceptions for connectedness and meaning in some analyses; its tables contain copying errors, and safety, which the protocol planned to follow, was not assessed. The card may be cited for the between-arm and within-arm estimates with their intervals, the absence of a depression difference after month 1, the follow-up treatment shares (with their denominators), response and remission as shares of all randomized patients, and the lack of safety data; not for durable superiority of psilocybin over escitalopram, nor for attributing either arm's lasting improvement to its treatment.

key_findings.finding: Of 59 randomized (30 psilocybin, 29 escitalopram), none was lost to week 6; 25 of 30 and 21 of 29 completed the 6-month follow-up questionnaire. Missing at months 1 to 6: 1, 2, 9, 4, 3 and 5 in the psilocybin arm and 4, 4, 11, 10, 8 and 8 in the escitalopram arm, reasons unknown.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Findings (p. 1); Fig. 1 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Between-arm difference in QIDS-SR-16 change from baseline (psilocybin minus escitalopram): week 6 −1.28 (95% CI −3.93 to 1.36); month 1 (10 weeks) −3.58 (−6.31 to −0.85; p=0.011, FDR-adjusted p=0.021); months 2 to 6 between 0.13 and 1.80, all intervals including zero; month 6 1.51 (−1.35 to 4.38; p=0.311), a numerically larger improvement with escitalopram.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Findings (p. 1); Results › Depressive symptomology, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Table 3, panel 1A (p. 9)
key_findings.note: The week-6 estimate from this model (−1.28) differs from the original trial's primary result (−2.0, 95% CI −5.0 to 0.9, per the companion card); the paper does not explain the difference.

key_findings.finding: Within-arm QIDS-SR-16 change from baseline: psilocybin −6.48 at month 3 (d 1.24) and −5.27 at month 6 (d 1.33); escitalopram −6.59 at month 3 (d 1.33) and −6.83 at month 6 (d 1.35).
key_findings.locator: Results › Depressive symptomology, 2nd paragraph (p. 7); Table 3, panels 1B–1C (p. 9)
key_findings.note: Single-arm, uncorrected before-after changes with no untreated comparison; the escitalopram-arm confidence intervals in Table 3 are inconsistent with the coefficients and standard errors (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Responders (at least 50% QIDS-SR-16 reduction) and remitters (QIDS-SR-16 of 5 or less), psilocybin vs escitalopram, Supplementary Table 6 (cited in the article as S7): response at week 6 70% vs 48% (p = .05), month 1 53% vs 31%, month 2 53% vs 48%, month 3 50% vs 41%, month 4 50% vs 38%, month 5 53% vs 55% and month 6 43% vs 48% (p = .70); remission at week 6 57% vs 28% (p = .01), month 1 53% vs 21% (p = .01), month 2 47% vs 24%, month 3 37% vs 24%, month 4 40% vs 24%, month 5 33% vs 41% and month 6 37% vs 34% (p = .86). The text states that remitters were significantly more frequent in the psilocybin arm at month 1, and the Discussion gives escitalopram-arm response around 50% and remission around 30% at 6 months and psilocybin-arm response of 43%.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Table 6 (file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf); Fig. 2B–C (p. 8); Results › Depressive symptomology, 2nd paragraph (p. 7); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 12) and 16th paragraph (p. 14)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: every percentage is a whole count of all 30 and 29 randomized patients, and the printed p values equal uncorrected chi-square tests on those counts at 12 of 14 time points, so missing patients were counted as non-responders or imputed (not stated). At week 6 the table's percentages (57% psilocybin remission, 48% escitalopram response, as in the original trial per the companion card) differ from Fig. 2 (60.1% and 44.6%, re-measured on the 298-ppi figure image) and from the table's own week-6 p values, which fit the figure's counts (reporting issues). The editors' earlier figure readings for months 1–6 agree with the table.

key_findings.finding: Work and social functioning (WSAS, lower is better), between-arm difference favouring psilocybin: week 6 −7.53 (95% CI −12.1 to −2.94), month 3 −10.29 (−15.5 to −5.08), month 6 −7.46 (−12.4 to −2.47); within-arm change at month 6 −12.73 (d 1.69) with psilocybin vs −5.26 (d 0.66) with escitalopram.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Findings (p. 1); Results › Work and social functioning (p. 7); Table 3, panels 1A–1C (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Connectedness (WCS) and meaning in life (MLQ) improved more with psilocybin at week 6, month 3 and month 6 (month 6: WCS 11.02, 95% CI 1.25 to 20.83; MLQ 4.86, 0.67 to 9.05); in the escitalopram arm the MLQ change was not significant at any time point (month 6: 2.12, d 0.31). Flourishing (FS) improved in both arms (month 6: 12.72 vs 8.89) with no significant Time × Condition interaction (F(3,147)=1.79, p=0.15).
key_findings.locator: Results › Meaning in life (p. 7, continued on p. 8), Connectedness and Flourishing (p. 8, Flourishing continued on p. 10); Table 3, panels 1A–1C (pp. 9–10)

key_findings.finding: 37 of 59 trial patients (62.7%) received some form of additional intervention during follow-up. Among respondents, psilocybin vs escitalopram arm: medication 8 (30.7%) vs 10 (43.5%), p=0.53; psychedelics 8 (30.8%) vs 4 (17.4%), p=0.45; therapy 12 (46.2%) vs 9 (40.9%), p=0.94 (chi-square tests).
key_findings.locator: Results › Potential treatment confounds during follow-up; Table 2
key_findings.note: Denominators (editors' sums of the yes and no counts in Table 2): 26 in the psilocybin arm and 23 (22 for therapy) in the escitalopram arm. The 62.7% uses all 59 randomized patients as denominator although only 48–49 answered; editors' calculation: 37 of 49 respondents, about 76%.

key_findings.finding: Repeating the analyses with imputation favouring escitalopram (worst follow-up score for psilocybin, best for escitalopram), the between-arm differences at month 6 were QIDS-SR-16 2.27 (SE 1.34, p = .09), WSAS −7.12 (2.20, p < .001), WCS 11.02 (4.33, p = .04) and MLQ 4.10 (1.85, p = .02); with covariates for follow-up medication, psychedelics and therapy they were 2.56 (1.58, p = .10), −6.90 (2.60, printed p < .009), 10.30 (4.98, printed as 110.30; p = .04) and 4.29 (2.15, p = .04). The month-1 depression difference remained (−2.91, printed p = .01; −3.19, p = .04). The article describes these results as consistent with the uncorrected analyses for all measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Impact of attrition bias and potentially confounding variables on the results (p. 10, continued on p. 11); the supplement's second Supplementary Table 7 (pp. 189–191) and Supplementary Table 9 (pp. 191–194), cited in the article as S8–S9 (file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf)
key_findings.note: Editors' checks: neither table reports the Flourishing Scale although their captions list it; the imputed WCS estimates in the second Supplementary Table 7 repeat the unimputed ones (Table 9's differ); several t values are copied from Supplementary Table 3, and the month-1 difference (−2.91, SE 1.34) gives p of about .03, not .01 (reporting issues). Positive QIDS-SR-16 values favour escitalopram.

key_findings.finding: Safety was not assessed during follow-up; the authors call the absence of a systematic assessment of side effects a limitation.
key_findings.locator: Summary › Methods (p. 1); Discussion, 16th paragraph (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: In each arm, participants received about 20 h of in-person therapeutic support during the 6-week trial (screening, preparation, two dosing days of about 6–8 h with two therapists, integration), plus up to six optional integration calls taken up equally in both arms.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph (two therapists, about 6–8 h per dosing day) and 2nd paragraph (about 20 h of support, optional calls)

key_findings.finding: 34% of the escitalopram arm reported continuing or resuming medication during follow-up; escitalopram was given for only 6 weeks, and the authors state that a better comparison would arguably have continued escitalopram throughout follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 12); 12th paragraph (p. 13)
key_findings.note: 34% matches 10 of 29 randomized patients, whereas Table 2 gives 10 of 23 respondents (43.5%).

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that correlations between change at 6 weeks and change at later follow-ups were larger and more consistent in the psilocybin arm (for example exceeding r=0.30) than in the escitalopram arm, and infer that the escitalopram arm's later improvement may owe more to other interventions or chance changes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 15th paragraph (p. 13, continued on p. 14); Supplementary Table 11A (file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf; unnumbered landscape page after p. 197)
key_findings.note: Supplementary Table 11A: correlation of week-6 change with later change, escitalopram 0.57 (month 1), 0.13, 0.73, 0.38, 0.19 and 0.25 (month 6); psilocybin 0.70, 0.61, 0.47, 0.47, 0.55 and 0.33; no sample sizes, intervals or test of the difference between arms. Editors' calculation (Fisher z): if computed on the 21 and 25 month-6 respondents, r = 0.25 has a 95% interval from about −0.2 to 0.6 and r = 0.33 from about −0.1 to 0.6. Correlations of earlier with later change do not show that either treatment caused the later scores.

key_findings.finding: Response in the psilocybin arm at 6 months (43%) was lower than the 79% at 6 months reported in an earlier follow-up of psilocybin therapy for major depressive disorder (Gukasyan et al., 2022), which the authors relate to that study's open-label design, baseline severity or type of support.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 16th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Both protocol versions in the supplement (pre-trial V5 and V7 at trial completion) state that patients would be told their allocation at the end of the week-6 visit, describe the 6-month follow-up as unblinded and intended to assess safety and enduring effects, and plan a consultation with the study psychiatrist at that visit about continuing escitalopram or returning to usual treatment after controlled withdrawal (escitalopram arm) or about treatment options (psilocybin arm). The article mentions neither the unblinding nor these consultations, and reports that safety was not assessed during follow-up (p. 1).
key_findings.locator: Supplement: Protocol V5 §1.1 Basic study design, 2nd paragraph (p. 44); §2.1.2 Escitalopram, last two paragraphs (p. 48); Visit 7 (p. 59, continued on p. 60); §13 Breaking of blind (p. 79). Protocol V7: the same passages (pp. 93, 97, 108–109, 129)

key_findings.finding: Prespecification: the protocols list the MLQ, Flourishing Scale and WSAS among measures taken before and after treatment, and a self-constructed connectedness questionnaire, but do not name the WCS or say which scales would be collected at follow-up beyond monthly QIDS-SR-16 and more comprehensive assessments at 1, 3 and 6 months after the first dosing session. Both statistical analysis plans (November and December 2020) analyse only change to week 6, list the FS and WSAS but not the WCS or MLQ among secondary outcomes, and plan no follow-up analysis.
key_findings.locator: Protocol V5 §2.2.1 Outcome Measures (p. 48), Assessments at 1–6 months (p. 60), §2.7 Psychological outcome measures (pp. 61–62); Protocol V7, the same sections (pp. 97, 109–111); SAP of November 2020, Outcome Measures (p. 146) and Efficacy (pp. 151–155); SAP of December 2020 (pp. 163–171); file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf

key_findings.finding: Missing data by questionnaire (Supplementary Table 1): at month 3, 9 psilocybin and 11 escitalopram patients lacked the QIDS-SR-16, while 5–7 and 9–11 lacked the 3-monthly scales; at month 6, 5 and 8 lacked the QIDS-SR-16 and 4–7 and 7–8 the other scales. 16 of 30 psilocybin and 12 of 29 escitalopram patients completed at least 85% of the QIDS-SR-16 follow-ups; 2 escitalopram patients and no psilocybin patient completed none (Supplementary Materials 2).
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Materials 2, 1st paragraph (p. 179); Supplementary table 1 (pp. 179–180); file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: The table's percentages fit denominators of 31 (psilocybin) and 60 (total), not 30 and 59 (editors' calculation; reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Item-level WSAS (the first Supplementary Table 7; cited in the article as S6 on p. 7 and S7 on p. 12): the Time × Condition interaction was significant for home management (F = 4.02, p = .009), social leisure (6.11, p = .001), private leisure (3.42, p = .019) and maintaining relationships (6.16, p = .001), not for ability to work (0.91, p = .438); 3 numerator degrees of freedom, uncorrected.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Table 7 (item-level analysis of WSAS); file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses whose results the article does not report (Supplementary Table 12A): excluding patients with missing data or follow-up psychedelic use (n = 30 at month 3 and 33 at month 6), the between-arm differences at months 3 and 6 were QIDS-SR-16 0.40 (SE 1.88, p = .83) and 2.37 (2.00, p = .25); WSAS −9.67 (3.65, p = .01) and −7.24 (3.48, p = .04); WCS 12.43 (6.90, p = .08) and 14.12 (6.42, p = .03); MLQ 1.93 (2.94, p = .52) and 4.17 (1.93, p = .03). With imputation, follow-up covariates and a missingness covariate (Table 12B), the QIDS-SR-16 differences were 2.73 (1.78, p = .13) and 2.57 (1.67, p = .13), WSAS −9.43 (2.77, printed p = 0.00) and −7.31 (2.91, p = .02), and WCS 13.77 (5.23, p = .01) and 10.31 (5.64, p = .07).
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Table 12A–B (unnumbered landscape pages after p. 197; PDF pp. 200–201); file Erritzoe_2024_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: Positive QIDS-SR-16 values favour escitalopram. In Table 12B the 3-month MLQ panel repeats the 6-month one (4.29, SE 2.11), so the 3-month MLQ result is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The QIDS-SR-16 omnibus Time × Condition test is printed as F(7, 279)=7.33, p=0.006, and the MLQ omnibus test as F(3,143)=5.31, p<0.001 (p. 7). Editors' calculation: that F on those degrees of freedom gives p of about 0.00000004 for the QIDS-SR-16 test and about 0.002 for the MLQ test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the F values or the p values are misprinted; the false discovery rate adjustments built on them cannot be checked. The supplement prints no unadjusted omnibus test; in its sex-disaggregated model the QIDS-SR-16 time × condition test is F(7, 317.4) = 2.59, p = 0.013 (Supplementary Table 11, p. 197), nearer the printed p than the printed F.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3, panel 1C, the 95% confidence intervals for the escitalopram arm's QIDS-SR-16 change do not match the coefficients and standard errors at any of the seven time points; for example month 2, B −7.24 (SE 1.03) with a printed interval of −13.28 to −5.51, and week 6, −6.37 (SE 0.98) with −9.94 to −2.45. The escitalopram WCS interval at month 6 (5.53 to 16.35) does not fit its printed SE of 3.69. The psilocybin-arm and between-arm intervals agree with their coefficients and standard errors. Editors' calculation: B ± 1.96 SE gives about −9.26 to −5.22 at month 2 and −8.29 to −4.45 at week 6, and the WCS interval implies an SE of about 2.76.
reporting_issues.consequence: The escitalopram-arm intervals cannot be used; the coefficients, standard errors and effect sizes agree with the text. For the escitalopram QIDS-SR-16 changes, the two-arm model in Supplementary Table 3 gives intervals consistent with B ± 1.96 SE (for example week 6 −6.37, 95% CI −8.27 to −4.48; month 2 −7.23, −9.22 to −5.25; pp. 181–182), which can be cited instead. For the escitalopram WCS change at month 6 the supplement does not settle the error: Supplementary Table 4 prints SE 3.69 with t = 3.93, which implies an SE of about 2.79 (consistent with the article's interval), and p = .003, which fits SE 3.69 (p. 185).

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the escitalopram arm's WSAS change as −1.00 at month 3 and −3.10 at month 6 (p. 7), whereas Table 3 gives −1.80 and −5.26 (p. 9); the text values equal the ratio of each coefficient to its standard error (−1.80/1.79 and −5.26/1.69), i.e. the test statistics.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text understates the escitalopram arm's improvement in functioning; Table 3 should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and text give p<0.001 for the 6-month WSAS between-arm difference (pp. 1, 7), but B −7.46 with SE 2.58 gives z of about 2.89 and p of about 0.004 (editors' calculation), and Table 3 marks it at the p<0.01 level.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the difference remains significant, but less strongly than printed. Supplementary Table 3 prints the same estimate with t = −2.88 and p < .001 (p. 183).

reporting_issues.issue: Denominators for treatment during follow-up are used inconsistently: the Results count 37 of 59 patients (62.7%) as receiving an additional intervention (p. 7), whereas Table 2 has only 48–49 respondents; the Discussion attributes 63% to the psilocybin arm (p. 11) and gives 34% of the escitalopram arm as continuing or resuming medication (p. 12), against 10 of 23 respondents (43.5%) in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation: about three-quarters of respondents (37 of 49) had other treatment during follow-up; the 63% is not specific to the psilocybin arm, and the share of escitalopram respondents on medication is 43.5%, not 34%.

reporting_issues.issue: Response and remission during follow-up are given only as percentages, in Fig. 2B–C and in Supplementary Table 6 (cited in the article as S7), without counts, denominators or a stated method for missing data, although Fig. 1 shows patients missing at every follow-up point. Editors' calculation: every percentage in Supplementary Table 6 is a whole count of all 30 and 29 randomized patients, and its p values equal uncorrected chi-square tests on those counts at 12 of 14 time points. At week 6, however, the table prints psilocybin remission 57% (17 of 30) and escitalopram response 48% (14 of 29), as in the original trial (per the companion card), whereas Fig. 2 plots 60% and about 45% (re-measured on the 298-ppi figure image: 60.1% and 44.6%, that is 18 of 30 and 13 of 29), and the table's own week-6 p values (.01 and .05) fit the figure's counts (p = 0.012 and 0.050) rather than its percentages (0.024 and 0.089); Supplementary Table 2B implies 18 psilocybin remitters and 14 escitalopram responders.
reporting_issues.consequence: The follow-up response and remission rates count all randomized patients, so missing patients were treated as non-responders or imputed (not stated); they cannot be compared directly with rates among respondents in other studies. At week 6 the article's figure and the supplement disagree by one patient in two cells; the table's percentages agree with the original trial report.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 implies 9 of 30 psilocybin patients (30%) missing at month 3, whereas the text gives a QIDS-SR-16 range up to 29% and, for the 3-monthly scales collected at the same time points, a range of 13–23% in the psilocybin arm (pp. 5, 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Supplementary Table 1 (pp. 179–180) reconciles the counts: at month 3, 9 psilocybin patients lacked the QIDS-SR-16 but only 5–7 lacked the 3-monthly scales. Its percentages, however, fit denominators of 31 for the psilocybin arm and 60 overall in every cell, not the 30 and 59 randomized (editors' calculation; 9 of 31 is 29%), which is where the article's 29% comes from; the averages in the article are little affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor inconsistencies: eligible ages 18–80 in the abstract and 18–85 in the Methods (pp. 1, 3); recruitment described as from a hospital in the UK (p. 1); the Methods state there were no baseline differences although Table 1 shows imbalances in illness duration, baseline QIDS-SR-16 and alcohol use (pp. 4–5); the Procedures describe the escitalopram arm as taking placebo capsules on other days (p. 4); a 40% relapse rate is cited to Kato et al. (2021), who are not in the reference list (p. 12); results are referred to Table 1 where Table 3 is meant (p. 7); Table 3's panels are labelled 1A–1C; the item-level functioning analysis is placed in Supplementary Table S6 on p. 7 and S7 on p. 12; significance symbols differ between Table 3 (two asterisks for p<0.001) and the figures (p<0.005). The article's supplementary table numbers also differ from the supplement's: response and remission are in Supplementary Table 6 (cited as S7), the item-level WSAS analysis in the first Supplementary Table 7 (cited as S6 on p. 7 and S7 on p. 12), the imputation analyses in a second Supplementary Table 7 and in Table 9 (cited as S8–S9; there is no Table 8), and the correlations in Table 11A (cited as S11); the supplement's own text sends readers to Supplementary Table 3 for the completer comparison, which is in Table 2A/B (Supplement pp. 179, 188–198).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the main estimates, but descriptions of the sample and cross-references need checking against the trial report.

reporting_issues.issue: The article calls the study a follow-up of a double-blind trial and never states that patients were told their allocation at week 6, which both protocol versions specify (Protocol pp. 44, 59, 79; 93, 108, 129).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot tell from the article that all follow-up ratings, and the treatment choices made after week 6, came from patients who knew their allocation; this weighs most on the self-rated connectedness and meaning-in-life outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: Both protocol versions planned the unblinded follow-up to assess safety as well as enduring effects (Protocol pp. 44, 93), and the pre-trial protocol states that follow-ups would detect prolonged or delayed adverse events (Protocol p. 76); the article reports that safety was not assessed during follow-up (p. 1) without noting the departure. Structured interviews planned at 6 months (V5, p. 48) or at 1 and 6 months (V7, p. 97), the 1-month interview added by an amendment to capture the experience of escitalopram withdrawal (Supplement p. 141), are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Harms after week 6, including any during escitalopram withdrawal or after psychedelic use in follow-up, are unknown; the omission departs from the protocol.

reporting_issues.issue: Completer tables contain copying errors. In Supplementary Table 2A (p. 180) the psilocybin panel's week-6 response row repeats the escitalopram values (7, 58.3%; 7, 41.2%), its remission counts (10 and 11) add up to the arm's 21 responders, its education percentages are swapped between columns, and it shows a column of 2 non-completers although the text says there were none (p. 179). Table 2B (p. 181) gives 13 escitalopram patients with every follow-up completed against 12 with at least 85% in Table 2A and the text. In Table 10B (p. 196) the model for baseline QIDS-SR-16 repeats the age model's numbers (intercept 36.8, impossible on a 0–27 scale).
reporting_issues.consequence: The article's statement that completers and non-completers did not differ (p. 7) rests on tables that cannot be checked as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The imputation and sensitivity tables have further problems: neither imputation table (the second Supplementary Table 7 and Table 9, pp. 189–194) reports the Flourishing Scale although their captions list it; the imputed WCS between-arm estimates (19.35, 14.18, 11.02) are identical to the unimputed ones of Supplementary Table 3 despite 16 and 11 patients missing at months 3 and 6; several t values are copied from Supplementary Table 3 (for example a month-1 QIDS-SR-16 change of −4.62 with SE 0.96 printed with t = −3.92) and some p values do not fit their estimates (month-1 difference −2.91, SE 1.34: p about .03, printed .01); a WCS estimate is printed as 110.30 for 10.30 (p. 194); and in Supplementary Table 12B the 3-month MLQ panel repeats the 6-month one (p. 200). In Supplementary Table 3 the baseline condition term (−1.91, SE 1.46, t = −1.30) is printed with p = .597 instead of about .19 (p. 181).
reporting_issues.consequence: The article's statement that the imputation results were consistent with the uncorrected results for all measures (pp. 10–11) cannot be verified for the Flourishing Scale or the WCS; the direction and significance of the other imputed results can be read, with their p values treated as approximate.

design_detail: Two-page viewpoint by a single author, Natalie Gukasyan of the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, on the phase 2 trial of single-dose psilocybin (25, 10 or 1 mg) in treatment-resistant depression (Goodwin et al., 2022). No data of its own and no search; ten references, chosen by the author. It argues that the trial missed the chance to assess blinding and expectancy, places its efficacy in context, and raises concern about suicidal behaviour in the 25-mg arm, with possible mechanisms for further study.
can_establish: What a psychedelic-trial researcher outside the trial team argued soon after publication about the trial's blinding, its comparison conditions and its suicidality findings, and which explanations and data she proposed for future studies.
cannot_establish: Whether 25 mg psilocybin raises the risk of suicidal behaviour (three events in one arm, no analysis), whether blinding failed in this trial (no data were collected), or any effect size beyond figures taken from the trial and from other studies, which are cited without appraisal.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (viewpoint). The trial discussed: 233 participants at 22 sites in Europe and North America, randomized to a single dose of 25, 10 or 1 mg of a proprietary psilocybin formulation, with 1 mg as the placebo-like condition, after 2–4 failed medication trials in the current episode (p. 8, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; sources chosen by the author (ten references: the trial, two earlier psilocybin studies in depression, STAR*D, a 2021 item by the trial group of Carhart-Harris cited on antidepressant use before psilocybin, an article on blinding and expectancy confounds in psychedelic trials, a psilocybin trial in alcohol use disorder, a funding notice from the US National Institute of Mental Health, a paper on adverse behavioural effects of antidepressants in children and adolescents, and a piece on psychedelic hype).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author to support two arguments (missing blinding data; suicidality). The efficacy context draws on STAR*D and two smaller earlier psilocybin studies with higher reported efficacy; the blinding argument on one article on blinding and expectancy and one alcohol use disorder trial; the suicide-risk discussion on a paper about antidepressant effects in children and adolescents.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no data). As described: a single dose of 25, 10 or 1 mg of a proprietary psilocybin formulation (p. 8).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The viewpoint notes that 67% of the trial sample had been tapered off an antidepressant at entry (p. 8).

comparison.controls: In the trial discussed, the 1-mg dose served as the control condition; the author argues that the 10-mg arm could have informed expectancy effects if shown to be a convincing comparison with 25 mg (p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; refers to the trial's response, remission, sustained response and adverse events (p. 8).

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited (pp. 8–9): response of 37% at 3 weeks in the 25-mg group, lower than in two earlier studies of psilocybin-assisted therapy for depression; response rates of 30.6%, 13.7% and 13.0% for second-, third- and fourth-line treatments in STAR*D (Rush et al., 2006, as cited); 67% of the trial sample tapered off an antidepressant at entry; correct identification of treatment after the first dose by 94% of participants and 92% of staff in a trial of psilocybin versus diphenhydramine in alcohol use disorder (Bogenschutz et al., 2022, as cited); about 11 h of supportive psychotherapy between preparation and 1-month follow-up in Davis et al. (2021); suicidal behaviour in three participants, all in the 25-mg arm, about 1–2 months after dosing, all non-responders at 3 weeks with previous suicide attempts or non-suicidal self-injury.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable; the trial's adverse-event rates are characterized as relatively high without figures (p. 8).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data of its own. Its statements about the trial (233 participants, three doses, 25 mg but not 10 mg better than 1 mg at 3 weeks, key secondary end points not significant, 67% tapered off antidepressants, suicidal behaviour in three participants of the 25-mg arm after the 3-week end point, no blinding data) agree with the companion card's reading of the trial (sc_goodwin_2022).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The standfirst says the trial results "suggest modest efficacy but raise concerns about potential for serious adverse effects" (p. 8). Points where the argument could be overstated: the STAR*D comparison (p. 8) sets a 3-week response rate in a treatment-resistant sample against response rates of later treatment lines in a different study, population and schedule, the same comparison the trial authors made (per the companion card); the remark that antidepressant effects were evident 1 day after treatment (p. 8) does not mention that, per the companion card, the 1-mg group also improved sharply by day 2; and the statement that all suicidal behaviour occurred in the high-dose arm (pp. 8–9) holds for events coded as suicidal behaviour, but the companion card records serious adverse events of suicidal ideation or intentional self-injury in the 10-mg arm before week 3, one intentional self-injury in the 1-mg arm after week 3, and worsening of suicidal state by week 3 most often with 10 mg (17%, against 14% with 25 mg and 9% with 1 mg). The demoralization explanation, the role of aftercare and the contribution of challenging experiences are offered as possibilities, not findings (p. 9). A headline version (psilocybin raises suicide risk) would overstate from three events in one arm of 79 participants; so would a headline that the trial's blinding was shown to have failed, since no blinding data exist.

timeline.event: The trial discussed: one 25-mg dose better than 1 mg on clinician-rated depression at 3 weeks, 10 mg not; blinding not assessed; serious adverse events including suicidal ideation, self-injury and suicidal behaviour
Psilocybin versus diphenhydramine in alcohol use disorder, cited here for 94% of participants and 92% of staff identifying treatment correctly after the first dose

Notice of Information from the US National Institute of Mental Health (NOT-MH-23-125, 16 November 2022), cited here as stating that psychedelic trials without rigorous assessment of blinding integrity would be of low funding priority; not read

Randomized trial of psilocybin-assisted therapy in major depressive disorder (Davis et al., 2021, JAMA Psychiatry), cited here for higher efficacy, two doses and about 11 h of supportive psychotherapy; not read
STAR*D outcomes of sequential treatment steps (Rush et al., 2006, Am J Psychiatry), cited for response rates of 30.6%, 13.7% and 13.0% at steps 2 to 4; not read

replication.where_it_stands: The viewpoint's two concerns, missing blinding data and suicidality at the higher doses, are acknowledged in the trial report itself (per the companion card: blinding not tested; worsening of suicidal state by week 3 in 14%, 17% and 9% of the 25-, 10- and 1-mg groups). Whether psilocybin raises the risk of suicidal behaviour cannot be settled from one trial's three events; phase 3 results from the same sponsor were not among the files. The project's psilocybin list says a correction to this viewpoint was published, but none was among the files.

funding.funder: Support for the author was provided by Tim Ferriss, Matt Mullenweg, Craig Nerenberg, Blake Mycoskie and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation; the funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (p. 9).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 9): the author is a co-investigator on a study of psilocybin for major depressive disorder funded by Usona Institute. Not named there: the author is also an author of Raison et al. (2023), the Usona-funded phase 2 trial of psilocybin for major depressive disorder (byline p. 843; affiliation p. 851 of that article), and reports grants from the Usona Institute during that study (p. 852 of that article).
funding.affiliations_note: Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine (p. 8). The author is first author of the 12-month follow-up of the Davis et al. (2021) trial (Gukasyan et al., 2022, as listed in Erritzoe et al., 2024, reference 42, p. 15), a trial the viewpoint cites for higher efficacy and more psychotherapeutic support than the trial it criticizes. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the viewpoint.

what_would_settle_it: Psilocybin trials that record every participant's and staff member's guess of allocation after each dose, use comparison conditions designed to be convincing (several doses or an active placebo), and collect suicidal ideation and behaviour prospectively with their timing and related symptoms (insomnia, anxiety, irritability) for at least 3 months, pooled across trials so that rare events can be compared by dose.

domains.note: A viewpoint with no search or selection criteria; ten references chosen by the author.

The trial under discussion is appraised critically, but the comparators (STAR*D response rates, the higher efficacy of two smaller earlier studies, the blinding figures from an alcohol use disorder trial) are cited without regard to differences in population, measures or timing.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the author's own studies is cited; one cited trial (Davis et al., 2021) is one whose 12-month follow-up she led (per Erritzoe et al., 2024, reference 42).
Mechanisms (progression of depression, activation syndrome, mixed or manic states, demoralization, aftercare, challenging experiences) are presented as possibilities to study.

domains.domain: Balance of the trial's efficacy and harm findings
domains.note: Under-represented: suicidality-related events at the lower doses. The safety concern is framed as a high-dose signal, without the serious adverse events of suicidal ideation and self-injury in the 10-mg arm, the self-injury in the 1-mg arm, or the most frequent worsening of suicidal state at 10 mg (per the companion card); adverse-event rates are called relatively high without figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a viewpoint (METHODS §5.3). The piece is explicit that its mechanisms are speculative and its factual statements about the trial agree with the trial report as read for the companion card, but its selection is unsystematic and its safety argument presents a dose pattern more cleanly than the trial's own counts allow. Cite it for the argument that the trial collected no blinding data, for the observation that all three participants with suicidal behaviour were in the 25-mg arm, non-responders at 3 weeks and had a history of suicide attempts or self-injury, and for the research proposals; the figures it quotes from other studies should be cited from those studies.

key_findings.finding: The viewpoint summarizes the trial as 233 participants at 22 sites in Europe and North America, randomized to a single dose of 25, 10 or 1 mg of a proprietary psilocybin formulation (1 mg as the placebo-like condition) after 2–4 failed medication trials in the current episode; 25 mg but not 10 mg reduced depressive symptoms more than 1 mg at 3 weeks, and response and remission at 3 weeks and sustained response at 12 weeks did not differ significantly.
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: To put the 37% response at 3 weeks with 25 mg in context, the author notes that it was numerically higher than the response rates of 30.6%, 13.7% and 13.0% for second-, third- and fourth-line treatments in STAR*D, that effects were evident 1 day after treatment, and that the 25-mg group improved more than the 1-mg group although 67% of the sample had been tapered off an antidepressant at entry; she adds that the trial used fewer doses and less psychotherapeutic support than two smaller earlier open-label studies with higher efficacy, and that whether repeated doses add benefit remains open.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Calling blinding the most glaring problem, the author notes that the trial collected no data on blinding integrity, that the 10-mg arm could have informed expectancy effects had it been shown to be a convincing comparison condition, and that in a trial of psilocybin versus diphenhydramine in alcohol use disorder 94% of participants and 92% of staff identified the treatment correctly after the first dose; she cites a funding notice of the US National Institute of Mental Health, issued less than 2 weeks after the trial's publication, giving low priority to psychedelic trials without rigorous assessment of blinding integrity.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Suicidal behaviour occurred in three participants, about 1–2 months after treatment; all three had not responded at 3 weeks and had previous suicide attempts or non-suicidal self-injury, and all suicidal behaviour in the trial occurred in the 25-mg arm, which the author says should be taken seriously although such histories and treatment-resistant depression carry elevated risk.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (p. 8, continued on p. 9)
key_findings.note: Per the companion card, the trial also recorded serious adverse events of suicidal ideation and intentional self-injury in the 10-mg arm before week 3 and one intentional self-injury in the 1-mg arm after week 3.

key_findings.finding: The author recalls that increased suicide risk with serotonergic antidepressants has been a concern since at least the 1960s, typically in younger people early in treatment, with proposed explanations including progression of depression, antidepressant-induced activation syndrome and shifts into mixed or manic states, and calls for prospective collection of the timing of worsening suicidal ideation and of related symptoms such as insomnia, anxiety and irritability.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (continued from p. 8)

key_findings.finding: As mechanisms possibly specific to psychedelics, the author proposes a demoralization reaction in patients who believe they received a much-publicized treatment and do not improve, the type, timing and frequency of aftercare, and challenging psychedelic experiences; she notes that the trial offered less support than Davis et al. (2021), which provided about 11 h of supportive psychotherapy between preparation and 1-month follow-up.
key_findings.locator: 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author concludes that the trial is an important step, that blinding integrity and adequate comparison conditions will be key for future studies, and that the risk of serious adverse events such as suicide should be carefully studied and may have contributing factors unique to this treatment.
key_findings.locator: 6th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 1 gives the trial's journal as J. Med. (p. 9); the trial was published in the New England Journal of Medicine, 387, 1637–1648 (reference record goodwin_2022).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation error.

reporting_issues.issue: Adverse events are called relatively high (p. 8) without any figures or comparison group, and the timing of the suicidal behaviour (about 1–2 months after treatment) is given without its source; the companion card records the events only as occurring after week 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers must take adverse-event rates and timing from the trial report (per the companion card: any adverse event in 84%, 75% and 72% of the 25-, 10- and 1-mg groups).
