design_detail: Secondary, exploratory analysis (not pre-registered) by the trial's own team of data from the phase 2 randomized trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram for major depressive disorder (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021). Pre-treatment efficacy expectancy for each treatment (one unvalidated 0–100 visual-analogue item per treatment, rated the day before the first dosing day), trait suggestibility (Short Suggestibility Scale) and absorption (Modified Tellegen Absorption Scale) were examined as non-randomized predictors of change from baseline to week 6 on six scales (HAM-D, MADRS, BDI, QIDS-SR-16, STAI-T, WEMWBS), separately within each arm (28 escitalopram, 27 psilocybin), with linear mixed models; the between-arm comparison was then refitted with adjustment for expectancy or suggestibility. Appraised as a cohort nested in a trial, because the exposures of interest (expectancy, suggestibility, absorption) were not randomized; the predictors were all measured before the first dose.
can_establish: How much improvement these 55 trial patients expected from each treatment before the first dosing day, and whether, within each arm, patients with higher expectancy, suggestibility or absorption improved more by week 6 (associations only).
cannot_establish: Whether expectancy or suggestibility caused any part of the improvement (neither was manipulated, and prognostic factors such as treatment history were not adjusted for), whether the effect of psilocybin therapy is independent of expectancy (equivalence tests could not exclude an association of 0.5 standardized mean difference, and beliefs about allocation after dosing were never recorded), or whether the trial's between-arm differences were expectancy artefacts (the adjustment uses a covariate that differs between arms by construction).

sample.recruitment: Patients of the trial (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021); the authors state that most were self-referred and that many were probably seeking psilocybin treatment in particular (PDF p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As in the trial: moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder; details referred to the trial report (PDF p. 2). Data from 55 patients were used (PDF p. 1) of the 59 randomized in the trial (per the companion card sc_carhart_harris_2021); Figures 2 and 3 give 28 escitalopram and 27 psilocybin patients (PDF pp. 4–5). Why four patients were not analysed is not stated in the main text. The supplement's degrees of freedom imply that the suggestibility analyses used 27 escitalopram and 28 psilocybin patients and the absorption analyses all 59 randomized patients (Tables S1–S3, Supplement pp. 2–4; editors' inference: for the predictor × timepoint terms the degrees of freedom equal the number of patients minus 2), although the article and Figure 3 give 55 (28 and 27).
sample.demographics: Not reported in this paper; see the trial report.
sample.attrition: Four of 59 randomized patients (1 escitalopram, 3 psilocybin) not analysed, reasons not given in the main text (PDF pp. 1, 4). This applies to the expectancy analyses; by the degrees of freedom in the supplement, 2 escitalopram and 2 psilocybin patients were missing from the suggestibility analyses and none from the absorption analyses (Supplement pp. 2–4; editors' inference). The supplement gives no reasons either.
sample.selection_effects: Mostly self-referred patients who sought out a psilocybin trial (PDF p. 6); in both arms expectancy for psilocybin far exceeded that for escitalopram (PDF p. 3). The four patients not analysed are unbalanced by arm (3 vs 1).

exposure.measurement: Expectancy: the day before each dosing day, patients rated how much improvement in their mental health they expected at the end of the trial after 6 weeks of daily escitalopram, and 3 weeks after the second of two full strong doses of psilocybin, each on a 0–100 visual analogue scale anchored at 0% and 100% improvement; this analysis uses the ratings given before the first dosing day (PDF p. 2). The covariate is the expectancy for the treatment actually allocated (received treatment expectancy), so it is escitalopram expectancy in one arm and psilocybin expectancy in the other (PDF pp. 2–3). Suggestibility (Short Suggestibility Scale) and absorption (Modified Tellegen Absorption Scale) were measured at baseline (PDF p. 2). All covariates were centred on the median and divided by the SD (PDF p. 3). The authors state that the expectancy measure was not a validated survey (PDF p. 7). The supplement adds that using received-treatment expectancy assumes patients learned their allocation from conspicuous drug effects, whereas an averaged, treatment-agnostic expectancy (assuming they did not) gave the same qualitative conclusions, with output only in the code repository (Supplement p. 1; not consulted). Before the first session the received-treatment expectancy averaged 29.7 (SE 4.1) in the escitalopram arm and 57.1 (SE 3.9) in the psilocybin arm (Supplement p. 1; Table S1, p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions of the trial: psilocybin arm, two 25-mg doses of COMP360 psilocybin 3 weeks apart with 6 weeks of daily placebo capsules; escitalopram arm, two 1-mg psilocybin doses 3 weeks apart (viewed by the research team as a placebo) with daily oral escitalopram, 10 mg for 3 weeks then 20 mg for 3 weeks; psychological support in both arms (PDF p. 2).

comparison.controls: Within-arm analyses compare patients with higher and lower predictor scores in the same arm; between-arm models compare the randomized arms with adjustment for the predictor and its interactions.
comparison.matching: Arms randomized 1:1 in the trial. No significant between-arm differences in expectancy (allocation effect −3.2 ± 5.7, p=0.580), suggestibility (−2.5 ± 2.8, p=0.368) or absorption (4.4 ± 4, p=0.272) (PDF p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Factors that could shape both expectancy and prognosis were not included in the models: previous experience of antidepressants (patients had used about two psychiatric medications before, per Erritzoe et al., 2024, Table 1), previous psilocybin use, illness duration and baseline severity.

outcomes.instruments: Change from baseline to week 6 on the HAM-D and MADRS (clinician-rated), the BDI (called clinician-rated in this paper), the QIDS-SR-16 (the trial's primary outcome, self-rated), the STAI-T and the WEMWBS (self-rated) (PDF p. 2); figures plot change from week 0 to week 6 (PDF pp. 4–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard depression, anxiety and well-being scales. The expectancy items were not validated (PDF p. 7). This paper calls the Beck Depression Inventory clinician-rated (PDF p. 2), whereas the same team's QIDS paper describes the BDI-IA used in the trial as a 21-item self-report scale (Weiss et al., 2023, p. 721).
outcomes.operationalization: Within-arm association: the predictor × timepoint interaction, i.e. the change in outcome per 1 SD of the predictor, with patient as random effect (PDF p. 3). Between-arm effect: the treatment × timepoint interaction in models that also contain the predictor and its interactions, estimated at the median of the predictor (PDF p. 3). Equivalence: two one-sided tests against bounds of ±0.5 standardized mean difference, taken as the minimum important difference (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni across the six outcomes within each model (PDF p. 3; Supplementary Tables S2–S5 and S7 print both, and each adjusted p is six times the unadjusted one, capped at 1). No correction across the model families (three predictors, two arms, two sets of adjusted between-arm models and their three-way interactions).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: No allocation-guess data were collected from patients or assessors, so blinding integrity could not be evaluated (PDF p. 7).

analysis.effect_sizes: Estimates ± SE, Bonferroni-adjusted p (PDF pp. 3–6). Expectancy, psilocybin minus escitalopram, whole sample: 25.8 ± 3.5, p<0.001 (estimated means 54 vs 28.2 on the 0–100 scale). Escitalopram arm (n=28), change per 1 SD (about 22 points) of expectancy: HAM-D −3.91 ± 0.9 (p=0.001), BDI −5.47 ± 1.61 (p=0.013), MADRS −4.87 ± 1.52 (p=0.022), STAI-T −5.2 ± 1.68 (p=0.028), QIDS-SR-16 −2.46 ± 0.98 (p=0.115), WEMWBS 2.95 ± 1.76 (p=0.641). Psilocybin arm (n=27): HAM-D 1.16 ± 1.05, BDI 1.14 ± 2.4, MADRS 1.69 ± 1.81, QIDS-SR-16 0.56 ± 1.25, STAI-T 0.64 ± 2.66, WEMWBS −2.96 ± 2.44 (all p=1); equivalence tests non-significant on all scales. Psilocybin arm, change per 1 SD (about 10 points) of suggestibility: HAM-D −3.46 ± 0.92 (p=0.005), BDI −7.16 ± 1.94 (p=0.006), MADRS −6.36 ± 1.37 (p=0.001), QIDS-SR-16 −3.31 ± 1.04 (p=0.022), STAI-T −9.64 ± 2.1 (p=0.001), WEMWBS 6.44 ± 2.02 (p=0.022); escitalopram arm none significant. Absorption: no association in either arm. Between-arm difference adjusted for expectancy: HAM-D −3.06 ± 1.67 (p=0.438), BDI −3.32 ± 3.49 (p=1), MADRS −4.52 ± 2.85 (p=0.711), QIDS-SR-16 0.82 ± 1.93 (p=1), STAI-T −3.03 ± 3.92 (p=1), WEMWBS 7.82 ± 3.61 (p=0.214). Adjusted for suggestibility: HAM-D −5.88 ± 1.44 (adjusted p = 0.001 in Table S5; printed <0.001 in the article), BDI −7.48 ± 2.7 (p=0.047), MADRS −7.36 ± 2.09 (p=0.006), QIDS-SR-16 −1.37 ± 1.46 (p=1), STAI-T −8.17 ± 2.75 (p=0.027), WEMWBS 9.34 ± 2.59 (p=0.004). Editors' note: in the expectancy-adjusted models the point estimates still favour psilocybin on five of six scales (all except QIDS-SR-16) with larger standard errors than in the suggestibility-adjusted models. Unadjusted between-arm differences (Table S7, Supplement p. 7): HAM-D −6.0 ± 1.5 (adjusted p 0.002), BDI −7.6 ± 2.9 (0.069), MADRS −7.9 ± 2.4 (0.013), QIDS-SR-16 −1.3 ± 1.5 (1), STAI-T −8.2 ± 3.3 (0.089), WEMWBS 9.5 ± 2.9 (0.01). Unadjusted p values for every model are in Tables S1–S5 and S7 (for example escitalopram-arm expectancy and QIDS-SR-16, p = 0.019 before correction). Psilocybin arm, absorption (Table S3): all six estimates in the direction of more improvement with higher absorption, BDI −5.19 ± 2.08 (p = 0.019) and MADRS −3.45 ± 1.65 (p = 0.046) before correction, none after (adjusted 0.112–0.831).
analysis.covariates: Within-arm models: patient as random effect, timepoint, one predictor and its interaction with timepoint. Between-arm models: patient as random effect, timepoint, treatment, the predictor and their interactions (PDF p. 3). No adjustment for baseline severity, illness duration or treatment history.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The trial is registered (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03429075, PDF p. 1); this analysis was not pre-registered and the authors call its results exploratory rather than confirmatory (PDF p. 7).
analysis.selective_reporting: All six outcomes are reported for every model, with Bonferroni-adjusted p values in the article and unadjusted p values and model formulas in Supplementary Tables S1–S7 (read for this update). The treatment-agnostic expectancy analysis is described in one sentence, with its output only in the code repository (Supplement p. 1; not consulted). Data and analysis scripts are said to be in a public repository (PDF p. 3; not consulted).
analysis.power: No power calculation; the authors state that the trial was not powered to reject effects as small as the minimum important difference, so the failed equivalence tests may reflect the small sample (PDF p. 7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Before the first dose, patients in both arms expected far more improvement from psilocybin (estimated mean 54 on a 0–100 scale) than from escitalopram (28.2). In the escitalopram arm, higher escitalopram expectancy went with more improvement on four of six scales, not on the trial's primary outcome (QIDS-SR-16); in the psilocybin arm no association was found, but the equivalence tests could not exclude one of 0.5 standardized mean difference. Higher suggestibility went with more improvement on all six scales in the psilocybin arm, not in the escitalopram arm. After adjustment for expectancy, none of the six between-arm differences was significant (point estimates still favouring psilocybin on five); after adjustment for suggestibility, five of six were significant. Without adjustment for any predictor, the between-arm differences were significant after Bonferroni correction on three of six scales (HAM-D −6.0, MADRS −7.9, WEMWBS 9.5) and at uncorrected p < 0.05 on five (Table S7); adjustment for expectancy shrank the estimates by 43–63% on HAM-D, BDI, MADRS and STAI-T and by 18% on WEMWBS, reversed the sign on the QIDS-SR-16 and enlarged the standard errors by 13–27% (editors' calculation from Table S7).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that psychedelic therapy "may be less vulnerable to expectancy biases than previously suspected" (PDF p. 1) and does not mention that adjusting for expectancy removed every significant between-arm difference; the authors themselves say they can neither rule out nor confirm expectancy effects in the psilocybin arm and that no allocation-guess data were collected (PDF pp. 6–7). The Discussion states that the expectancy imbalance biased the results in favour of psilocybin's superiority and that low escitalopram expectancy can be read as a nocebo effect (PDF p. 6), causal readings that the Limitations disclaim (relationships correlational, not causal, PDF p. 7). The Introduction restates the original trial as showing psilocybin superior on all mental-health secondary outcomes with greater than 95% confidence (PDF p. 1), although the trial applied no correction for multiplicity, drew no conclusions from its secondary outcomes, and its response difference had an interval including zero (per the companion card). Editors' reading: because received treatment expectancy is psilocybin expectancy in one arm and escitalopram expectancy in the other, it differs between arms by construction, and the adjusted between-arm estimate is the difference between the arms' fitted lines at a common median expectancy, a level above most escitalopram patients' ratings and below most psilocybin patients' ratings (Figure 1); its loss of significance therefore depends on the fitted slopes and does not by itself show that the original differences were expectancy artefacts. The supplement explains that the received-treatment measure assumes patients learned their allocation from conspicuous drug effects, and reports that an averaged, treatment-agnostic expectancy gave the same qualitative conclusions, with output only in the code repository (Supplement p. 1; not consulted). Before the first session the arms' received-treatment expectancies averaged 29.7 and 57.1 (Supplement p. 1), the distance across which the adjusted comparison extrapolates. The Discussion's statement that the unadjusted models showed significant between-arm differences on all depression outcomes except the QIDS-SR-16 (PDF p. 6) holds only before the Bonferroni correction the paper uses elsewhere (BDI adjusted p = 0.069; Table S7). Headlines in either direction (psilocybin works regardless of expectations; the advantage of psilocybin was all expectation) would overstate.

timeline.event: The trial analysed here: no significant difference on the primary outcome; secondary outcomes favouring psilocybin, uncorrected; blinding not assessed
Self-blinding microdosing study by the same first author and colleagues, cited here among studies suggesting that positive expectancy may play an important role in responses to microdosing
Psilocybin versus diphenhydramine in alcohol use disorder, cited here for 94% of participants guessing their allocation correctly

Same team's reanalysis of the same trial: facet-level advantages of psilocybin on depressed mood and anhedonia reported to persist after controlling for relative expectancy (psilocybin minus escitalopram expectancy); a different expectancy variable and different outcomes from those used here
Same team's observational 6-month follow-up of the trial: no between-arm difference in depression after month 1

replication.where_it_stands: Among the papers read, no psilocybin trial has measured validated expectancy both before and after dosing together with allocation guesses. The same team's two analyses of this trial's expectancy data point in different directions: facet-level advantages for psilocybin persisted after controlling for relative expectancy (Weiss et al., 2023), whereas here every scale-level between-arm difference lost significance after adjusting for received treatment expectancy. The suggestibility finding has not been tested in another trial among the papers read.

what_would_settle_it: A trial that measures validated expectancy for each treatment before randomization and again after each dose, records each patient's guess of allocation and their confidence, includes a placebo arm, and ideally varies expectancy experimentally (for example through the information given to patients), with pre-registered analyses adjusted for treatment history and baseline severity and powered to exclude associations smaller than 0.5 standardized mean difference.

domains.note: The expectancy–outcome and suggestibility–outcome associations are unadjusted for factors that could drive both, such as earlier experience with antidepressants (low expectancy for an SSRI may reflect, and predict, past non-response), illness duration and baseline severity.

Expectancy rests on one unvalidated 0–100 item per treatment (PDF pp. 2, 7); suggestibility and absorption on published scales. The covariate used is the expectancy for the allocated treatment, which differs between arms by construction. Before the first session the received-treatment expectancy averaged 29.7 in the escitalopram arm and 57.1 in the psilocybin arm (Supplement p. 1).

55 of 59 randomized patients analysed for expectancy (the four exclusions unexplained and unbalanced by arm: 3 psilocybin, 1 escitalopram); by the supplement's degrees of freedom, a different 55 (27 escitalopram, 28 psilocybin) for suggestibility and all 59 for absorption (Supplement pp. 2–4; editors' inference); a mostly self-referred sample seeking psilocybin.

Expectancy was measured before the first dose only; after dosing, patients could probably tell 25 mg from 1 mg, and allocation guesses, which may modify how expectancy acts on outcomes, were not recorded (PDF p. 7).

Four of 59 patients missing without reasons; handling of any missing week-6 outcomes not described in the main text. Fractional degrees of freedom for some scales in Tables S2–S5 suggest that a few week-6 scores were missing within the analysed patients and were handled by the mixed models (editors' inference).

Four of six outcomes are self-rated (counting the BDI, which this paper calls clinician-rated), and response tendencies that raise expectancy ratings may also raise reported improvement; the clinician-rated scales were scored by raters whose knowledge of allocation was not assessed.

Not pre-registered; three predictors, two arms and two sets of adjusted between-arm models, with Bonferroni correction only within each set of six outcomes. All six outcomes are reported for every model, which limits selective reporting. Unadjusted p values and model formulas for every model are in Supplementary Tables S1–S7.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design can show associations within each arm between pre-treatment expectancy or suggestibility and improvement, but they are unadjusted for prognostic factors and rest on an unvalidated expectancy item in 27–28 patients per arm. The null association in the psilocybin arm is inconclusive by the authors' own equivalence tests, and the expectancy-adjusted between-arm models depend on extrapolating each arm to a common expectancy level. The card may be cited for the size of the pre-treatment expectancy gap (54 vs 28.2), for the within-arm associations as exploratory correlations, and for the fact that expectancy adjustment removed the significance of the three between-arm differences that were significant after correction without adjustment (HAM-D, MADRS, WEMWBS; Table S7), with that caveat; not for the claim that psilocybin therapy is free of expectancy effects, nor for the claim that the trial's secondary outcomes were expectancy artefacts.

key_findings.finding: Before the first dosing day, patients expected much more improvement from psilocybin than from escitalopram: difference 25.8 ± 3.5 points, p<0.001, estimated means 54 vs 28.2 on a 0–100 scale; no effect of allocation (−3.2 ± 5.7, p=0.580) or interaction with expectancy type (9.3 ± 6.9, p=0.183), so the imbalance was present in both arms; expectancies did not change significantly between the first and second dosing sessions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pre-treatment between-group differences, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
key_findings.note: The Discussion gives the average psilocybin expectancy as 51% (PDF p. 6); this is not the whole-sample mean (54 ± 2.8 before the first session, Supplement p. 1) but matches the escitalopram arm's psilocybin expectancy in Table S1 (29.71 + 21.25 = 50.96, editors' calculation); the psilocybin arm's was 57.1. Changes between sessions are in a separate key finding.

key_findings.finding: Suggestibility (−2.5 ± 2.8, p=0.368) and absorption (4.4 ± 4, p=0.272) did not differ between arms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pre-treatment between-group differences, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the escitalopram arm (n=28), higher pre-treatment escitalopram expectancy went with greater improvement at week 6 on the HAM-D (−3.91 ± 0.9 points per SD of expectancy, about 22 points; adjusted p=0.001), BDI (−5.47 ± 1.61, p=0.013), MADRS (−4.87 ± 1.52, p=0.022) and STAI-T (−5.2 ± 1.68, p=0.028), but not on the QIDS-SR-16 (−2.46 ± 0.98, p=0.115) or WEMWBS (2.95 ± 1.76, p=0.641).
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-treatment-arm association between expectancy and therapeutic outcomes, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Unadjusted p values (Table S2, Supplement p. 3): HAM-D <0.001, BDI 0.002, MADRS 0.004, QIDS-SR-16 0.019, STAI-T 0.005, WEMWBS 0.107, so five of six scales before correction.

key_findings.finding: In the psilocybin arm (n=27), pre-treatment psilocybin expectancy was not associated with improvement on any scale (HAM-D 1.16 ± 1.05, BDI 1.14 ± 2.4, MADRS 1.69 ± 1.81, QIDS-SR-16 0.56 ± 1.25, STAI-T 0.64 ± 2.66, WEMWBS −2.96 ± 2.44; all adjusted p=1), and equivalence tests were non-significant on all scales, so an association as large as 0.5 standardized mean difference could not be ruled out.
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-treatment-arm association between expectancy and therapeutic outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Equivalence bounds (0.5 SMD) in points: HAM-D 2.3, BDI 4.7, MADRS 3.9, QIDS-SR-16 2.6, STAI-T 5.1, WEMWBS 2.5; equivalence p 0.112–0.362 before correction (Table S6, Supplement p. 7). All six point estimates lie in the direction of less improvement with higher expectancy.

key_findings.finding: In the psilocybin arm, higher baseline suggestibility went with greater improvement on all six scales (per SD, about 10 points on the Short Suggestibility Scale: HAM-D −3.46 ± 0.92, adjusted p=0.005; BDI −7.16 ± 1.94, p=0.006; MADRS −6.36 ± 1.37, p=0.001; QIDS-SR-16 −3.31 ± 1.04, p=0.022; STAI-T −9.64 ± 2.1, p=0.001; WEMWBS 6.44 ± 2.02, p=0.022); in the escitalopram arm on none (for example HAM-D 0.9 ± 1.07, p=1; MADRS 2.78 ± 1.53, p=0.490). Absorption was associated with improvement in neither arm.
key_findings.locator: Results › Within-treatment-arm association among suggestibility, absorption, and therapeutic outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 4, 2nd continued on p. 5) and 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 5); Figure 3 (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: Equivalence tests for the escitalopram-arm suggestibility association were non-significant on four scales and significant on the BDI and STAI-T only before correction (p = 0.028 and 0.014; adjusted 0.168 and 0.084), so the escitalopram-arm null is inconclusive (PDF p. 4; Table S6, Supplement p. 7). By the degrees of freedom, these models included 27 escitalopram and 28 psilocybin patients, not the 28 and 27 labelled in Figure 3 (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for pre-treatment expectancy, the between-arm difference in change to week 6 was not significant on any scale: HAM-D −3.06 ± 1.67 (adjusted p=0.438), BDI −3.32 ± 3.49 (p=1), MADRS −4.52 ± 2.85 (p=0.711), QIDS-SR-16 0.82 ± 1.93 (p=1), STAI-T −3.03 ± 3.92 (p=1), WEMWBS 7.82 ± 3.61 (p=0.214); equivalence tests were also non-significant. The treatment × timepoint × expectancy interaction was significant on the HAM-D (6.02 ± 1.63, p=0.003) and MADRS (7.79 ± 2.78, p=0.043).
key_findings.locator: Results › Between-treatment difference in models adjusted for expectancy and suggestibility, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Supplementary Tables 4, 6 and 7 (file Szigeti_2024_Supplement.pdf)
key_findings.note: Point estimates still favour psilocybin on five of six scales. Table S7 (Supplement p. 7) sets these beside the unadjusted estimates (HAM-D −6.0 ± 1.5, BDI −7.6 ± 2.9, MADRS −7.9 ± 2.4, QIDS-SR-16 −1.3 ± 1.5, STAI-T −8.2 ± 3.3, WEMWBS 9.5 ± 2.9; see the Table S7 finding). The equivalence tests for these adjusted differences used bounds of 2.9–6.2 points and gave p 0.165–0.747 (Table S6).

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for suggestibility, the between-arm differences favoured psilocybin and were significant on five of six scales (HAM-D −5.88 ± 1.44, adjusted p = 0.001 in Table S5, printed <0.001 in the article; BDI −7.48 ± 2.7, p=0.047; MADRS −7.36 ± 2.09, p=0.006; STAI-T −8.17 ± 2.75, p=0.027; WEMWBS 9.34 ± 2.59, p=0.004), not on the QIDS-SR-16 (−1.37 ± 1.46, p=1); the treatment × timepoint × suggestibility interaction was significant on all six scales.
key_findings.locator: Results › Between-treatment difference in models adjusted for expectancy and suggestibility, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 5, continued on p. 6); Supplementary Table 5, rows tp(wk6):trt(P) (file Szigeti_2024_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the expectancy adjustment as showing that the expectancy imbalance biased the trial's results in favour of psilocybin, through low expectancy in the escitalopram arm (a nocebo effect) rather than benefit from high expectations in the psilocybin arm, and read the suggestibility finding as possible evidence that extra-pharmacological factors, demand characteristics or the Hawthorne effect contribute to response to psilocybin.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph and 7th paragraph (PDF p. 6, 7th continued on p. 7)

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: the analysis was not pre-registered and is exploratory; all relationships are correlational; the equivalence tests cannot rule out an expectancy effect of 0.5 standardized mean difference and the trial was not powered to do so; the expectancy measure was not validated; no allocation-guess data were collected from patients or assessors, so blinding integrity and its interaction with expectancy could not be evaluated.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and future work, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Between-arm differences in change to week 6, psilocybin minus escitalopram, without adjustment (Table S7): HAM-D −6.0 ± 1.5 (p < 0.001; Bonferroni-adjusted 0.002), BDI −7.6 ± 2.9 (0.011; 0.069), MADRS −7.9 ± 2.4 (0.002; 0.013), QIDS-SR-16 −1.3 ± 1.5 (0.402; 1), STAI-T −8.2 ± 3.3 (0.015; 0.089), WEMWBS 9.5 ± 2.9 (0.002; 0.01); adjusted for expectancy: −3.1 ± 1.7 (0.073; 0.438), −3.3 ± 3.5 (0.347; 1), −4.5 ± 2.9 (0.119; 0.711), 0.8 ± 1.9 (0.674; 1), −3.0 ± 3.9 (0.444; 1), 7.8 ± 3.6 (0.036; 0.214). After correction, three unadjusted differences were significant (HAM-D, MADRS, WEMWBS) and none of the adjusted ones.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Table 7 (read from the embedded image and at 300 dpi); file Szigeti_2024_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: adjustment shrank the estimates by 43–63% on HAM-D, BDI, MADRS and STAI-T and by 18% on WEMWBS, reversed the QIDS-SR-16 estimate and enlarged the standard errors by 13–27%. The unadjusted QIDS-SR-16 estimate (−1.3) is close to the week-6 estimate of the same team's follow-up (−1.28, Erritzoe et al., 2024) and differs from the trial's published primary result (−2.0, per the companion card); the models and samples differ.

key_findings.finding: Expectancy did not change significantly between the two dosing sessions: escitalopram expectancy 28.2 ± 2.8 before the first and 25.9 ± 3.4 before the second session in the whole sample, and 29.7 ± 4.1 and 26.9 ± 4.8 in the escitalopram arm; psilocybin expectancy 54 ± 2.8 and 52.7 ± 3.4 in the whole sample, and 57.1 ± 3.9 and 62.1 ± 4.6 in the psilocybin arm, the last change reported with a paired t-test, t = 0.244, df = 52, p = 0.81 (means ± SE). The first values in each arm are the received-treatment expectancies used in the models.
key_findings.locator: Changes in expectancy between dosing sessions, 2nd paragraph; file Szigeti_2024_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: Editors' check: df = 52 cannot belong to the 27 psilocybin-arm patients, and a 5-point mean rise with t = 0.244 in 27 pairs would need an SD of differences above 100 on a 0–100 scale; the test fits the whole-sample change (54 to 52.7) instead. The second rating in each arm came after the first dosing session.

key_findings.finding: In the psilocybin arm (30 patients by the degrees of freedom), higher absorption went with more improvement on all six scales, at uncorrected p < 0.05 on the BDI (−5.19 ± 2.08, p = 0.019) and MADRS (−3.45 ± 1.65, p = 0.046) and at p = 0.056–0.139 on the others; none survived Bonferroni correction (adjusted 0.112–0.831). In the escitalopram arm all p ≥ 0.35.
key_findings.locator: Supplementary Tables 2 and 3, models score~(1|patient_id)+tp*abs, component tp(wk6):abs; file Szigeti_2024_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: The article reports only that no absorption association was significant (PDF p. 5).

reporting_issues.issue: The Beck Depression Inventory is described as clinician-rated (PDF p. 2), whereas the same team's analysis of the same trial describes the BDI-IA as a 21-item self-report scale (Weiss et al., 2023, p. 721).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers comparing self-rated and clinician-rated outcomes would misclassify one of the four outcomes on which escitalopram expectancy predicted response.

reporting_issues.issue: Data from 55 patients were analysed (27 psilocybin, 28 escitalopram, PDF pp. 1, 4) out of the trial's 59, without a reason for the four exclusions in the main text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the four excluded patients were in the psilocybin arm; whether they differed in expectancy or outcome cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction states that psilocybin therapy was superior on all mental-health secondary outcomes with greater than 95% confidence (PDF p. 1); the trial's response difference had an interval including zero (22 percentage points, 95% CI −3 to 48, per the companion card), and the same team's QIDS paper counts 14 of 16 efficacy outcomes as favouring psilocybin (Weiss et al., 2023, p. 717). The Discussion's statement that unadjusted models gave significant between-arm differences on all depression outcomes except the QIDS-SR-16, as originally reported (PDF p. 6), refers to secondary outcomes for which the trial report gave no P values (per the companion card).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's description of the trial results it reanalyses overstates them. Table S7 (Supplement p. 7) now shows the comparison: in the paper's own unadjusted models, after the Bonferroni correction it applies throughout, only HAM-D, MADRS and WEMWBS differed (BDI adjusted p = 0.069, STAI-T 0.089), so the Discussion's statement about all depression outcomes except the QIDS-SR-16 holds only before correction; adjusting for suggestibility raised the number of Bonferroni-significant differences from three to five (Table S5).

reporting_issues.issue: Psilocybin expectancy is given as an estimated mean of 54 (PDF p. 3, Figure 1 legend) and as an average of 51% (PDF p. 6) without saying how the two differ; in the suggestibility results, an adjusted p of 0.001 is marked with one asterisk for STAI-T and three for MADRS (PDF p. 5); MADRS is misspelt MARDS several times (PDF pp. 5–6). The supplement explains part of this: the whole-sample mean before the first session was 54 ± 2.8 (Supplement p. 1), and 51 matches the escitalopram arm's psilocybin expectancy in Table S1 (29.71 + 21.25 = 50.96, editors' calculation). Also: the suggestibility-adjusted HAM-D difference is given as adj. p < 0.001 in the article (PDF p. 5) but adjusted p = 0.001 in Table S5 (Supplement p. 6); and the paired t-test on Supplement p. 1 (t = 0.244, df = 52, p = 0.81), reported for the psilocybin arm's rise from 57.1 to 62.1, cannot belong to its 27 patients (it fits the whole-sample change from 54 to 52.7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 3 labels 28 escitalopram and 27 psilocybin patients (PDF p. 5), the numbers of the expectancy analysis, but the degrees of freedom of the suggestibility models imply 27 and 28 patients (25 and 26 for the suggestibility × timepoint term, Tables S2–S3), and those of the absorption models all 59 randomized (27 and 28 within arm; 57 for the between-arm comparison in Table S1), whereas the article says data from 55 patients were used (PDF p. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Each predictor appears to have been analysed in a different set of patients; why patients lacked expectancy or suggestibility scores is not stated (editors' inference from the degrees of freedom, which equal the number of patients minus 2 for these terms when data are complete).

design_detail: Post hoc psychometric reanalysis, by the trial's own team, of baseline and week-6 data from the phase 2 randomized trial of psilocybin therapy (n=30) versus escitalopram treatment (n=29) for major depressive disorder (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021), motivated by the trial's null primary outcome. Part 1 compares the QIDS-SR-16 (the pre-registered primary outcome) with the MADRS, HAM-D-17 (HRS) and BDI-IA item by item (each item rescaled to 0–1), examines the QIDS-SR-16 compound criteria (sleep, weight/appetite and psychomotor scored by the highest of several items), and compares standard errors and variances of the scales' mean-scores. Part 2 re-tests the between-arm difference on newly derived outcomes: seven depression facets built by allocating items of five scales (with the SHAPS) to a published factor structure (Ballard et al., 2018), and a single depression factor from an exploratory factor analysis of four scales. Linear mixed models, Time × Condition, baseline to week 6 (QIDS-SR-16 items also at week 5). The authors label all analyses exploratory.
can_establish: How the QIDS-SR-16 items behaved relative to comparable items of other depression scales in this trial's data, and, as exploratory comparisons of the randomized arms on outcomes defined after the results were known, which items and derived facets differed most between the arms at week 6.
cannot_establish: That the QIDS-SR-16 measured depression less validly than the other scales (no external criterion was used, and the authors concede that its higher variance may reflect real differences between patients), or that psilocybin therapy is superior to escitalopram on depressed mood, anhedonia or a core depression factor (outcomes derived after a null primary outcome, eight composite outcomes and dozens of items tested without correction, 59 patients, and clinician ratings possibly influenced by clinicians' expectations).

sample.recruitment: The trial's patients; ethics, patient characteristics and eligibility are referred to the trial report (p. 721).
sample.attrition: Factor analysis on 57 patients, because two lacked MADRS and HAM-D data (p. 722; note 1, p. 730); expectancy data for 55 (p. 722); the number of patients in each facet model is not stated (degrees of freedom of 57 for the time terms, Table 4, p. 728).
sample.selection_effects: As in the trial: mostly self-referred volunteers seeking a psilocybin trial (per the companion card sc_carhart_harris_2021). The analysis itself was undertaken because the primary outcome was null while other outcomes favoured psilocybin (p. 717).

exposure.measurement: Randomized allocation in the trial; investigators and medication-administering staff unaware of assignment (p. 721).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions of the trial: 25 mg COMP360 psilocybin at visit 2 and again 3 weeks later with daily placebo capsules, or 1 mg psilocybin at the same visits with escitalopram 10 mg daily for 3 weeks and then 20 mg daily for 3 weeks (p. 721).

comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1 in the trial (per the trial report).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomized. Patients' relative expectancy (psilocybin minus escitalopram expectancy, each one 0–100 item rated the day before the first dosing day, p. 722) was added as a moderator in supplementary models for the significant outcomes (Supplemental Materials II, not read). Clinicians' expectancies were not measured (p. 730).

outcomes.instruments: QIDS-SR-16 (self-report; Cronbach's α 0.75 at baseline, 0.89 at weeks 5 and 6); MADRS (10-item, clinician-administered; α 0.65 at baseline, 0.91 at week 6); HAM-D-17 (clinician-administered; α 0.15 at baseline, 0.81 at week 6); BDI-IA (21-item self-report; α 0.75, 0.94); SHAPS (14-item self-report anhedonia scale; α 0.85, 0.96) (p. 721). Seven facets (Amotivation, Reduced Appetite, Impaired Sleep, Suicidal Thoughts, Negative Cognition, Depressed Mood, Anhedonia; the Tension facet dropped) with α 0.66–0.86 at baseline and 0.74–0.95 at week 6 (p. 722). Depression factor: one factor forced from 64 items of four scales, items and composites loading above 0.40 averaged (15 items/composites), explaining 15% of the variance; α 0.84 at baseline and 0.95 at week 6 (pp. 722, 727).
outcomes.validity_norms: The facet structure comes from an exploratory factor analysis in 119 people that has not been confirmed (p. 730); items new to that structure were allocated by the authors' judgment, and items were dropped by endorsement and item–total correlation rules within this sample (pp. 721–722). The depression factor was derived in the same 57 patients in whom it was then tested.
outcomes.operationalization: Between-arm difference in change from baseline to week 6: the Time × Condition coefficient, standardized (b) and unstandardized on the 0–1 item scale (B) (pp. 722–723).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: p<0.05, two-tailed (p. 723); the authors note that post hoc analyses risk type I error and call the results exploratory (pp. 721, 730). The count of 8 is the seven facets and the depression factor; item-level comparisons across 64 items of four scales were also reported. Editors' calculation: with a Bonferroni threshold for eight tests (0.05/8, about 0.006), only the anhedonia facet (p=0.001) would remain significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Clinician-rated scales were scored by raters whose expectancies were not measured; the authors preferred the self-report BDI-IA for item comparisons partly because it is insulated from clinician expectancies favourable to psilocybin therapy, which they say may have played a role in clinician-rated measurement (p. 722), and list unmeasured clinician expectancies as a limitation (p. 730). Blinding was not assessed in the trial (per the companion card).

analysis.effect_sizes: Facets and factor, Time × Condition, psilocybin vs escitalopram (Table 4, p. 728): Depressed mood b −0.68 (SE 0.26), B −0.11 (SE 0.04), t(57) −2.57, p=0.013; Anhedonia b −0.79 (0.22), B −0.12 (0.03), t −3.61, p=0.001; Depression factor b −0.55 (0.25), B −0.09 (0.04), t −2.17, p=0.035; no significant difference on the other five facets (p. 727; full results in Supplemental Table S6, not read). Items most favourable to psilocybin therapy (B on the 0–1 scale): HAM-D Libido −0.38, BDI Guilt −0.23, HAM-D Somatic energy −0.21, MADRS Reported sadness −0.20, BDI Dissatisfaction with life −0.19, BDI Reduced sexual interest −0.19, MADRS Lassitude −0.18, HAM-D Work and interests −0.18, HAM-D Agitation −0.18, BDI Worthlessness −0.16 (p. 723). QIDS-SR-16 Weight/appetite criterion B 0.13, favouring escitalopram (p. 725). Scale-level standard errors of the Time × Condition coefficient (0–1 scale): MADRS 0.04, HAM-D 0.02, BDI-IA 0.03, QIDS-SR-16 0.04 (Table 3, p. 726). Editors' note: on a 0–1 item scale, a B of −0.11 corresponds to about a tenth of an item's response range.
analysis.covariates: None in the main models; for outcomes with a significant interaction, supplementary models with a Time × Condition × Relative expectancy term (p. 723; Supplemental Materials II, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The trial is registered (NCT03429075), with mean change on the QIDS-SR-16 as its pre-registered primary depression outcome (p. 717); the item, facet and factor analyses here were post hoc and not pre-registered (pp. 721, 730).
analysis.selective_reporting: The outcomes were constructed by the trial's own team after the primary outcome was null, with the stated aim of explaining the discrepancy between the QIDS-SR-16 and the other scales (p. 717). Items were excluded by endorsement and item–total rules within the same data, and the factor was derived in the same sample (p. 722). Full facet results (Supplemental Table S6), item-factor allocations (Table S1), composites (Table S3), factor loadings (Table S4) and the expectancy-moderation models (Materials II) are only in the supplement (not read).
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors note the small sample (pp. 722, 730).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this trial's week-6 data, several items of the clinician-rated scales and the BDI-IA (libido, guilt, energy, reported sadness) differed between arms more than comparable QIDS-SR-16 items, and the QIDS-SR-16 mean-score had larger baseline and change variances and a larger standard error than the other scales. Removing the compound criteria from the QIDS-SR-16 changed its between-arm estimate only marginally. On post hoc composites, the psilocybin arm improved more on depressed mood (0.68 SD), anhedonia (0.79 SD) and a single depression factor (0.55 SD), but not on five other facets, without correction for multiple testing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 14 of 16 major efficacy outcomes favoured psilocybin therapy and that the reanalysis was suggestive of its superior efficacy on depressed mood, anhedonia and a core depression factor (p. 717); the Conclusion lists five sources of the QIDS-SR-16 discrepancy, chief among them higher variance and compound items (p. 730), although the authors' own test found that excluding compound items did not meaningfully alter the estimates (p. 728) and they concede that the higher variance could equally reflect greater precision in capturing real variation between patients (p. 730). The Introduction describes the trial report's caution as readers being "editorially instructed to draw no conclusions" (p. 717). The 14 of 16 favourable outcomes are uncorrected secondary results (per the companion card), several from clinician-rated scales that the authors themselves consider exposed to clinicians' expectations favouring psilocybin therapy (p. 722). The authors recommend the HAM-D for lower measurement error (p. 730), although its baseline internal consistency in this trial was 0.15 (p. 721). A headline version (the trial really showed psilocybin beating escitalopram, and only the primary questionnaire missed it) would overstate: the primary outcome was pre-registered precisely so that outcomes are not chosen after the results are known, and the alternative outcomes here were built from the same data by the trial's own team.

timeline.event: The trial reanalysed here: QIDS-SR-16 difference −2.0 (95% CI −5.0 to 0.9), secondary outcomes favouring psilocybin without correction for multiplicity

Same team's expectancy analysis of the same trial: adjusting the scale totals for received treatment expectancy left no significant between-arm difference on any of six scales, in contrast with the facet results reported here as robust to relative expectancy
Same team's 6-month follow-up, which cites this paper's critique of the QIDS-SR-16 as a possible reason for the null depression comparisons at 6 weeks and during follow-up

replication.where_it_stands: The facet and factor results have not been tested in another trial among the papers read; the authors call them exploratory and dependent on replication (p. 730). Whether the QIDS-SR-16 is less sensitive to treatment differences than other scales would need comparison across many trials, which this single-trial analysis cannot provide.

funding.funder: A private donation from the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust and the founding partners of Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research (p. 730). COMPASS Pathways provided the psilocybin (COMP360); the Pharmacy Manufacturing Unit at Guy's and St Thomas' Hospital provided escitalopram and placebo capsules (p. 721).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 730): RCH reports receiving consulting fees from Entheon Biomedical and Mindstate Design Lab. DE reports receiving consulting fees from Aya, Mindstate Design Lab and Clerkenwell Health. DN reports advisory roles at COMPASS Pathways, Psyched Wellness, Neural Therapeutics and Alvarius. BW and BG declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: A secondary analysis by the trial's own team: all five authors at the Centre for Psychedelic Research, Imperial College London, R. L. Carhart-Harris (the trial's first author) also at the University of California San Francisco (p. 717). BW designed and conducted the analysis (p. 730). Data available on request from the corresponding author, not publicly (p. 730). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A new trial comparing psilocybin therapy with an SSRI that pre-registers facet-level outcomes (for example depressed mood and anhedonia composites defined from named items) alongside the total scores, with clinician ratings made by raters unaware of allocation and allocation guesses recorded; and, for the questionnaire question, a comparison of the QIDS-SR-16 with other scales across several trials or an individual-participant meta-analysis.

domains.note: The trial's randomization (per the companion card: random-number generator run outside the research team).
As in the trial: patients could probably tell 25 mg from 1 mg and blinding was not assessed; 4 of 29 stopped escitalopram because of adverse events (per the companion card).
Few missing: 57 of 59 for the factor analysis (two lacking MADRS and HAM-D data); degrees of freedom of 57 in the facet models.

Self-rated items come from patients who were probably aware of allocation and largely preferred psilocybin; clinician-rated items, which supplied many of the largest differences (libido, energy, sadness), came from raters whose expectancies the authors themselves say may have favoured psilocybin therapy (pp. 722, 730).

Composite outcomes defined after the pre-registered primary outcome was null, by the trial's own team, with item exclusions and a factor derived from the same data; eight composites and dozens of items tested without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomization is sound, but the between-arm comparisons reported here are on outcomes chosen after the primary result was known, without correction for multiplicity, and on ratings open to patients' and clinicians' expectations. The psychometric part (variance, compound criteria, item content) has no standard appraisal instrument and rests on one small trial; the authors' own tests did not support compound items as a sufficient explanation. The card may be cited for how QIDS-SR-16 items compared with other scales in this trial, for the item- and facet-level differences as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and for the authors' acknowledgment of clinician-expectancy concerns; not as evidence that psilocybin therapy is superior to escitalopram, nor that the QIDS-SR-16 is invalid.

key_findings.finding: The authors motivate the analysis by stating that 14 of 16 major efficacy outcome measures of the trial favoured psilocybin therapy with greater than 95% confidence, while the two that did not came from the QIDS-SR-16, the pre-registered primary depression outcome; they reproduce the trial's supplementary figure of 11 continuous outcomes, on which only the QIDS-SR-16 interval crosses zero.
key_findings.locator: Abstract and Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 717); Figure 1 (p. 720)
key_findings.note: The intervals are uncorrected for multiplicity (per the companion card), and the suicidality interval shown in Figure 1 is the one the companion card found irreconcilable with the group intervals.

key_findings.finding: Items most favourable to psilocybin therapy (unstandardized difference on a 0–1 item scale) came mainly from clinician-rated scales and the BDI-IA: HAM-D Libido −0.38, BDI Guilt −0.23, HAM-D Somatic energy −0.21, MADRS Reported sadness −0.20, BDI Dissatisfaction with life −0.19, BDI Reduced sexual interest −0.19, MADRS Lassitude −0.18, HAM-D Work and interests −0.18, HAM-D Agitation −0.18, BDI Worthlessness −0.16.
key_findings.locator: Results › Examining most differentially responsive symptoms, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: QIDS-SR-16 items that favoured psilocybin therapy (Falling asleep −0.15, Sleeping too much −0.11, Feeling slowed down −0.08, Feeling restless −0.08) all sit inside compound criteria scored by the highest item, while the Weight/appetite criterion favoured escitalopram (B 0.13).
key_findings.locator: Results › Examining most differentially responsive symptoms, 3rd paragraph (p. 723); Evidence of differences in QIDS-SR16 item functioning, weight/appetite paragraph (p. 725)

key_findings.finding: The item scored highest within a compound criterion changed between baseline and week 6 in 13 patients (22%) for sleep, 11 (19%) for weight/appetite and 4 (7%) for psychomotor items; recomputing the QIDS-SR-16 without the compound scoring changed the between-arm estimate only marginally (reported as ΔB −0.12 and −0.08) while its standard error fell by 18% and 17%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Examining compound criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 726); Table 2 (p. 719)

key_findings.finding: On a common 0–1 scale, the QIDS-SR-16 mean-score had a standard error of the between-arm coefficient 19% higher than the BDI-IA, 21% higher than the MADRS and 76% higher than the HAM-D; a baseline SD 47%, 74% and 135% higher; and an SD of change 11%, 14% and 58% higher.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of standard error and variance; Table 3
key_findings.note: Table 3 prints these values to two decimals (for example SE 0.04 for both QIDS-SR-16 and MADRS), so the percentages cannot be recomputed from it; the authors concede that higher variance may reflect real variation between patients rather than measurement error (p. 730).

key_findings.finding: Baseline internal consistency was low for the clinician-rated scales: HAM-D α 0.15 and MADRS α 0.65 (0.81 and 0.91 at week 6), against 0.75 for the QIDS-SR-16 and the BDI-IA.
key_findings.locator: Method › Measures › Primary clinical outcome and Secondary clinical outcomes

key_findings.finding: Among seven derived facets, the psilocybin arm improved more on Depressed mood (b −0.68, B −0.11, p=0.013) and Anhedonia (b −0.79, B −0.12, p=0.001), i.e. 0.68 and 0.79 SD more than the escitalopram arm; no significant difference on Amotivation, Negative cognition, Reduced appetite, Impaired sleep or Suicidal thoughts.
key_findings.locator: Results › Depression facets across five depression and anhedonia scales, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 727); Table 4 (p. 728)

key_findings.finding: On a single depression factor (15 items and composites from four scales, explaining 15% of the variance), the psilocybin arm improved 0.55 SD more (b −0.55, B −0.09, t(57) −2.17, p=0.035).
key_findings.locator: Method › Depression factor score, 4th paragraph (p. 722); Results › Single factor across four depression scales, 2nd paragraph (p. 727); Table 4 (p. 728)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the facet-level differences were present even when controlling for relative expectancy (psilocybin minus escitalopram expectancy, available for 55 patients).
key_findings.locator: Method › Expectancy (p. 722); Discussion › Understanding differential treatment response, 6th paragraph (p. 729)
key_findings.note: Models only in Supplemental Materials II, not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors judge that excluding compound items did not meaningfully alter the between-arm estimates, so compound criteria are unlikely to account fully for the discrepancy between scales, and that the QIDS-SR-16's higher variance cannot be straightforwardly interpreted.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › What accounts for the discrepancy between the QIDS-SR16 and other depression scales?, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: clinicians' expectancies and other rating biases were not measured; the facet structure (from 119 people) has not been confirmed; post hoc analyses in a small sample risk false positives and are exploratory; conclusions about the QIDS-SR-16 should be moderated; and its higher variance could equally reflect greater precision in capturing real variation between patients.
key_findings.locator: Limitations

key_findings.finding: The authors chose the BDI-IA as the main comparison for QIDS-SR-16 items partly because, as a self-report scale, it is insulated from clinician expectancies favourable to psilocybin therapy, which they say may have played a role in the clinician-rated measures.
key_findings.locator: Method › Analytic plan, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The figure numbers in the text do not match the captions: the text's Figure 2 (item differences across the four scales, and scale mean-score errors) is captioned Figure 3, Scale-level comparison, and the text's Figure 3 (11 QIDS-SR-16 content areas) is captioned Figure 2, Item-level comparison (pp. 723–726). The reproduced trial figure is called Supplemental Figure S4 in the text (p. 717) and Figure S6 in its source line (p. 720).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; readers must match figures by content.

reporting_issues.issue: The change in the QIDS-SR-16 between-arm estimate after removing compound scoring is given as ΔB −0.12 and −0.08 and called marginal (p. 726), without saying whether ΔB is an absolute change on the 0–1 scale or a proportion; on the 0–1 scale, item-level differences of −0.1 to −0.2 are described elsewhere as substantial.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the change cannot be judged, so the conclusion that compound scoring does not explain the discrepancy rests on an undefined quantity.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4, the t value for the Anhedonia intercept (25.80) equals the unstandardized B divided by its SE, whereas the other intercept t values (4.25, 4.30) equal the standardized b divided by its SE; the note defines Time as the difference between conditions in outcome scores for the escitalopram condition, which describes neither a time effect nor a condition effect.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Time × Condition rows, on which the conclusions rest, are internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The trial's baseline is described as visit 1, one day before the first dosing day (p. 721), whereas the same team's follow-up paper places the pretreatment baseline 7–10 days before dosing day 1 (Erritzoe et al., 2024, Table 1 footnote, p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear from which assessment the week-6 changes here are computed.

reporting_issues.issue: Note 3 cites a specific suicidality scale as significantly favouring psilocybin therapy in the trial report (p. 730), and Figure 1 shows its interval as excluding zero (p. 720); the companion card found the printed suicidality (SIDAS) difference interval irreconcilable with the group intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The suicidality result should not be counted among the outcomes favouring psilocybin.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 614 (round-2 check): missed item: Interpretation gap: the Discussion reads non-significant facet differences as suggesting the two treatments may be equivalent on reduced appetite and suicidality (p. 729, 6th paragraph of 'Understanding differential treatment response'), and reads the uncorrected item-level libido difference (a coefficient with no test in the text) as psilocybin therapy's superiority in remediating sexual function (p. 729) and a potential key advantage in avoiding SSRI sexual side effects (Conclusion, p. 730).
disagreements.resolution: Recorded by the AI co-editor (13 November 2026) for the card's next revision.
