design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject (two-period crossover) study from Buenos Aires, Argentina, stated as registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05160220). 34 adults who were planning to start microdosing with their own Psilocybe cubensis mushrooms each had one psilocybin week and one placebo week, separated by a week without measurements. The order was set by each participant drawing one of two identical coded envelopes at the start and keeping the other for the second period, with a third party in charge of blinding holding the key to the codes (supplement, pp. 2–3); the article says the third party randomized the order (p. 2). In each measurement week a gel capsule was taken on Wednesday and on Friday: 0.5 g of ground, homogenized dried Psilocybe cubensis (active) or the same weight of a dried edible mushroom (for example Suillus granulatus) prepared the same way (placebo). Testing on dosing days took place in a house that hosted only the researchers and the participant. Outcomes: 21 visual analogue items of acute effects, 13 questionnaires, three creativity tests, six computer tasks of perception and cognition, resting EEG and an auditory event-related potential paradigm, and wristband physical activity. Participants guessed their condition after each week, and results were also split by whether the guess was correct.
can_establish: Whether two 0.5 g doses of dried psilocybin mushrooms, taken double-blind by people already planning to microdose, changed same-day ratings of acute effects, mood and well-being questionnaires, creativity, task performance, EEG and daily activity compared with an edible-mushroom placebo over one week.
cannot_establish: Effects of microdosing over weeks or months (two doses per condition), effects in people with depression or other conditions (healthy volunteers only), the amount each person actually received (one pooled analysis of three mushroom sources), or whether expectation produced the effects seen only in correct guessers, because guessing is itself shaped by what people feel and the expectation data were collected but not analysed.

sample.recruitment: Community volunteers recruited by word of mouth, social media advertising and visits to workshops on psilocybin mushrooms and microdosing, December 2019 to August 2020; people who were planning to start a microdosing protocol with their own mushroom material and who agreed to the study's standardized schedule and dose; no payment (p. 2, Introduction, last paragraph; Materials and Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Per the supplement, people who contacted the researchers by e-mail were briefed by phone on the study and its criteria, received the consent form with a written explanation that included why a blinded, randomized placebo condition was needed, and after consenting had a psychological interview screening for the exclusion criteria (Supplement p. 1, Recruitment process).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Main text: fluent Spanish speakers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision (p. 2, Participants, 1st paragraph). Supplement (p. 1, Selection criteria): planning to start microdosing with their own Psilocybe cubensis material; as conditions of inclusion, agreeing to the pre-arranged dosing schedule, to abstain from psychoactive drugs, including alcohol and caffeine, during the study weeks, and not to eat in the 3 h before each capsule. A non-diagnostic psychiatric interview following Johnson et al. (2008) excluded people meeting DSM-5 criteria for schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder or bipolar I or II disorder (also when present in first- or second-degree relatives), substance abuse or dependence in the past 5 years (nicotine excepted), depressive disorders or recurrent depressive episodes, obsessive-compulsive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, dysthymia, panic disorder, bulimia or anorexia, or with a history of neurological disorder; anyone taking psychiatric medication was excluded.
sample.demographics: 11 of 34 participants female; age 31.26 (SD 4.41) years; weight 74 (SD 17) kg. Mean 11 (SD 14.9) previous experiences with serotonergic psychedelics, 1.5 (SD 2.3) of them rated challenging; only 6 reported significant previous microdosing experience (p. 2, Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: The paper states that all participants completed all parts of the experiment (p. 2), but the blinding analysis counts 64 measurement weeks rather than the 68 expected from 34 people in two periods (p. 4); the gap is not explained (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people with considerable psychedelic experience who were about to microdose, recruited partly at microdosing workshops: positive expectations are likely and prior familiarity with psilocybin effects makes the active capsule easier to recognise. Healthy volunteers, so the authors note ceiling effects on mood and cognition are possible (p. 9). Results do not generalize to people seeking treatment for a condition. The supplement confirms that people with depressive or anxiety disorders, or taking any psychiatric medication, were excluded, and that candidates were told in writing before consenting why a blinded placebo condition was needed (Supplement p. 1).

exposure.measurement: Assigned in coded form. Per the supplement, the two active capsules and the two placebo capsules were each sealed in an airtight plastic bag inside identical paper envelopes holding a folded paper code; each participant randomly picked one envelope at the start and kept the other for the second period; after the data had been collected, scored and analysed, participants reported their codes and the third party in charge of blinding matched them to conditions for the final analyses, after which the order was revealed to participants (Supplement pp. 2–3, Blinding procedure, steps 1–5). The article says instead that a third party randomized the order and kept the capsule identity from participants and researchers (p. 2, Experimental design); the order was revealed to participants after the study ended (p. 2, Participants, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Psilocybin week: an oral gel capsule of 0.5 g of ground, homogenized dried Psilocybe cubensis on Wednesday and again on Friday (two capsules). Placebo week: capsules of the same weight and preparation made with an edible mushroom. The two measurement weeks were separated by one week without measurements (p. 2, Experimental design; Fig. 1a–b, p. 3; p. 4, Chemical characterization of samples). Alkaloid content of pooled samples and the authors' estimate per capsule are given in the key findings. Supplement (study conditions): the placebo material was a dried edible mushroom, for example Suillus granulatus (p. 3, Blinding procedure, step 2); a 150 mg sample was kept from each mushroom source for analysis (pp. 2–3, step 1); participants were asked not to eat in the 3 h before each capsule (p. 1, Selection criteria); measurements on dosing days began 1.5 h after the capsule (p. 3, Measurements per day of the week); participants were driven to and from the study house on those days (p. 2, Experimental setting).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were asked to abstain from psychoactive drugs, including alcohol and caffeine, during the study weeks; substance abuse or dependence in the past 5 years (nicotine excepted) and any psychiatric medication were exclusions (Supplement p. 1, Selection criteria). Adherence to the abstention was not checked or reported: no testing is described in the article or the supplement.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable in the usual sense: outcomes were measured on the dosing days and the days after within each measurement week; a week without measurements separated the two conditions (p. 2). The supplement asks participants to abstain from psychoactive drugs during the study weeks (p. 1) but does not say whether this covered the week between conditions or the time before the study, and adherence was not checked.

comparison.controls: Each participant served as their own control: one week of placebo capsules (the same weight of an edible mushroom, prepared the same way) (p. 2, Experimental design).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; order set by each participant's random pick of one of two identical coded envelopes (Supplement p. 3, Blinding procedure, step 4), not by a third party as the article states (p. 2). The number of participants in each order is reported neither in the article nor in the supplement, and the envelope method does not force balanced orders.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for a within-person comparison. Period and order effects cannot be checked from the article or the supplement because the numbers per sequence are not given.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants; other drug use not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Acute effects: 21 visual analogue items adapted from Carhart-Harris et al., summed to a total, rated Wednesday to Saturday (p. 2, Acute effects; Fig. 1d–e, p. 3). Questionnaires in Spanish: Big Five Inventory, STAI-T and Short Suggestibility Scale at baseline; STAI-S, PANAS, Perceived Stress Scale, Tellegen Absorption Scale, BIEPS well-being scale, Mind Wandering Questionnaire, Flow State Scale, Creative Personality Scale, TECA empathy test and Cognitive Flexibility Scale on Fridays (Table 1, p. 4). Creativity: Remote Associates Test, Alternative Uses Task and Wallach–Kogan test on Fridays. Tasks: binocular rivalry, backward masking, attentional blink, Go/No-Go and Stroop on Wednesdays; Trail Making on Fridays. EEG: 24-channel mobile system, eyes open and closed (5 min each), spectral power by band and broadband Lempel-Ziv complexity; Local–Global auditory ERP paradigm (pp. 3–4). Physical activity: Fitbit Charge 4 steps, distance, resting and activity time every day (p. 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Supplement (pp. 4–7): validated Spanish versions of the BFI, STAI, PANAS, Perceived Stress Scale and Flow State Scale; BIEPS and TECA developed in Spanish; Short Suggestibility Scale, Tellegen Absorption Scale, Mind Wandering Questionnaire, Cognitive Flexibility Scale and Creative Personality Scale translated by the authors with no validation reported; Spanish versions of the Remote Associates, Alternative Uses and Wallach–Kogan tests without validation details. The 21 VAS items (listed on Supplement p. 2) were chosen from studies of larger psychedelic doses; the authors note that such effects could help participants break the blind (Supplement p. 2). The article scales most questionnaire scores to 0–10 for display (p. 5).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit or harm was defined as a difference between the psilocybin and placebo weeks on paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Mann–Whitney U tests for the unpaired correct-guess and wrong-guess subsets), reported at uncorrected p < 0.05 with a statement of whether Bonferroni correction removed it, and complemented by Bayes factors (BF10 with a JZS prior; above 3 favours a difference, below 1/3 favours none) (p. 4, Statistical analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. Bonferroni within some families (4 days for the summed acute-effect rating, 21 single items, 4 EEG bands); otherwise uncorrected p < 0.05 with Bonferroni status stated (p. 4). No primary outcome is named. 27 is the number of measures in Table 1 (p. 4); most yield several scores (21 acute items, 5 personality traits, 9 creativity scores, several task measures, EEG bands under two eye conditions, daily activity), so the total number of tests is larger and is not stated.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and investigators did not know the capsule contents until the last steps of data analysis (Fig. 1a legend, p. 3; Introduction, last paragraph, p. 2). Most outcomes were self-rated or computer-scored; participants correctly identified their condition in most weeks (see key findings). Per the supplement, the codes were linked to conditions only after the data had been collected, scored and analysed (p. 3, Blinding procedure, step 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals are given in the article or the supplement. Supplementary Tables S1–S4 give means ± SEM, p-values (paired Wilcoxon for all weeks; Mann–Whitney for the guess subsets) and BF10. All weeks, psilocybin vs placebo (Table S1, Supplement p. 10): summed acute-effect rating on Wednesday 65.52 ± 5.84 vs 38.97 ± 2.95 (p = 7e-5, BF10 143.5) and on Friday 60.55 ± 4.30 vs 40.05 ± 3.48 (p = 9e-5, BF10 52.86); Thursday and Saturday no difference (p = 0.83 and 0.58). Questionnaires: conscientiousness 29.76 vs 28.14 (p = 0.01, BF10 0.36) and Short Suggestibility Scale 3.34 vs 3.02 (p = 0.03, BF10 0.51), both trait measures taken before that week's first capsule; all other p ≥ 0.10. Creativity (Table S3, p. 13): Alternative Uses fluency lower with psilocybin, 8.76 ± 0.62 vs 9.52 ± 0.61 (p = 0.03, BF10 0.34); Wallach–Kogan elaboration 0.02 vs 0.01 (p = 0.04, BF10 1.28); other scores p ≥ 0.22. Guess subsets (Tables S2 and S4, pp. 11–12, 14): see key findings; no questionnaire or creativity score differed at p < 0.05 in either subset. The six computer tasks, EEG and wristband measures have no supplementary table; the article reports them as significant or not (pp. 6–7): attentional blink, Stroop and Trail Making part A slightly worse at uncorrected p < 0.05; eyes-closed theta power lower after Bonferroni over 4 bands; Lempel-Ziv complexity, ERPs and activity unchanged. Approximate values read from Fig. 1d and Fig. 3c are in the key findings. Editors' check: the BF10 values appear to have been computed without the within-person pairing (reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: None; paired non-parametric comparisons within person.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper states the study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov before it started (NCT05160220; p. 2, Participants, 2nd paragraph). The registry record was not read here, so the registration date (to be compared with data collection from December 2019 to August 2020) and the registered primary outcome were not checked; the paper itself names no primary outcome.
analysis.selective_reporting: No primary outcome. The supplement gives numbers (means ± SEM, p, BF10) only for the VAS totals, questionnaires and creativity tests (Tables S1–S4); the six computer tasks, EEG and wristband measures, and the single VAS items, are reported in the article only as significant or not and otherwise referred to the OSF files (Supplement p. 10; not consulted). The article names only conscientiousness among questionnaires at uncorrected p < 0.05 (p. 5), but Table S1 also shows the Short Suggestibility Scale at p = 0.03. Participants' expectations of change were collected but their analysis is deferred to a future publication (p. 2), although the abstract's conclusion is about expectation. The Fig. 2 caption states there were no differences at uncorrected p < 0.05 while the text reports two (pp. 5–6).
analysis.power: Not estimated; the authors say they did not know what effect size to expect (p. 4, Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph). Bayes factors in the wrong-guess subset were inconclusive, which the authors attribute to its small size (p. 5).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 34 people who each took two capsules of 0.5 g dried psilocybin mushrooms in one week and two placebo capsules in another, summed ratings of acute effects were higher on psilocybin dosing days (all weeks: 65.5 vs 39.0 on Wednesday, 60.6 vs 40.1 on Friday), clearly so only in weeks when people correctly guessed what they had taken (67.9 vs 37.3 and 63.7 vs 34.8); in the 19 weeks with a wrong guess the comparison was inconclusive, with a 16-point difference on Wednesday (59.0 vs 43.0, p = 0.16) and none on Friday (51.8 vs 52.8). No questionnaire of mood, stress, well-being or empathy, no creativity test and no physical-activity measure differed after correction; two task measures were slightly worse with psilocybin at uncorrected thresholds and a third (Trail Making part A) was reported as worse with no p-value or correction stated; eyes-closed EEG theta power was lower. Two trait measures taken before each week's first capsule (conscientiousness and suggestibility) differed at uncorrected p < 0.05, which cannot reflect that week's capsules.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "expectation underlies at least some of the anecdotal benefits" of microdosing (abstract, p. 1). This is not tested: participants' expectations were collected but not analysed (p. 2); a correct guess is likely to follow from noticing a drug effect, so splitting weeks by guess cannot show whether belief produced the ratings or the ratings produced the belief; and with no benefit found under any condition, the study observed no benefit whose source could be attributed to expectation. The Discussion's own conclusion is more cautious: until further research is done, it says, expectation or confirmation bias cannot be ruled out as the source of any desirable effects of long-term microdosing (last paragraph, p. 9), and the authors state that two doses in one week could not show cumulative effects and that benefits in people with existing impairments remain possible (8th paragraph, p. 9). The same closing paragraph calls the subjective effects reliable and significant (p. 9), which sits uneasily with the authors' statements that the acute effect lacked consistency across participants (p. 7) and was inconclusive in wrong-guess weeks (p. 5). A headline version (microdosing is just placebo) overstates: the study shows no detectable benefit on these measures over one week, with two capsules of mushrooms of approximately known content, in healthy, experienced volunteers.

timeline.event: Yanakieva et al.: randomized trial of low LSD doses; changes in time estimation without other changes in perception or concentration (as described by Cavanna et al., Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 8).
Bershad et al.: three low LSD doses vs placebo at weekly intervals; higher vigour ratings at the highest dose, no differences in mood, cognition or physiological measures (as described, p. 8).
Hutten et al.: dose-dependent positive effects on mood together with anxiety and cognitive impairment after low LSD doses (as described, p. 8).

Szigeti et al.: self-blinding citizen-science study of microdosing; positive effects on its primary outcome that Cavanna et al. say could be explained by participants breaking the blind (as described, p. 8)
van Elk et al.: pre-registered field and laboratory study of psilocybin-truffle microdosing; more than 60% of participants broke the blind (as described, p. 8).
This study: no detectable benefit on mood, creativity, cognition or activity; acute effects clear only in correct-guess weeks; correct guessing in most weeks.

replication.where_it_stands: On the authors' account of placebo-controlled studies (Discussion, pp. 8–9), low doses of LSD or psilocybin can produce noticeable acute effects, but evidence of benefit on mood, creativity or cognition beyond placebo is inconsistent, and participants often identify the active condition. This study is not a direct replication of any earlier trial. Longer schedules and clinical populations were untested here.

funding.funder: Grant PICT-2019-02294 awarded by Agencia Nacional de Promoción Científica y Tecnológica (Argentina); partial funding from the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (grant no. NU21-04-00307) and the Grant Agency of the Czech Republic (grant no. 20-25349 S) (Acknowledgements, p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests (Conflict of interest, p. 11).
funding.affiliations_note: Academic physics, neuroscience and forensic-chemistry groups in Buenos Aires, Tilburg, Prague and Santiago de Chile (p. 1); two authors (Janeckova, Kuchar) contributed the chemical analysis from the University of Chemistry and Technology Prague (p. 11). Data files are posted on the Open Science Framework (p. 9). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger pre-registered placebo-controlled trial of microdosing over several weeks to months with a named primary outcome, analysis of the psilocybin content of each batch of capsules, expectations measured before dosing and guesses recorded after every dose, and a design that separates belief from drug (for example a balanced-placebo arm in which what people are told is varied independently of what they receive), run in healthy people and in people with depression.

domains.note: Per the supplement, each participant randomly picked one of two identical coded envelopes for the first period (a form of drawing lots), and only the third party could link codes to conditions, so the sequence was random and allocation concealed (Supplement pp. 2–3, Blinding procedure, steps 3–5); the article's statement that a third party randomized the order (p. 2) differs. The number of participants in each order is not reported in either document.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: A week without measurements separated the conditions, which makes drug carryover unlikely, but knowledge carried over: guessing was at chance after the first week and well above chance after the second (p. 5). Period effects were not analysed and numbers per sequence are not given.

Matched mushroom placebo in identical capsules and identical envelopes (Supplement pp. 2–3), but participants identified their condition in most weeks; participants were asked to abstain from psychoactive drugs, alcohol and caffeine during the study weeks (Supplement p. 1) and adherence was not checked; no deviations from the assigned capsules are reported.
All participants are said to have completed (p. 2), but the blinding analysis uses 64 rather than 68 weeks and the numbers analysed per outcome are only in the supplement.

For the self-rated outcomes (acute-effect ratings, questionnaires), the participants were the assessors and correctly identified their condition in most weeks, which can shape their ratings. EEG, computer tasks and wristband data are less exposed (some concerns).
No primary outcome named; 27 measures with many scores; results mostly in the supplement; registry record not checked here; expectation data collected but not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design was sound in its essentials (third-party randomization, coded identical capsules, matched mushroom placebo, within-person comparison), but participants identified their condition in most weeks, especially after the second week, and the central outcomes are self-rated, so the self-reported results are at high risk of bias from knowledge of the condition. The absence of differences on objective measures (EEG complexity, tasks, activity) is less affected. No primary outcome and partial correction across many measures add concerns. The card may be cited for what was given and measured, the rate of correct guessing, the absence of detectable benefits over one week, and the acute-effect difference confined to correct-guess weeks; not for the size of any effect (none is reported with an interval), and not as a test of whether expectation explains anecdotal benefits. The supplement's Bayes factors appear not to use the within-person pairing (reporting issues), so Bayes factors below 1/3 should not be cited as paired evidence of no difference; the null findings rest on the uncorrected paired Wilcoxon tests.

key_findings.finding: Sample and design: 34 adults who were planning to start microdosing with psilocybin mushrooms (11 female; mean age 31.26, SD 4.41; on average 11 previous experiences with serotonergic psychedelics, SD 14.9; only 6 with significant microdosing experience) each had one psilocybin week and one placebo week in an order set by the participant's random pick of one of two identical coded envelopes (supplement; the article says a third party randomized it), double-blind, with a week without measurements in between; all are reported to have completed every part of the study.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph; Experimental design (single paragraph); Supplement, Blinding procedure, step 4 (file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: What was given (study conditions): in the psilocybin week, an oral gel capsule of 0.5 g of ground, homogenized dried Psilocybe cubensis on Wednesday and again on Friday; in the placebo week, capsules of the same weight and preparation made with an edible mushroom.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Experimental design (p. 2); Fig. 1a–b (p. 3); Chemical characterization of samples (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Blinding: by the text, participants identified their condition correctly in 49 of 64 measurement weeks (75%): 25 of 34 psilocybin weeks (73.5%) and about 70% of placebo weeks. The chi-square test did not show guessing better than chance after the first week (chi-square with 1 df = 0.09, p = 0.76) but did after the second week (chi-square = 11.53, p = 0.0006), which, the authors say, could indicate that information on the previous week's condition helped identify the current one.
key_findings.locator: Results › Unblinding of the experimental condition (single paragraph, p. 4 right column, continuing on p. 5)
key_findings.note: The subset sizes in the Fig. 1d legend (p. 3) are 25 psilocybin and 24 placebo weeks with a correct guess and 9 and 10 with a wrong guess, 68 weeks in all, which gives 49 of 68 correct (72%, editors' calculation); see reporting issues. The supplement (Blinding procedure, pp. 2–3) describes how capsules were coded and allocated but not when or how guesses were recorded, so the 64-versus-68-weeks question stays open.

key_findings.finding: Acute effects: the summed rating of the 21 acute-effect items was higher with psilocybin than with placebo on both dosing days (Bonferroni over 4 days; all weeks, Table S1: Wednesday 65.52 ± 5.84 vs 38.97 ± 2.95, p = 7e-5, BF10 143.5; Friday 60.55 ± 4.30 vs 40.05 ± 3.48, p = 9e-5, BF10 52.86), not on the following days (p = 0.83 and 0.58), and did not differ between the first and second dosing day. Split by guess, the difference was present in weeks with a correct guess (Bayes factors above 30; Table S2: 83.36 on Wednesday, 1e4 on Friday) but inconclusive in weeks with a wrong guess (Bayes factors between 1/3 and 3; Table S2: 0.70 and 0.40); the trend the article reports for the first dosing day corresponds to p = 0.16 (Table S2). The authors say the inconclusive result was possibly due to the comparatively small size of that subset.
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 1d (p. 3); Supplement Fig. S1 (p. 4), Table S1 rows VAS (Wed)–VAS (Sat) (p. 10) and Table S2 VAS rows (p. 11) (file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Acute-effect totals by guess (Table S2; the Fig. 1d legend gives 25 psilocybin and 24 placebo weeks with a correct guess and 9 and 10 with a wrong guess, and the wrong-guess means are multiples of 1/9 and 1/10, consistent with these sizes, editors' check): correct guess, Wednesday 67.88 vs 37.29 (p = 0.0002, BF10 83.36) and Friday 63.72 vs 34.75 (p = 2e-6, BF10 1e4); wrong guess, Wednesday 59.00 vs 43.00 (p = 0.16, BF10 0.70) and Friday 51.77 vs 52.80 (p = 0.83, BF10 0.40). The editors' earlier reading of Fig. 1d (about 68 vs 37, 64 vs 35, 59 vs 43 and 52 vs 53) agrees. Placebo weeks that people took for psilocybin were rated higher than correctly identified placebo weeks, and psilocybin weeks taken for placebo lower than correctly identified psilocybin weeks; no test of these differences between subsets is reported.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1d; Table S2, VAS rows (file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf)
key_findings.note: The subsets are weeks grouped after the fact by the participant's own guess, not randomized groups. The SEMs printed for these VAS subsets in Table S2 are too small (reporting issues); the article's Fig. 1d error bars fit the corrected values.

key_findings.finding: Single acute-effect items (imagination, dreamlike quality, spatial distortions, mind-wandering) differed at uncorrected p < 0.05 on dosing days, but none survived Bonferroni correction for 21 items; the authors conclude there was no robust evidence of consistent changes in single items across participants.
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute effects, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1e (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Questionnaires of state anxiety, positive and negative affect, stress, absorption, well-being, mind-wandering, flow, creative personality, empathy and cognitive flexibility did not differ between psilocybin and placebo weeks at uncorrected p < 0.05 (Table S1: all p ≥ 0.10). Two trait measures taken before each week's first capsule (2 days before according to the Methods, p. 2; Table 1, p. 4, places the Short Suggestibility Scale on the Tuesday) differed at uncorrected p < 0.05: conscientiousness 29.76 vs 28.14 (p = 0.01, BF10 0.36), the only one the article names, and the Short Suggestibility Scale 3.34 vs 3.02 (p = 0.03, BF10 0.51), shown only in Table S1; neither survives correction. 15 of the 18 questionnaire scores had BF10 below 1/3 (the others 0.36, 0.43 and 0.51; editors' count from Table S1); in the wrong-guess subset all were inconclusive (0.40–0.66, Table S2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-reported scales and questionnaires (single paragraph); Fig. 2a; Table S1 and Table S2 questionnaire rows (file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf); Materials and Methods › Questionnaires and tasks, 1st paragraph (p. 2) and Table 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The BF10 values appear to have been computed without the within-person pairing (reporting issues), so values below 1/3 are not paired evidence of no difference.

key_findings.finding: Creativity (Remote Associates, Alternative Uses and Wallach–Kogan tests) did not differ between conditions except two scores at uncorrected thresholds, neither surviving Bonferroni correction. Table S3 gives their direction: Alternative Uses fluency was lower with psilocybin (8.76 ± 0.62 vs 9.52 ± 0.61; p = 0.03, BF10 0.34) and Wallach–Kogan elaboration higher (0.02 ± 0.01 vs 0.01 ± 0.01; p = 0.04, BF10 1.28); the other seven scores had p ≥ 0.22 and BF10 of 0.26–0.33. The article's statement that all creativity Bayes factors except Wallach–Kogan elaboration were below 1/3 is slightly off for Alternative Uses fluency (0.34).
key_findings.locator: Results › Creativity tests, 2nd paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6); Fig. 2b–d (p. 5); Table S3 (file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf)

key_findings.finding: Perception and cognition: three measures were worse with psilocybin: lower detection of the second target at a 300 ms lag in the attentional blink task and slower Stroop responses (on incongruent trials in Fig. 3e), both at p < 0.05 (BF10 > 1) only without correction for multiple comparisons, and more time for Trail Making part A, reported as significant with no p-value or correction stated (not marked in Fig. 3f); the Results paragraph names no difference on the other tasks. Editors' reading of Fig. 3c: second-target accuracy at that lag about 0.83 with placebo and 0.77 with psilocybin.
key_findings.locator: Results › Perception and cognition (single paragraph, both columns); Fig. 3

key_findings.finding: Brain activity: with eyes closed, EEG power in the theta band (4–8 Hz) was lower with psilocybin (p < 0.05, also after Bonferroni correction over 4 bands); no other band and no eyes-open difference is reported; broadband Lempel-Ziv complexity and the auditory Local–Global ERPs did not differ between conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Resting state EEG and Local-Global ERPs, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6, continuing on p. 7); Fig. 4 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Daily wristband measures (step count, distance, resting time and activity time) did not differ between psilocybin and placebo weeks on any day.
key_findings.locator: Results › Physical activity (single paragraph); Fig. 5 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Mushroom content: liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry of 150 mg samples from the three mushroom sources, analysed pooled, gave psilocybin 640.2 μg/g, psilocin 950.7 μg/g, baeocystin 50.4 μg/g and norbaeocystin 12.5 μg/g. The authors estimate an effective content of about 0.9 mg psilocybin per capsule, say it could have been higher or lower depending on each participant's source, did not adjust for body weight, and note that psilocybin can fall by up to 50% in the first months of storage, so the content when taken may have been higher than measured.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Chemical characterization of samples (p. 4); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Expectations were measured but not analysed: participants were asked about their expected change in seventeen domains (editors' count; including positive and negative emotion, anxiety, creativity, memory, sleep and spirituality), and the analysis is deferred to a future publication.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Questionnaires and tasks, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: no power calculation; two doses per condition within one week cannot show effects of longer microdosing schedules; participants were healthy, so the absence of effects could reflect ceiling effects, and benefits in people with existing impairments remain possible.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Discussion, 8th paragraph (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Recruitment and screening (supplement): people who contacted the researchers by e-mail were briefed by phone, received the consent form with a written explanation of why a blinded, randomized placebo condition was needed, and after consenting had a psychological interview screening for the exclusion criteria; start dates were then agreed.
key_findings.locator: Recruitment process (single paragraph); file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf

key_findings.finding: Selection criteria and study conditions (supplement): participants were planning to microdose with their own Psilocybe cubensis material and, as conditions of inclusion, were asked to follow the pre-arranged schedule, to abstain from psychoactive drugs, including alcohol and caffeine, during the study weeks, and not to eat in the 3 h before each capsule. A non-diagnostic psychiatric interview following Johnson et al. (2008) excluded people meeting DSM-5 criteria for psychotic or bipolar I or II disorder (also in first- or second-degree relatives), substance abuse or dependence in the past 5 years (nicotine excepted), depressive disorders or recurrent depressive episodes, obsessive-compulsive, generalized anxiety or panic disorder, dysthymia, bulimia or anorexia, or with a history of neurological disorder, and anyone taking psychiatric medication.
key_findings.locator: Selection criteria (single paragraph); file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: No check of adherence to the abstention or to the fasting condition is described.

key_findings.finding: Allocation and blinding (supplement): for each participant, two gel capsules of 0.5 g active material and two of 0.5 g dried edible mushroom (for example Suillus granulatus) were sealed in airtight plastic bags inside identical paper envelopes, each holding a folded code; the participant randomly picked one envelope at the start and kept the other for the second period; after the data were collected, scored and analysed, participants reported their codes, the third party in charge of blinding matched codes to conditions for the final analyses, and the order was then revealed to participants.
key_findings.locator: Blinding procedure, steps 1–5; file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf
key_findings.note: The article (p. 2) says the third party randomized the order; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Setting and schedule (supplement): testing took place in a house that hosted only the researchers and the participant, with separate rooms for the tasks, environmental sound kept low and noise-cancelling headphones offered; participants were driven to and from the house on dosing days. Trait questionnaires were completed on the first day of each condition week, the wristband was worn throughout, the daily subjective-effects scale was completed every day through a link sent by a messaging app, capsules were taken on Wednesday and Friday, and measurements started 1.5 h after the capsule.
key_findings.locator: Experimental setting (pp. 1–2); Measurements per day of the week, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf

key_findings.finding: In the correct-guess and wrong-guess subsets taken separately, no questionnaire or creativity score differed between psilocybin and placebo weeks at p < 0.05 (Mann–Whitney tests; smallest p = 0.09, Wallach–Kogan elaboration in wrong-guess weeks).
key_findings.locator: Table S2 questionnaire rows; Table S4; file Cavanna_2022_Supplement.pdf

reporting_issues.issue: Denominators for correct guessing do not agree. The text gives 49 correct guesses in 64 measurement weeks (75%), 25 of 34 psilocybin weeks (73.5%) and 70% of placebo weeks (p. 4), while the Fig. 1d legend gives 25 + 24 correct and 9 + 10 wrong guesses (p. 3). Editors' calculation: 34 participants in two periods, and the four legend counts, both give 68 weeks; 49 of 64 is 76.6%, not 75%; 49 of 68 is 72.1%; 70% for placebo matches 24 of 34 (70.6%) rather than 24 of 30 (80%), which 64 weeks would imply.
reporting_issues.consequence: On the figure's counts about 72% of weeks were correctly identified; the difference from the printed 75% (repeated in the Discussion, p. 8) is small, but whether any weeks lacked a guess is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fig. 2 caption says no differences were found at uncorrected p < 0.05 (p. 5), while the text reports two among the measures shown in Fig. 2b and 2d: Alternative Uses fluency (p = 0.03) and Wallach–Kogan elaboration (p = 0.04) (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the caption overstates the null; neither difference survived correction.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fig. 3 caption states, under the Go/No-Go panel, that response times were slower with psilocybin (uncorrected), but the asterisk in the figure is on the Stroop response-time panel (incongruent trials), which is what the text reports; the text also reports slower Trail Making part A, which is not marked in Fig. 3f, and the caption describes both Trail Making panels as error rates although one shows completion time.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which task measures differed has to be taken from the text; the Go/No-Go statement in the caption appears misplaced.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1e marks five item-by-day differences at uncorrected p < 0.05 (four on Wednesday, one on Friday) (p. 3), while the text refers to four comparisons with Bayes factors above 30 matching the significant differences in Fig. 1e; Bayes factors above 30 are called very strong in the 2nd paragraph of Acute effects and strong in the 3rd (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Item-level results cannot be reconciled from the article: the supplement gives only the VAS totals (Tables S1–S2) and lists the 21 items (p. 2), referring further p-values and Bayes factors to the OSF files (p. 10; not consulted).

reporting_issues.issue: The beta band is defined as 12–30 Hz in the Methods (p. 3) and labelled so in Fig. 4d, but as 12–20 Hz in the Results (p. 6) and the Fig. 4b caption (p. 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no beta difference was reported under either definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion refers to Fig. 2A for the acute-effect totals in unblinded participants; those totals are shown in Fig. 1d.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor cross-reference error.

reporting_issues.issue: How the estimate of about 0.9 mg psilocybin per capsule was derived is not shown, and the samples from the three sources were analysed pooled (both stated on p. 9; p. 4 gives a single set of concentrations for the three sources). Editors' calculation from the concentrations printed on p. 4: 0.5 g contains about 0.32 mg psilocybin and 0.48 mg psilocin. The supplement adds only that a 150 mg sample was kept from each mushroom source (Supplement pp. 2–3, Blinding procedure, step 1); it gives no per-source results and no derivation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The amount each participant received is uncertain; the null findings apply to an approximately known and possibly variable amount.

reporting_issues.issue: No primary outcome is named, and neither the article nor the supplement gives effect sizes or confidence intervals. The supplement gives means ± SEM, p-values and Bayes factors for the VAS totals, questionnaires and creativity tests (Tables S1–S4) but none for the computer tasks, EEG or activity measures, which it refers to the OSF files (Supplement p. 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and precision of the task, EEG and activity results cannot be checked from the article or the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Alternative Uses fluency is reported as differing at uncorrected p = 0.03 (p. 6), and Table S3 prints its BF10 as 0.34 (Supplement p. 13), just above 1/3, beside a lower mean with psilocybin (8.76 vs 9.52). Editors' calculation (JZS prior with pingouin's default scale r = 0.707; the paper names the library, p. 4): a paired t-test of 34 pairs at p = 0.03 corresponds to a BF10 of about 1.7, and at p = 0.04 to about 1.4; a BF10 of 0.34 is what two independent groups of 34 give from the printed means and SEMs (t = −0.87), which points to the explanation in the issue on the Bayes factors of Tables S1 and S3 below.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Bayes factor and the p-value describe different comparisons. The Alternative Uses difference did not survive correction either way, so the card's reading of no robust creativity difference stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods compute spectral power in five bands, including gamma (30–40 Hz) (p. 3), but the Results, Fig. 4 and the Bonferroni correction cover only four (delta, theta, alpha and beta; pp. 6–7); the gamma band is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The eyes-closed theta result was corrected over four bands rather than the five computed; its exact p-value is not given in the main text, so whether it would survive correction over five cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Bayes factors in Tables S1 and S3 appear to treat the two conditions as independent groups. Editors' calculation: a JZS Bayes factor for two independent groups of 34 (scale 0.707) computed from the printed means and SEMs reproduces the printed BF10 to within about 0.02 in 24 of the 28 rows recomputed; for agreeableness, whose printed means are identical in both conditions and agree with the Table S2 subsets, the printed 0.25 is the value for two independent groups of 34, whereas 34 pairs at t = 0 give 0.18 (neuroticism and openness also print identical means with 0.25, but the Table S2 subset means imply unequal means for both). Exceptions: the VAS totals for Wednesday and Friday (143.5 and 52.86 printed; about 173 and 63 recomputed, or about 145 and 54 if the printed SEMs used divisor n), conscientiousness (0.36 vs 0.55; about 0.36 from the mushroom-week mean of 29.26 that the Table S2 subsets imply) and Wallach–Kogan elaboration (1.28 vs 0.31, from coarsely rounded means). The p-values come from paired Wilcoxon tests (captions of Tables S1 and S3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Bayes factors probably ignore the within-person pairing that the design and the p-values use, so they cannot be read as paired evidence for or against a difference. The error does not run one way: where means are nearly equal a paired Bayes factor would be lower (0.18 against 0.25 at t = 0), and where the paired difference is larger it would be higher (about 1.7 at p = 0.03), which fits p-values of 0.01–0.03 beside BF10 of 0.34–0.51. Approximate paired values from the printed p-values (editors' calculation) stay below 1/3 for most rows but not for TAS, RAT correct answers and RAT time (about 0.49, 0.38 and 0.34). The OSF files (not consulted) would settle it.

reporting_issues.issue: The article states that no questionnaire differed at uncorrected p < 0.05 except conscientiousness (p. 5), but Table S1 also shows the Short Suggestibility Scale at p = 0.03 (3.34 vs 3.02, BF10 0.51).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: a second trait measure, taken before each week's first capsule, differed without correction; neither survives correction and neither can reflect that week's capsules.

reporting_issues.issue: The article says a third party randomized the order of conditions (p. 2), whereas the supplement says each participant randomly picked one of two identical coded envelopes at the start, and the third party in charge of the blinding later used the codes to match envelopes to conditions (Supplement p. 3, Blinding procedure, steps 4–5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Allocation was still random and concealed, but by the participant's draw, with no balancing of orders described; the number in each order is not reported, so period effects cannot be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: The SEMs printed for the acute-effect totals in the correct-guess and wrong-guess subsets (Table S2, VAS rows) are smaller than the subsets' data imply. Editors' calculation: the two subsets combine to the all-weeks SEMs of Table S1 only if each subset's SD was divided by the square root of 34 instead of by the subset's own size (for example psilocybin Wednesday 5.77 vs 5.84 printed, against 4.68 with the subsets' sizes); the printed p-values and Bayes factors agree with the corrected SEMs (wrong-guess Wednesday: t about 1.35 and BF10 about 0.75, vs 0.70 printed), and so do the error bars of the article's Fig. 1d (wrong-guess psilocybin Wednesday about ±10 around 59, read from the figure, against 4.93 printed). The questionnaire rows of Table S2 and the creativity rows of Table S4 fit ordinary SEMs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The VAS subset SEMs in Table S2 understate uncertainty by a factor of about 1.2 (correct guess) and 1.9 (wrong guess); the tests and Fig. 1d are unaffected, so the subset means should be cited with the figure's error bars or the tests, not with the table's SEMs.

reporting_issues.issue: Further slips in the supplement: in Table S4, Wallach–Kogan originality in wrong-guess weeks is printed as 0.39 ± 0.03 vs 0.07 ± 0.02 with p = 0.96 (followed by a stray mark), values that cannot all be right; the captions of Tables S2 and S4 list the subsets in the reverse order of their columns; the backward-masking stimulus onset asynchronies are listed as 16, 32, 478, 64 and 80 ms, where 48 is presumably meant (p. 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no finding on the card rests on these values.

disagreements.first_pass: Acute effects: the summed rating of the 21 acute-effect items was higher with psilocybin than with placebo on both dosing days (Bonferroni over 4 days), not on the following days, and did not differ between the first and second dosing day. disagreements.first_pass: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-subject (two-period crossover) study from Buenos Aires, Argentina, stated as registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05160220). 34 adults who were planning to start microdosing with psilocybin mushrooms each had one psilocybin week and one placebo week, separated by a week without measurements, in an order randomized by a third party. In each measurement week a gel capsule was taken on Wednesday and on Friday: 0.5 g of ground, homogenized dried Psilocybe cubensis (active) or the same weight of an edible mushroom prepared the same way (placebo). Outcomes: 21 visual analogue items of acute effects, 13 questionnaires, three creativity tests, six computer tasks of perception and cognition, resting EEG and an auditory event-related potential paradigm, and wristband physical activity. Participants guessed their condition after each week, and results were also split by whether the guess was correct.
