design_detail: Self-blinding citizen-science study run online from Imperial College London: a randomized, placebo-controlled, three-arm parallel-group comparison carried out by the participants themselves without clinical supervision, with within-person comparisons of capsule days and weeks. People who already planned to microdose with their own psychedelic put their usual microdose into opaque capsules alongside identical-looking empty placebo capsules, packed weekly sets into envelopes with QR codes, and drew four envelopes by a constrained random procedure. This assigned each person, with probability 1/3, to 4 placebo weeks (PL), 2 placebo and 2 microdose weeks (half-half, HH) or 4 microdose weeks (MD), with two microdoses in each microdose week (0, 4 or 8 in total) and placebo capsules mixed into microdose weeks; capsules were taken on four days a week. Scanning the QR codes let the researchers, but not the participants, decode what was taken when. Over 10 weeks (weeks 0–9): questionnaires and online cognitive tasks at baseline, week 5 (primary endpoint) and an optional week-9 follow-up; weekly post-acute measures on Sundays, 48–72 h after the last capsule; acute measures on Thursdays, 2–6 h after a capsule. Participants guessed the type of capsule on each capsule day and the type of week at the end of each week, and the acute and post-acute analyses were repeated with these guesses. Filed under psilocybin, but 75% of participants used LSD or an LSD analogue and 24% psilocybin mushrooms.
can_establish: Whether, among self-selected people with psychedelic experience who microdosed with their own substance, those randomized to 4 weeks of microdosing differed from those randomized to placebo in well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction, paranoia, personality and online cognitive tasks at week 5 and week 9, and whether self-ratings on microdose days or weeks differed from those on placebo days or weeks.
cannot_establish: What substance or amount anyone took (nothing was verified); whether the improvement seen in all groups was a placebo effect rather than natural change, regression to the mean or repeated testing (there was no untreated group); whether beliefs about the capsule caused the score differences, because guesses were recorded after the assessments and can follow from perceived drug effects or from feeling better; or effects in people with a mental-health condition, over longer schedules, or of psilocybin specifically (the psilocybin subgroup is described only as matching the combined results).

sample.recruitment: Advertisements on relevant online and offline forums; sign-up and informed consent through the study website, which carried the study manual and explainer videos; no payment (p. 5, Materials and methods › Recruitment and inclusion criteria; p. 7, Ethical considerations). Study dates are not stated; the authors refer to drug-checking data from 2018 and 2019 as covering the period when the study was running (p. 14, Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph). Of 1630 people who signed up, 246 started; 4 did not scan their QR codes and 2 withdrew and asked for their data to be deleted, leaving 240 at baseline (Figure 3, p. 8). Ethics approval: Imperial College Research Ethics Committee, ICREC reference 18IC4518 (p. 7).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Over 18 years; good understanding of English; intention to microdose with psychedelics; previous experience with psychedelics (microdoses or full doses); no psychedelic use other than the study microdoses from a week before the start until the week-5 timepoint; willingness to follow the protocol (p. 5). No health screening is described. Five participants who chose their own schedule and took three or one microdoses in microdose weeks were excluded from analysis, and three participants who set up together and drew an invalid sequence (3 placebo weeks and 1 microdose week) were dropped from the between-group analyses but kept in the acute and post-acute analyses (Appendix 1 › Additional information on the self-blinding setup and data collection, pp. 22–23).
sample.demographics: At baseline (n=240): mean age 33.5 (SD 9.4); 70% male, 19% female, 1% other (these sum to 90%; see reporting issues); described as mostly educated and from western countries. 33% reported at least one past psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety disorder 13%, depression 13%, PTSD 7%) and 7% a current diagnosis. 74% agreed or strongly agreed that they were active advocates of psychedelic drug use and 90% of the therapeutic use of psychedelics (p. 7, Results › Demographics, randomization, and completion rate, 2nd paragraph). Mean baseline expectation score for microdosing 68 (SD 19) on a 0–100 scale (Appendix 1 › Attitude toward psychedelics and microdosing, p. 24). Full demographics are in Supplementary file 1, not read.
sample.attrition: Completed the week-5 primary endpoint: 191 of 240 (80%): PL 65 of 78 (83%), HH 57 of 71 (80%), MD 69 of 91 (77%). Optional week-9 follow-up: 159 (66%): 53 (68%), 44 (62%), 62 (68%) (Figure 3, p. 8). Completion did not differ by group (chi-square 0.64, 12 df, N=240, p=0.99; p. 7). Reasons for dropping out and comparisons of completers with non-completers are not reported; the mixed models used all available data. Participants who withdrew without asking for deletion stayed in the analyses (Appendix 1, p. 22).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people who already intended to microdose with their own supply, recruited through psychedelic-interest forums, with strongly positive attitudes and expectations (74% self-described advocates of psychedelic drug use; expectation score 68 of 100). Only 246 of the 1630 who signed up (15%, editors' calculation) started. Mostly healthy, with little room to improve on well-being, as the authors note (p. 14). Results describe enthusiastic, experienced people microdosing in daily life, not people seeking treatment.

exposure.measurement: Each participant used their own psychedelic: LSD 147 (61%), LSD analogues 33 (14%), psilocybin-containing mushrooms 57 (24%), other 3 (LSA 1, DOB 2) (p. 8, Results › Microdoses). Participants were told to use the microdose amount they would use outside the study (p. 5, Microdose preparation); placebo capsules were empty or, for people microdosing with mushrooms, filled with the same weight of a non-psychoactive mushroom (Appendix 1, p. 22). The capsule type taken on each day was known to the researchers from the scanned QR codes (pp. 4–5). Substance identity, purity and amount were not verified, and intake and adherence to the schedule could not be confirmed (p. 14, Discussion › Limitations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions. Oral capsules (vials for liquids) on four days a week during the 4-week dose period, two of them microdoses in each microdose week: 0, 4 or 8 microdoses in total for PL, HH and MD (pp. 3, 5; Appendix 1, p. 22). Amounts were self-chosen and self-reported: mean 13 (SD 5.5) µg for LSD and LSD analogues and 0.2 (SD 0.12) g for psilocybin mushrooms (p. 8); Appendix 1—figure 3 gives 12.8 µg for 180 people and 0.19 g for 56 people (p. 25). For analyses of amount, mushroom amounts were converted to an assumed LSD equivalent (p. 7).
exposure.polysubstance: No psychedelic use other than the study microdoses from a week before the start to week 5 (inclusion criterion, self-reported). Recreational drug use was recorded and compared between groups in Supplementary file 2 (not read); alcohol, cannabis and other drugs during the study are not reported and were not otherwise controlled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable as such: acute measures were taken 2–6 h after a capsule and post-acute measures 48–72 h after the last capsule (p. 3, Materials and methods › Outcomes).

comparison.controls: Participants randomized to 4 placebo weeks (PL, n=78 at baseline) for the accumulative outcomes; for the acute and post-acute outcomes, scores obtained on placebo days or at the end of placebo weeks, within and between people.
comparison.matching: Randomization by the self-blinding draw (probability 1/3 per group). The authors report no statistically significant baseline differences in demographics, recreational drug use or baseline scores (Supplementary files 1–3, not read) (p. 7). Group sizes at baseline were 78, 71 and 91.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Randomized, so pre-existing differences should balance in expectation; expectations were measured at baseline (expectation score) and tested as a covariate. Whether participants could tell capsules apart, or kept track of envelopes during the draw, could not be checked.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same inclusion rule for all groups; other drug use reported only in Supplementary file 2 (not read).

outcomes.instruments: Accumulative (baseline, week 5, week 9): Ryff's psychological well-being scales (RPWB, 42 items), Cognitive and Affective Mindfulness Scale (CAMS), Satisfaction With Life (SWL), Green Paranoid Thought Scales (GPTS, social-reference subscale), Big Five personality with an added intellect trait, and a cognitive performance score (CPS) from six online Cambridge Brain Sciences tasks (spatial span, paired associates, rotations, odd one out, spatial planning, feature match). Post-acute (Sundays): Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (WEMWB), Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptomatology (QIDS), Spielberger's anxiety inventory (trait form, STAI-T) and Social Connectedness Scale (SCS). Acute (Thursdays): PANAS (positive minus negative affect), six study-made visual analogue scales on 0–100 (drug intensity, mood, temper, energy, focus, creativity) and the CPS (p. 3, Materials and methods › Outcomes; Table 1, p. 5; Appendix 1, pp. 20–22).
outcomes.validity_norms: Published scales except the six visual analogue items, which were made for the study. The RPWB was given by mistake with a seven-step instead of six-step response scale, and scores were rescaled by 6/7 (Appendix 1, p. 21). The CPS expresses each person's task z-scores relative to the placebo group's mean at the same timepoint, to remove practice effects (Appendix 1, p. 20), so within-group CPS change is not an independent pre–post measure.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit = change from baseline in accumulative scores, compared within groups over time and between groups (PL vs HH, PL vs MD) at week 5 and week 9; acute and post-acute effects = differences between scores obtained on microdose versus placebo days or at the end of microdose versus placebo weeks. Breaking blind = a correct forced-choice guess of the day's capsule (acute) or the week's type (post-acute), asked as the last question after the assessments (pp. 6, 14).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported. Editors' count of main outcomes: 11 accumulative (RPWB, CAMS, SWL, GPTS, six personality traits, CPS), 4 post-acute and 8 acute (PANAS, six visual analogue scales, CPS), plus subscales and six cognitive subtests, each tested within groups over two intervals and between groups at two timepoints; the acute and post-acute outcomes were also tested in models with guesses and in four strata comparisons each.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: All outcomes were self-completed online by participants, whose blinding was partial (72% correct capsule guesses); the cognitive tasks were scored automatically.

analysis.effect_sizes: PL vs MD at week 5, adjusted treatment difference ±95% CI, without/with the number of microdose guesses as covariate: RPWB 2.5 ± 5.6 (p=0.37)/0.9 ± 5.7 (p=0.76); CAMS 0.8 ± 1.5 (p=0.32)/0.4 ± 1.5 (p=0.65); GPTS −1.6 ± 2.5 (p=0.21)/−1.2 ± 2.5 (p=0.36); SWL 0.4 ± 1.7 (p=0.67)/0.2 ± 1.8 (p=0.83); personality traits between −0.3 and 0.8, all p≥0.24 without guesses (pp. 9–10). Acute, microdose vs placebo days, adjusted mean difference ±95% CI without guess: PANAS 2.2 ± 1.4 (Cohen's d 0.19), drug intensity 12.5 ± 3.0 (d=0.58), mood 4.6 ± 2.9 (d=0.20), energy 5.3 ± 2.7 (d=0.27), creativity 4.7 ± 2.6 (d=0.25); with guess in the model only drug intensity stayed significant, 3.4 ± 2.0 (Table 2, p. 11; p. 10). Post-acute STAI-T −1.5 ± 1.3 in Table 2 (−1.4 ± 1.3, p=0.03, in the text), −0.1 ± 0.6 with guess. Cohen's d was below 0.3 for every scale except drug intensity (p. 10).
analysis.covariates: Each model was adjusted for whichever of these baseline variables were significant: age, sex, education, baseline score, dose, total dose, suggestibility, expectation score, number of past psychiatric diagnoses, number of current psychiatric medications, lifetime full-dose experiences and lifetime months of microdosing (pp. 6–7, Materials and methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). The covariates retained in each model are in supplementary files not read; selection was data-driven.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned in the paper (registries not searched); the transparent reporting form listed among the additional files (p. 16) was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: A primary endpoint (week 5) is named but no single primary outcome. The guess-adjusted accumulative analysis is called post hoc (p. 9) and the strata comparisons post hoc (p. 7). Detailed results are in eight supplementary files (not read); the LSD and psilocybin subgroups are described only as matching the combined results, without numbers (pp. 8, 10). The data are shared publicly on GitHub (p. 17, Data availability).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation was made beforehand. From their own data the authors calculated that 90% power at alpha 0.05 would need 1508 participants for RPWB, 1638 for CAMS, 4918 for SWL, 1392 for GPTS and 366 for CPS (p. 15, Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph). The upper 95% limit of the RPWB difference at week 5 is 8.1 points (editors' calculation from 2.5 ± 5.6), so a modest benefit on this scale is not excluded.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 240 self-selected, mostly healthy people with psychedelic experience who microdosed with their own unverified substance (three-quarters LSD or LSD analogues), well-being, mindfulness, life satisfaction and paranoia scores improved from baseline in the microdose group, but mindfulness and paranoia also improved in the placebo group, and at week 5 and week 9 no between-group difference was significant on any accumulative scale or on the cognitive score. On capsule days, microdoses were rated as more intense (d=0.58) and slightly better on affect, mood, energy and creativity (d 0.19–0.27), and weeks with microdoses were followed by slightly lower trait-anxiety scores. Participants guessed the day's capsule correctly on 72% of capsule days; with guesses in the models only drug intensity remained, and scores followed what people believed they had taken in 21 of 22 comparisons.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the acute and post-acute differences can be explained by participants breaking blind, and that the findings suggest anecdotal benefits "can be explained by the placebo effect" (abstract, p. 1); the Discussion says the results strongly suggest that beliefs about the capsules' content, not the content, determined the differences (p. 13). Gaps: (1) guesses were recorded after the assessments and can themselves follow from feeling better or from perceptible drug effects, which the intensity ratings show were real; models that adjust for or stratify by guess condition on a variable affected by the treatment and cannot show that belief caused the scores, as the authors concede for the strata analysis (p. 14). (2) There was no untreated group, so the improvement in all groups cannot be attributed to a placebo effect rather than natural change, regression to the mean, repeated testing or reporting tendencies. (3) The week-5 intervals include modest benefits (RPWB up to 8.1 points, editors' calculation), so the result is no detectable difference in this sample, not proof of no effect; the statement that the differences are not clinically meaningful (p. 15) rests on point estimates. (4) Substance identity and amount were unverified. A headline version (microdosing is just placebo) overstates: the study found no detectable benefit over placebo after 4 weeks in enthusiastic, mostly healthy people using their own LSD or mushrooms, alongside a measurable acute effect on perceived drug intensity.

timeline.event: Yanakieva et al. and Bershad et al. (2019a, 2019b), followed in 2020 by Family et al. and Hutten et al.: small double-blind laboratory studies of single low LSD doses in healthy volunteers; by this paper's account (p. 2) no robust support for the anecdotal benefits, some dose-related self-rated drug effects, variable LSD blood levels and raised BDNF; not read.
This study: no between-group difference after 4 weeks of self-blinded microdosing; small acute and post-acute differences that followed participants' guesses.

Cavanna et al.: randomized double-blind crossover trial of two psilocybin-mushroom microdoses against placebo in 34 people planning to microdose; no benefit on mood, creativity or cognition, and acute effects clear mainly in weeks with a correct guess (project card sc_cavanna_2022).

replication.where_it_stands: Against the companion card sc_cavanna_2022: this study adds a larger, longer randomized comparison (240 people, up to 8 microdoses over 4 weeks, follow-up to week 9) with the same two results, no detectable benefit over placebo and partial unblinding with effects that follow the guess. It also qualifies how Cavanna et al. describe this study (positive effects on its primary outcome, as recorded in that card's timeline): the paper names week 5 as its primary endpoint, at which no between-group difference was significant; its positive findings were within-group changes, seen in the placebo group as well, and small acute and post-acute differences. Neither study tested people with a mental-health condition or schedules longer than 4 weeks, and this study's evidence is mostly about LSD.

funding.funder: The Funding section states that no external funding was received for this work (p. 16); the Acknowledgements thank the Beckley Foundation for providing funds for the study (p. 16), and author Amanda Feilding (Beckley Foundation) is credited with funding acquisition (p. 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that no competing interests exist (p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Psychedelic Research, Data Science Institute, Center for Complexity Science and Centre for Psychiatry, Imperial College London; Beckley Foundation, Oxford (p. 1). The funding statement and the acknowledgements disagree (see reporting issues). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, adequately powered randomized trial of repeated microdosing with study-supplied, verified substance and amount, an active placebo, guesses about allocation collected before (or separately from) the outcome assessments, a no-treatment arm to separate placebo response from natural change, and participants with room to improve (for example people with depressive symptoms), followed for several months.

domains.note: Sequence generated by the participant's own shuffling of sealed envelopes, a dice roll and QR scans, constrained to three possible group outcomes; concealment depended on participants not marking or tracking envelopes and could not be verified (three participants who set up together drew an invalid sequence). Baseline comparisons are reported as non-significant in supplements not read; group sizes 78, 71 and 91.

Self-sourced, unverified substances and self-chosen amounts; intake and schedule adherence could not be confirmed; participants partly identified their capsules. Five participants with non-protocol schedules were excluded and three with invalid sequences dropped from between-group analyses; small numbers relative to 240.
20% missing at the week-5 primary endpoint and 34% at week 9, similar across arms; reasons and comparisons of completers with non-completers not reported; mixed models assume data missing at random.

All outcomes except the cognitive tasks were self-rated by participants who often knew or believed they knew their capsule; the paper's own analyses show scores followed beliefs. RPWB given on a non-standard response scale.
No registration or single prespecified primary outcome; many outcomes and models; data-driven covariates; post hoc guess analyses; detailed results only in supplements. Data are publicly shared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applied to the randomized comparisons. The week-5 between-group null is the most robust result, because the main biases here (partial unblinding, enthusiastic participants rating themselves) would tend to favour a microdose benefit rather than hide one; it is still imprecise and specific to self-sourced, unverified amounts in mostly healthy people. The acute and post-acute differences are at high risk of bias from self-rating under partial unblinding, and their attribution to belief rests on guesses recorded after the outcomes. Cite for: no detectable difference from placebo after 4 weeks of self-administered microdosing in this sample; partial blinding (72% correct capsule guesses against 62% expected from a guesser who knew the capsule ratio); higher self-rated drug intensity on microdose days. Not for: microdosing being ineffective in general or in clinical populations, belief causing the effects, or psilocybin specifically.

key_findings.finding: Design: the self-blinding draw assigned participants with probability 1/3 to 4 placebo weeks, 2 placebo and 2 microdose weeks, or 4 microdose weeks, with two microdoses per microdose week (0, 4 or 8 in total) and placebo capsules mixed into microdose weeks; primary endpoint at week 5, optional follow-up at week 9; QR codes let only the researchers decode which capsule was taken when.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Self-blinding setup procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Figure 1 (p. 4); Figure 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Flow: 1630 signed up, 246 started, 4 did not scan QR codes and 2 withdrew with data deleted, leaving 240 at baseline (PL 78, HH 71, MD 91); 191 (80%) completed the week-5 primary endpoint (65, 57 and 69) and 159 (66%) the optional week-9 follow-up (53, 44 and 62); completion did not differ by group (chi-square 0.64, 12 df, p=0.99).
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics, randomization, and completion rate, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Figure 3 (p. 8)
key_findings.note: The text says 240 started; Figure 3 shows 246 started and 240 after removals. The group counts are printed in Figure 3 and were read from the rendered page (they are not in the text layer).

key_findings.finding: Participants: mean age 33.5 (SD 9.4); 70% male, 19% female, 1% other; 33% with a past and 7% with a current psychiatric diagnosis; 74% agreed or strongly agreed that they were active advocates of psychedelic drug use and 90% of therapeutic use; mean expectation score 68 (SD 19) of 100.
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics, randomization, and completion rate, 2nd paragraph (p. 7); Appendix 1 › Attitude toward psychedelics and microdosing (p. 24)
key_findings.note: The sex percentages sum to 90%.

key_findings.finding: Substances (study conditions): LSD 147 (61%), LSD analogues 33 (14%), psilocybin mushrooms 57 (24%), other 3; self-reported mean amounts 13 (SD 5.5) µg for LSD and analogues and 0.2 (SD 0.12) g for mushrooms; LSD and psilocybin subgroups are said to match the combined results, without numbers.
key_findings.locator: Results › Microdoses (single paragraph, p. 8); Accumulative outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 8); Acute and post-acute outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Within-group change, baseline to week 5 (adjusted mean ±95% CI): MD group RPWB +4.2 ± 3.9 (p=0.04), CAMS +2.4 ± 1.1 (p<0.001), SWL +1.2 ± 1.2 (p=0.04), GPTS −5.0 ± 1.7 (p<0.001), neuroticism −1.3 ± 0.9 (p<0.01), openness +0.9 ± 0.8 (p=0.03); placebo group CAMS +1.6 ± 1.1 (p<0.01), GPTS −3.4 ± 1.7 (p<0.001), neuroticism −1.0 ± 1.0 (p=0.04); HH group CAMS +1.3 ± 1.2 (p=0.02), GPTS −4.9 ± 1.9 (p<0.001); well-being and life satisfaction did not change significantly in the PL or HH groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › Accumulative outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 8, continuing on p. 9); Figure 4 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Cognition: the CPS did not change in the MD group and fell in the HH group (−0.16 ± 0.14, p=0.03); rotations (+0.34 ± 0.28) and odd one out (+0.52 ± 0.31) rose in the MD group, spatial span (−0.49 ± 0.30) and paired associates (−0.51 ± 0.30) fell in the HH group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Accumulative outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 8, continuing on p. 9)

key_findings.finding: No significant between-group difference at week 5 or week 9 on any accumulative scale or subscale, except lower paired-associates scores in the HH group (PL vs HH −0.55 ± 0.43, p<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Accumulative outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Figure 4

key_findings.finding: PL vs MD at week 5, adjusted treatment difference ±95% CI without/with the number of microdose guesses as covariate (post hoc): RPWB 2.5 ± 5.6 (p=0.37)/0.9 ± 5.7 (p=0.76); CAMS 0.8 ± 1.5 (p=0.32)/0.4 ± 1.5 (p=0.65); GPTS −1.6 ± 2.5 (p=0.21)/−1.2 ± 2.5 (p=0.36); SWL 0.4 ± 1.7 (p=0.67)/0.2 ± 1.8 (p=0.83); personality traits from −0.3 to 0.8 (all p≥0.24) without guesses. The number of microdose guesses was itself a significant covariate for RPWB (p<0.01), CAMS (p=0.02), agreeableness (p=0.02) and openness (p=0.03).
key_findings.locator: Results › Accumulative outcomes adjusted for number of microdose guesses (single paragraph, p. 9, continuing on p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Acute outcomes (microdose vs placebo capsule days; about 857 scores for questionnaires, 684 for the CPS): PANAS 16.2 vs 14.2 (adjusted difference 2.2 ± 1.4, p<0.01, d=0.19); drug intensity 21.4 vs 8.5 (12.5 ± 3.0, p<0.001, d=0.58); mood 4.6 ± 2.9 (d=0.20), energy 5.3 ± 2.7 (d=0.27), creativity 4.7 ± 2.6 (d=0.25), all p<0.001; focus, temper and the CPS did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute and post-acute outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 2 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Post-acute outcomes (end of microdose vs placebo weeks): only trait anxiety differed, lower after microdose weeks (STAI-T adjusted difference −1.5 ± 1.3 in Table 2; −1.4 ± 1.3, p=0.03, in the text; d=−0.04); WEMWB, QIDS and social connectedness did not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute and post-acute outcomes, 3rd paragraph (p. 10); Table 2 (p. 11)
key_findings.note: The text and Table 2 give different point estimates for STAI-T.

key_findings.finding: With guess added to the models, condition was no longer significant for any scale except drug intensity (3.4 ± 2.0, p<0.001); the guess × condition interaction was significant only for drug intensity (p<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Association between guess and acute/post-acute outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 10); Table 2, last column (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Strata (post hoc): with the guess held fixed, microdose and placebo scores did not differ on any self-rated scale except drug intensity (7.3 ± 3.1, p<0.001); with the capsule held fixed, scores differed by guess in 21 of 22 comparisons, all favouring a microdose guess (the exception was QIDS under placebo, p=0.06 in Figure 5); the cognitive score differed by neither.
key_findings.locator: Results › Association between guess and acute/post-acute outcomes, 2nd paragraph (p. 10); Figure 5 (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Shares of scores in each condition/guess stratum, printed in Figure 5: acute PANAS and mood 45% placebo/placebo-guess, 21% microdose/placebo-guess, 14% placebo/microdose-guess, 20% microdose/microdose-guess; post-acute 26%, 20%, 20% and 34%. By the editors' arithmetic, 49% of microdose-day scores and 24% of placebo-day scores came with a microdose guess, and 63% of microdose-week scores and 43% of placebo-week scores.
key_findings.locator: Figure 5 (labels under each panel)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations from the printed percentages; the strata means are plotted, and values read from the plots are not extracted.

key_findings.finding: Blinding: correct capsule guesses (break blind rate) 0.72 ± 0.18 (mean ± SD), specificity 0.82 ± 0.16, sensitivity 0.45 ± 0.30; a guesser who knew only the 3:1 ratio of placebo to microdose capsules would score 0.62, 0.75 and 0.25. By group (Appendix 1—table 1): the placebo group guessed microdose on 21% of capsule days; sensitivity was 0.54 in the HH and 0.41 in the MD group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinding integrity, 1st paragraph (p. 10, continuing on p. 11); Appendix 1—table 1 (p. 26)

key_findings.finding: Correct guessing rose with the self-reported microdose amount (F(1, 237)=7.4, p<0.01); the authors also estimate an amount above which guesses beat chance and compare it with a laboratory study (the value is not reproduced on this card, under the project's rule on amounts).
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinding integrity, 2nd paragraph (p. 11); Appendix 1 › Comparison to random guesser, last paragraph (p. 26)

key_findings.finding: Cues for guessing microdose (post-study survey, n=166): body or perceptual sensations only 24%, mostly bodily 31%, equally bodily and mental 22%, mostly mental 19%, mental only 4%; of 26 free-text answers, 15 mentioned muscle tingling or tension, 12 colour saturation or visual warping and 7 stomach discomfort, and 3 mentioned outcome-related effects. In the same survey 86% said they had been thinking about which capsule they took before being asked.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph (p. 14); Appendix 1 › Blind breaking cues (p. 25)
key_findings.note: The authors report a technical error: some participants were not invited to this survey and a few were invited twice.

key_findings.finding: Post hoc subsamples with the lowest 25% baseline well-being or the highest 25% neuroticism: no significant PL vs MD difference at week 5 on any accumulative outcome (for example RPWB −1.6 ± 13.6, p=0.81, and 4.8 ± 14.3, p=0.50).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 5th paragraph (p. 14, continuing on p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: no verification of the nature, purity or amount of the substance (62% bought on the illicit market, mostly LSD); adherence to the self-blinding procedure and the schedule could not be confirmed; guesses were recorded after the assessments, so the strata analysis cannot establish a causal link between guess and outcome; mostly healthy participants; the study may be underpowered, with the required sample sizes listed in the power field.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 2nd to 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The sex distribution is given as 70% male, 19% female and 1% other, which sums to 90%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex of about one in ten participants is unaccounted for; the full table is only in Supplementary file 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The Funding section says no external funding was received, while the Acknowledgements thank the Beckley Foundation for providing funds for the study and an author from the Beckley Foundation is credited with funding acquisition.
reporting_issues.consequence: The funding statement cannot be taken at face value; the Beckley Foundation should be recorded as a funder.

reporting_issues.issue: The post-acute trait-anxiety effect is −1.4 ± 1.3 (p=0.03) in the text but −1.5 ± 1.3 in Table 2; in the model with guess, the STAI-T interval (−0.1 ± 0.6) is half as wide as without guess and identical to the QIDS row, while the other rows keep similar widths.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the point estimate; the STAI-T entry in the guess model may be a transcription error, so the guess-adjusted anxiety result should be quoted with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites Figure 4 for the relation between reported amount and blind breaking and for the estimated detection threshold, but Figure 4 shows the accumulative outcomes; no figure in the paper shows amount against blind breaking.
reporting_issues.consequence: The amount–blinding relation can be checked only from the single F test (p. 11) and the appendix description (p. 26).

reporting_issues.issue: The main text defines specificity and sensitivity as correct guesses among all placebo or all microdose guesses (predictive values), while Appendix 1—table 1 defines and computes them per capsule type taken (the standard rates); sensitivity is 0.45 on p. 10 and 0.46 on p. 11.
reporting_issues.consequence: The numbers match the appendix definitions (editors' check: 0.12/0.27 and 0.59/0.72); the main-text definitions should not be used to interpret them.

reporting_issues.issue: The test that defines the authors' detection threshold is reported as t(317)=1.92, p=0.05; by the editors' calculation, the two-sided p for this t is about 0.056.
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold rests on a borderline test and should not be quoted as a firm estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix 1 describes five participants excluded for non-protocol schedules and three dropped from the between-group analyses, but the flow diagram (Figure 3) shows neither, and the text reports 240 started where the figure shows 246.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether the 240 at baseline include these eight participants, so the analysed numbers per group are uncertain by a few people.

reporting_issues.issue: People microdosing with mushrooms number 57 (24%) in the Results, 23% in the Limitations and 56 in Appendix 1—figure 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the psilocybin subgroup is small and its results are not reported separately.

reporting_issues.issue: The RPWB was administered with a seven-step response scale by mistake and rescaled by 6/7; the Limitations then describe its range as 0–252, which does not fit 42 items rated from 1 upwards.
reporting_issues.consequence: Comparisons of RPWB scores with other studies and the 1%-of-range illustration are approximate.
